every base change of $f$ is a closed map. It is *proper* if it is separated,
of finite type, and universally closed. An *open immersion* identifies its
source with an open subscheme of its target. For $y\in|Y|$, the geometric
fiber is

$$
 X_{\bar y}=X\times_Y\operatorname{Spec}\overline{\kappa(y)},
$$

where $\overline{\kappa(y)}$ is a chosen algebraic closure of $\kappa(y)$. A
*geometric point* of $Y$ is a morphism $\bar y:\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\to
Y$ whose field $\Omega$ is algebraically closed and contains the residue
field of the image point. A scheme of finite type over a field is one whose
structure morphism is of finite type. A morphism is *weakly etale* if it is
flat and its diagonal is flat. A subset of a scheme is *locally closed* if it
is the intersection of an open and a closed subset, and it is *constructible*
if it is a finite union of locally closed subsets. A locally closed
constructible subscheme means a subscheme whose underlying subset is locally
closed and constructible. A sheaf on a locally closed subscheme is locally
constant if it becomes a constant sheaf after pulling back along a covering
family in its pro-etale site; its stalk at a geometric point is the filtered
colimit of its sections over pointed neighborhoods.

Let $K$ be a field.
The sequence space $K^{\mathbf Z_{\geq0}}$ has coordinatewise addition
and scalar multiplication. A vector subspace is a subset containing
the zero sequence and closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

*Mathlib:* `Submodule`. A basic Mathlib notion, used throughout, so it is not mapped as the Lean declaration of this object.

attrs.title: Vector subspaces of a sequence space

objects.body:
Let $Y$ have the small pro-etale site
[def-weil-pbc-proetale-site], with the coefficient categories and
pullbacks of [def-weil-derived-pullback-tensor-hom]. For finite
$\Lambda=A_{E,n}$, a complex $K$ is *perfect on the coefficient site* if a
covering $\{U_\alpha\to Y\}$ makes each $K|_{U_\alpha}$ isomorphic to a
bounded complex of finite projective $\Lambda_{U_\alpha}$-modules. Here a
finite projective module is a direct summand of a finite sum
$\Lambda_{U_\alpha}^{\oplus m}$. At the integral stage use the completed
coefficient sheaf [def-weil-completed-integral-coefficients]
$\widehat{\mathcal O}_{E,U_\alpha}$. At the rational stage
[def-weil-rationalization-karoubi] use bounded complexes of direct summands
of finite sums of the unit $E_{U_\alpha}$ in that localized category. An
object of the common-stage $\Qlb$-category
[def-weil-algebraically-closed-coefficients] is site-perfect if some
finite-field representative is site-perfect. This condition requires a cover
of the site; perfectness of individual geometric stalks alone does not supply
one.

attrs.title: Perfect complexes on the coefficient site

objects.body:
Fix Grothendieck universes $\mathcal U\in\mathcal V$ containing the schemes
and coefficient rings under consideration. Replace every site by a
$\mathcal V$-small skeleton within the chosen bound. Derived categories and
filtered colimits are formed in $\mathcal V$.

Fix the finite-field datum $p,a,q,k_0,k$, where $q=p^a$. Let $X_0/k_0$ be
smooth, proper, geometrically connected of pure dimension $d\in\mathbf
Z_{\geq0}$, and put $X=X_0\times_{k_0}k$. For every prime $\ell\neq p$, write
$\Ql=\mathbf Q_\ell$, and let $K_{X,\ell}=(\Ql)_X$ be the constant Weil
sheaf, and let $F_\ell$ be the global geometric Frobenius on
$\RGamma(X,K_{X,\ell})$, using the geometric-Frobenius convention
[def-weil-frobenius-detailed]. Fix an indeterminate $T$. For every integer $i$ with
$0\leq i\leq2d$, define

$$
 V_{i,\ell}=H^i(X,\Ql),
\qquad
 F_{i,\ell}=F_\ell\vert_{V_{i,\ell}}.
$$

The finiteness of the spaces $V_{i,\ell}$, the invertibility of the operators
$F_{i,\ell}$, and the vanishing of $H^i(X,\Ql)$ outside $0\leq i\leq2d$ are
the cohomological-finiteness proposition, and are not part of the definition
of the family. Define

$$
 P_{i,\ell}(T)=
 \det(1-TF_{i,\ell}\mid V_{i,\ell})\in\Ql[T].
$$

It has constant coefficient $1$, degree $\dim_{\Ql}V_{i,\ell}$, and leading
coefficient $(-1)^{\dim V_{i,\ell}}\det(F_{i,\ell})$.

A *t-structure* on a triangulated category $\mathcal T$ is a pair $(\mathcal
T^{\le0},\mathcal T^{\ge0})$ of strictly full subcategories such that

1. $\mathcal T^{\le0}[1]\subseteq\mathcal T^{\le0}$ and $\mathcal
   T^{\ge0}[-1]\subseteq\mathcal T^{\ge0}$;
2. $\Hom_{\mathcal T}(A,B[-1])=0$ for all $A\in\mathcal T^{\le0}$ and
   $B\in\mathcal T^{\ge0}$;
3. every $K\in\mathcal T$ occurs in a distinguished triangle $A\to K\to
   B[-1]\to A[1]$ with $A\in\mathcal T^{\le0}$ and $B\in\mathcal T^{\ge0}$.

Write $\mathcal T^{\le n}=\mathcal T^{\le0}[-n]$ and $\mathcal T^{\ge
n}=\mathcal T^{\ge0}[-n]$. The *heart* is $\mathcal T^{\le0}\cap\mathcal
T^{\ge0}$, and the t-structure is *bounded* if every object of $\mathcal T$
lies in $\mathcal T^{\le n}\cap\mathcal T^{\ge m}$ for some $m\le n$. A
bounded t-structure carries truncation functors $\tau^{\le n},\tau^{\ge
n}:\mathcal T\to\mathcal T$ and distinguished truncation triangles

$$
 \tau^{\le n}K\longrightarrow K\longrightarrow
 \tau^{\ge n+1}K\longrightarrow\tau^{\le n}K[1],
$$

characterized by $\tau^{\le n}K\in\mathcal T^{\le n}$ and $\tau^{\ge
n+1}K\in\mathcal T^{\ge n+1}$.

(*Source note:* no Stacks Project entry states this form: Stacks defines no
t-structure on a triangulated category. Its nearest entries are the
truncation of a complex of an abelian category, Homological Algebra, Section
12.15 (Tag [0118](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0118)), where the
canonical truncations $\tau_{\le n}$, $\tau_{\ge n}$ of a (co)chain complex
are defined with the properties $H^i(\tau_{\le n}A^\bullet)=H^i(A^\bullet)$
for $i\le n$ and $0$ for $i>n$, and the canonical distinguished triangle
$\tau_{\le a}K^\bullet\to K^\bullet\to\tau_{\ge a+1}K^\bullet\to (\tau_{\le
a}K^\bullet)[1]$ of Remark 13.12.4 (Tag
[08J5](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/08J5), in $D(\mathcal A)$ for an
abelian $\mathcal A$). Difference: those entries truncate complexes of one
fixed abelian category inside $D(\mathcal A)$; they state no t-structure
axioms on an abstract triangulated category, no heart, no boundedness, and no
truncation functors on such a category — pages checked for a counterpart: the
tables of contents of Chapters 12, 13 and 21 and Sections 12.4, 12.5, 12.15,
13.11, 13.12 and 13.34, and the table of contents of Chapter 61. The
blueprint adds the axiom list together with the truncation functors
$\tau^{\le n},\tau^{\ge n}$ and their triangles, the structure on which the
integral and rational coefficient categories of this manuscript rest.)

Fix the finite-field datum [def-weil-finite-field-fiber] $p,a,q,k_0,k$, where
$q=p^a$, and a prime $\ell\neq p$. Write $\Ql=\mathbf Q_\ell$, choose an
algebraic closure $\Qlb$ of $\Ql$, and choose a finite extension $E/\Ql$
contained in $\Qlb$. Let $Y_0$ be a finite-type
[def-weil-scheme-morphism-properties] $k_0$-scheme, put
$Y=Y_0\times_{k_0}k$, and let $g_Y:Y\to Y$ be the geometric-Frobenius
automorphism from the geometric Frobenius convention
[def-weil-frobenius-detailed]. The category $\Sh_c(Y,E)$ is the
constructible heart [def-weil-constructible-heart]. On the small pro-etale
site [def-weil-pbc-proetale-site], its underlying constructibility
uses the finite-torsion constructibility convention
[def-weil-finite-torsion-constructibility]; a constructible $E$-Weil sheaf is
an object $\mathcal F\in\Sh_c(Y,E)$ together with an isomorphism formed using
the derived pullback [def-weil-derived-pullback-tensor-hom]

$$
 \theta:Lg_Y^*\mathcal F\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathcal F.
$$

Morphisms commute with $\theta$, and $D^b_{c,\mathrm W}(Y,E)$ is the
localization of bounded complexes of such sheaves at equivariant
quasi-isomorphisms; it is an ordinary triangulated category. Let $\mathcal
E_\ell$ be the directed set of finite extensions of $\Ql$ contained in
$\Qlb$. Define

$$
 D^b_{c,\mathrm W}(Y,\Qlb)=
 \underset{E\in\mathcal E_\ell}{\operatorname{2-colim}}
 D^b_{c,\mathrm W}(Y,E)
$$

with the common-stage coefficient construction
[def-weil-algebraically-closed-coefficients]. For each
$\Lambda\in\{E,\Qlb\}$ there is an exact forgetful functor

$$
 \operatorname{For}:D^b_{c,\mathrm W}(Y,\Lambda)
 \longrightarrow D^b_c(Y,\Lambda).
$$

An object $K$ carries, in addition to $\operatorname{For}(K)$, the derived
Frobenius isomorphism

$$
 \theta_K:Lg_Y^*\operatorname{For}(K)
 \xrightarrow{\sim}\operatorname{For}(K),
$$

represented termwise at a finite coefficient stage.

Let $A$ be an abelian variety over an
algebraically closed field of characteristic different from $\ell$. For
the torsion subgroup
$A[\ell^n]=\ker([\ell^n]:A\to A)$, define

$$
T_\ell A:=\varprojlim_n A[\ell^n](\overline k),
\qquad
V_\ell A:=T_\ell A\otimes_{\mathbf Z_\ell}\mathbf Q_\ell,
$$

where the transition map from level $n+1$ to level $n$ is
multiplication by $\ell$. Every endomorphism of $A$, and every
semilinear automorphism of $A$ over an automorphism of the ground field,
acts componentwise on these inverse limits; for the geometric Jacobian of a
curve these semilinear automorphisms are supplied by the next lemma.
The abelian-variety and torsion-subgroup conventions are those of
[def-sc-abelian-variety], [def-sc-mult-n].

In the notation of [def-tate-module-abelian-group], $T_\ell A=T_\ell\bigl(A(\overline k)\bigr)$ and $V_\ell A=V_\ell\bigl(A(\overline k)\bigr)$: the definition above is the Tate module of the abelian group $A(\overline k)$.

attrs.title: The Tate module used in the curve argument

objects.body:
For a closed algebraic subgroup $H\subseteq\operatorname{GL}(V)$, its
identity component $H^\circ$ is the connected component containing the
identity matrix. The set of connected components is denoted
$\pi_0(H)$. The next lemma proves, rather than builds into this
definition, that $H^\circ$ is a normal open-and-closed subgroup and
that $\pi_0(H)$ is the finite quotient group $H/H^\circ$.

An algebraic-group module is a finite-dimensional vector space together
with a morphism of algebraic groups $H\to\operatorname{GL}(M)$.

Choose $s\in W(X_0)$ with $\deg(s)=1$, and let
$\alpha(h)=\rho(s)h\rho(s)^{-1}$ be the automorphism of
$H_{\mathrm{geom}}$ furnished by
[lem-wf-conjugation-geometric-monodromy]. Define the locally
finite-type group scheme

$$
G_{\mathrm{arith}}(\rho)=
\bigsqcup_{m\in\mathbf Z}H_{\mathrm{geom}}\times\{m\},
\qquad (h,m)(h',n)=(h\alpha^m(h'),m+n),
$$

a disjoint union of finite-type pieces, with *degree map*

$$
\deg_G:G_{\mathrm{arith}}(\rho)(\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell)
\longrightarrow\mathbf Z,\qquad (h,m)\longmapsto m.
$$

That the displayed multiplication is a group law, and that $\deg_G$ is
then a group homomorphism, The
map to matrices is $(h,m)\mapsto h\rho(s)^m$. This map need not be
injective: the integer in the second coordinate is deliberately retained,
because it records the Weil degree even when two degree components have the
same matrix image.

For $b\in\Qlb^\times$, let $\mathcal B_b$ be the rank-one
Weil sheaf on a separated finite-type
$k_0$-scheme whose
Weil representation sends
$g\in W(X_0)$ to $b^{\deg(g)}$ and is trivial on
$\pi_1(X)$. Tensoring by $\mathcal B_b$ is called a *constant
Weil twist*.

For $m\in\mathbf Z$, put

$$
G^{[m]}=H_{\mathrm{geom}}\times\{m\}.
$$

An element of $G^{[m]}$ is called an
*algebraic-monodromy element of degree $m$*. The integer degree is
the component index in [def-wf-arithmetic-monodromy-extension]; it is
not a regular function on a finite-type algebraic group.

Let $X_0$ be a normal geometrically connected curve over $k_0$, fix
$\iota:\Qlb\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbf C$, and let $\mathcal V$ be an
irreducible lisse Weil sheaf of rank $r$. Choose a finite coefficient
field over which its representation is defined, and let $a$ be the
weight of [lem-wf-determinantal-weight-exists], so that the
determinant line
$\det(\mathcal V)$ is
punctually $\iota$-pure of weight
$a$. The *determinantal weight* of $\mathcal V$ is

$$
\dw_\iota(\mathcal V):=\frac{a}{r}.
$$

That this number does not depend on the chosen finite coefficient field is
[lem-wf-determinantal-weight-coefficient-field]. We use the same
notation for the associated representation $V$.

Let $X_0$ be a
separated finite-type
$k_0$-scheme, let $X=X_0\times_{k_0}k$, assume that $X$ is
connected, and choose a geometric point $\bar x\to X$. Let
$\mathcal F_0$ be a lisse
Weil sheaf, with underlying lisse
$\Qlb$-sheaf $\mathcal F$ on $X$ in the convention of
[def-weil-pbc-constructible-complexes]. Put
$V=\mathcal F_{\bar x}$. The underlying lisse sheaf first gives the
*geometric fundamental representation*

$$
\rho_{\mathrm{geom}}:\pi_1(X,\bar x)\longrightarrow\operatorname{GL}(V)
$$

by the equivalence of
*lisse $\Qlb$-sheaves on a connected scheme with continuous
$\Qlb$-representations of its etale fundamental group* of
[cor-galois-lisse-representations], the fundamental group being the
automorphism group of the fibre functor as in
[def-galois-fibre-functor]
($k$-torsion and adic levels are as in the coefficient conventions of
[def-weil-pbc-constructible-complexes]).

The Weil descent datum
$\varphi:\Phi_X^*\mathcal F\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathcal F$, with
$\Phi_X$ as in [def-tw-frobenius-action], supplies the missing
degree-one operator. More explicitly, let

$$
W(X_0,\bar x):=
\pi_1(X_0,\bar x)\times_{\operatorname{Gal}(k/k_0)}
\langle\Phi_X\rangle
$$

be the inverse image of the infinite cyclic subgroup generated by
geometric Frobenius, and choose a lift $s$ of $\Phi_X$. After the
usual transport of the stalk from $\Phi_X(\bar x)$ to $\bar x$, the
datum $\varphi$ gives an automorphism $T_s$ of $V$ satisfying

$$
T_s\rho_{\mathrm{geom}}(\gamma)T_s^{-1}
=\rho_{\mathrm{geom}}(s\gamma s^{-1})
\qquad(\gamma\in\pi_1(X,\bar x)).
$$

The *Weil fundamental representation* of $\mathcal F_0$ is the
extension of $\rho_{\mathrm{geom}}$ to $W(X_0,\bar x)$ defined by

$$
\rho(\gamma s^n):=\rho_{\mathrm{geom}}(\gamma)T_s^n
\qquad(\gamma\in\pi_1(X,\bar x),\ n\in\mathbf Z).
$$

That this formula defines a continuous representation, and that the
resulting representation depends on the auxiliary choices only up to the
change-of-base-point isomorphism, are recorded with the other properties
of this construction. Thus
every later expression $\rho:W(X_0)\to\operatorname{GL}(V)$ refers to
this extension, not merely to the geometric representation.

Let $\Pi=\pi_1(X,\bar x)$ be the geometric subgroup of the
Weil group and let
$\rho:W(X_0)\to\operatorname{GL}(V)$ be the representation attached to
a lisse Weil sheaf. The *geometric monodromy group* is the closed
linear algebraic subgroup

$$
H_{\mathrm{geom}}=\overline{\rho(\Pi)}^{\,\mathrm{Zar}}
\subseteq\operatorname{GL}(V).
$$

The closure is taken in the Zariski topology of the affine algebraic
group
$\operatorname{GL}(V)=\operatorname{Spec} \overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell[x_{ij},\det(x)^{-1}]$ of [def-sc-general-linear-group], not in the ambient
affine space of all matrices. Equivalently it is the common zero locus
in $\operatorname{GL}(V)$ of the regular functions vanishing on
$\rho(\Pi)$. That this closure is a subgroup is
[lem-wf-zariski-closure-subgroup].

The representation $\rho$ is *geometrically semisimple* if the
finite-dimensional $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$-representation
$V|_{\Pi}$ is a direct sum of irreducible $\Pi$-subrepresentations.
A lisse Weil sheaf is geometrically semisimple when its fundamental
representation has this property.

On $D(X,E)$ the internal Hom
$R\operatorname{Hom}_E(-,-)$ is computed from a $K$-injective
replacement in its second variable. For Weil complexes the
internal-Hom Frobenius is the conjugation

$$
\Phi_X^*R\mathcal Hom_E(K,L)\stackrel{\sim}{\to}
R\mathcal Hom_E(\Phi_X^*K,\Phi_X^*L)
\xrightarrow{R\mathcal Hom_E(\varphi_K^{-1},\varphi_L)}
R\mathcal Hom_E(K,L)
$$

of the conjugation displayed above; the Frobenius on the internal Hom is
recorded with the other properties of this construction.

Let $X_0$ be a separated finite-type $k_0$-scheme, fix
$\iota:\Qlb\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbf C$ as in
[def-weil-punctual-weights], and let $\mathcal F$ be a
constructible
Weil sheaf on $X_0$, with the
stalk Frobenius modules $(V_x,F_x)$ of
[def-weil-punctual-weights]. Reality is a pointwise condition on
those modules, so the definition is stated for constructible sheaves; the
lisse case is the classical one, and is the case in which the notion of
realizability below is applied. The *local characteristic
factor* of $\mathcal F$ at a closed point $x$ is

$$
P_x(T):=\prod_{\alpha\in S_x}(1-\alpha T)=\det(1-TF_x\mid V_x),
$$

where $S_x$ is the spectrum of $F_x$ counted with multiplicity.
The sheaf $\mathcal F$ is *$\iota$-real* if
$\iota(P_x(T))\in\mathbf R[T]$ for every closed point $x\in|X_0|$;
equivalently, the multiset of complex Frobenius eigenvalues is stable
under complex conjugation at every closed point. The sheaf $\mathcal F$
is *$\iota$-realizable* if it is a direct summand (in the category
of Weil sheaves) of an $\iota$-real lisse Weil sheaf
(*Deligne, Weil II, (1.2.13)*).

Let $X_0$ be a smooth geometrically connected affine curve over
$k_0=\mathbf F_q$ (the separated finite-type conventions of
[def-weil-pbc-scheme-conventions]), let $\mathcal F$ be a
constructible Weil complex
in the coefficient category of [def-weil-pbc-qbar-category],
and for $m\ge1$ let

$$
\|f_{\mathcal F}\|_m^2\;:=\;\sum_{y\in X_0(k_m)}
\left|\iota\sum_i(-1)^i
\operatorname{Tr}(F_y^{(m)}\mid\mathcal H^i(\mathcal F)_{\bar y})\right|^2
$$

(the square of the $L^2$-norm of the trace function of the
Frobenius of the $k_m$-basis). The *$L^2$-weight parameter*
of $\mathcal F$ (the $\|\cdot\|$ of the Ch. I route) is

$$
\|\mathcal F\|\;:=\;\sup\Bigl\{\beta\in\mathbf R:\
\limsup_{m\to\infty}\ \frac{\|f_{\mathcal F}\|_m^2}{q^{m(\beta+1)}}>0\Bigr\},
$$

the $\sup$ of the empty set being $-\infty$, the exponent $1$
being $\dim(X_0)$.

In the setting of [def-wf-l2-norm], the *$L^2$-series* is

$$
\varphi_{\mathcal F}(t)\;:=\;\sum_{m\ge1}\|f_{\mathcal F}\|_m^2\,t^{m-1}.
$$

Its radius of convergence $r_{\mathcal F}$ and the parameter
$\|\mathcal F\|$ of [def-wf-l2-norm] are related as recorded with
the other properties of this construction.

Let $k$ be a field. A *Lie algebra* over $k$ is a $k$-vector space $L$
with a bilinear map $[\,\cdot,\cdot\,]:L\times L\to L$ (the *bracket*)
that is alternating, $[x,x]=0$, and satisfies the Jacobi identity

$$
[x,[y,z]]+[y,[z,x]]+[z,[x,y]]=0 .
$$

For example $\operatorname{End}(V)$, for a $k$-vector space $V$, is a
Lie algebra with $[X,Y]=XY-YX$, and so is every subspace closed under
this bracket. For $x\in L$ put $\operatorname{ad}(x)y=[x,y]$.

For subspaces $I,J\subseteq L$, write $[I,J]$ for the linear span of the
brackets $[x,y]$ with $x\in I$, $y\in J$. A *subalgebra* is a subspace
$I$ with $[I,I]\subseteq I$, and an *ideal* is a subspace $I$ with
$[L,I]\subseteq I$. If $I$ is an ideal, the quotient $L/I$ is a Lie
algebra with $[x+I,y+I]=[x,y]+I$. The *derived sequence* of a Lie
algebra $I$ is $D^0I=I$, $D^{n+1}I=[D^nI,D^nI]$ (also written
$I^{(n)}$), and $I$ is *solvable* if $D^nI=0$ for some $n$. $L$ is
*perfect* if $L=[L,L]$.

A *Lie representation* of $L$ on a $k$-vector space $V$ is a linear map
$r:L\to\operatorname{End}(V)$ with

$$
r([x,y])=r(x)r(y)-r(y)r(x)\qquad(x,y\in L).
$$

A subspace $U\subseteq V$ is *Lie-invariant* if $r(x)U\subseteq U$ for
all $x\in L$. The representation is *faithful* if $r$ is injective,
*simple* (irreducible) if $V\neq0$ and its only invariant subspaces are
$0$ and $V$, and *semisimple* if $V$ is a direct sum of simple invariant
subspaces. The map $\operatorname{ad}:L\to\operatorname{End}(L)$ is a
Lie representation (the *adjoint representation*), by the Jacobi
identity.

attrs.title: Lie algebras, ideals, solvability and Lie representations

objects.body:
*Tangent spaces and differentials.* Let $X=\operatorname{Spec}A$ be a
finite-type affine $k$-scheme (for instance an affine variety, i.e.
$A$ finitely generated and reduced) and let $x\in X(k)$, with maximal
ideal $\mathfrak m_x\subseteq A$ of the functions vanishing at $x$. The
*tangent space* of $X$ at $x$ is

$$
T_xX=(\mathfrak m_x/\mathfrak m_x^2)^\vee
=\operatorname{Hom}_k(\mathfrak m_x/\mathfrak m_x^2,k).
$$

Equivalently, $T_xX$ is the set of $k$-algebra maps
$A\to k[\varepsilon]/\varepsilon^2$ reducing to evaluation at $x$
modulo $\varepsilon$: such a map is $f\mapsto f(x)+\varepsilon\,v(f)$
with $v$ a $k$-derivation at $x$, and $v\mapsto v|_{\mathfrak m_x}$
identifies these derivations with the linear forms on $\mathfrak m_x$
killing $\mathfrak m_x^2$ (the Leibniz rule forces
$v(\mathfrak m_x^2)=0$ and $v(1)=0$, and conversely every such form
extends uniquely via $A=k\oplus\mathfrak m_x$). A regular map
$\varphi:X\to Y$ with comorphism $\varphi^*:B\to A$ satisfies
$\varphi^*\mathfrak m_{\varphi(x)}\subseteq\mathfrak m_x$, hence induces
$\mathfrak m_{\varphi(x)}/\mathfrak m_{\varphi(x)}^2\to
\mathfrak m_x/\mathfrak m_x^2$; the dual linear map
$d\varphi_x:T_xX\to T_{\varphi(x)}Y$ is the *differential* of $\varphi$
at $x$. In the dual-number description it is composition with
$\varphi^*$; in particular $d(\psi\circ\varphi)_x=d\psi_{\varphi(x)}\circ
d\varphi_x$.

*Lie algebra of a matrix group.* Let $G\subseteq\operatorname{GL}(V)$ be
a closed subgroup scheme of finite type (see the last paragraph), for
example a smooth matrix group. For a commutative $k$-algebra $R$, the
$R$-points $G(R)$ are the matrices in $\operatorname{GL}(V\otimes_kR)$
satisfying the defining equations of $G$ over $R$. Its *Lie algebra* is
$\operatorname{Lie}(G)=T_1G$; by the dual-number description, and
identifying $T_1\operatorname{GL}(V)=\operatorname{End}(V)$ through
$X\mapsto1+\varepsilon X$,

$$
\operatorname{Lie}(G)=\{X\in\operatorname{End}(V):
1+\varepsilon X\in G(k[\varepsilon]/\varepsilon^2)\},
$$

a Lie algebra in the sense of [def-wf-lie-algebra] under the bracket
$[X,Y]=XY-YX$ of $\operatorname{End}(V)$. (That this subspace is
closed under the bracket, and that $dr$ below preserves brackets, is standard: compare
Milne, *Algebraic Groups* (2017), Chapter 10.)

*Rational actions.* A *rational representation* of $G$ is a regular
homomorphism $r:G\to\operatorname{GL}(M)$, i.e. an algebraic-group
module in the sense of [def-wf-algebraic-representations]. Its
differential at $1$ is the linear map
$dr:\operatorname{Lie}(G)\to\operatorname{End}(M)$ characterized by
$r(1+\varepsilon X)=1+\varepsilon\,dr(X)$ over
$k[\varepsilon]/\varepsilon^2$; it is a Lie representation of
$\operatorname{Lie}(G)$ on $M$ in the sense of [def-wf-lie-algebra],
i.e. $dr([X,Y])=dr(X)dr(Y)-dr(Y)dr(X)$. The *adjoint action*
is $\operatorname{Ad}(g)X=gXg^{-1}$ for $g\in G(k)$, preserving
$\operatorname{Lie}(G)$ because conjugation by $g$ preserves $G$; its
differential is $\operatorname{ad}(Y)X=[Y,X]$, since over
$k[\varepsilon]/\varepsilon^2$ one has
$(1+\varepsilon Y)X(1+\varepsilon Y)^{-1}=X+\varepsilon(YX-XY)$.

*Matrix group schemes and smoothness.* A *finite-type matrix group
scheme* is a closed subscheme $\mathcal G\subseteq\operatorname{GL}(V)$
cut out by a finitely generated, possibly nonradical, ideal, such that
the regular multiplication and inversion of $\operatorname{GL}(V)$
restrict to it; its coordinate algebra need not a priori be reduced,
and its tangent spaces and Lie algebra are defined by the same formulas
as above, directly from the defining equations. For a closed point $x$
of a finite-type affine $k$-scheme $X=\operatorname{Spec}A$, the *local
ring* is $\mathcal O_{X,x}=A_{\mathfrak m_x}$; it is *regular* if
$\dim_kT_xX=\dim\mathcal O_{X,x}$ (Krull dimension; the inequality
$\ge$ always holds), and $X$ is *smooth over $k$ at $x$* when
$\mathcal O_{X,x}$ is regular ($k$ being algebraically closed of
characteristic zero, hence perfect). A *smooth matrix group* is a
matrix group smooth at every closed point.

attrs.title: Tangent spaces, Lie algebras and rational actions

objects.body:
For a finite-dimensional Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$, its solvable
radical $\operatorname{rad}(\mathfrak g)$ is the sum of all solvable
ideals (solvability and ideals as in [def-wf-lie-algebra]), and its centre is

$$
\mathfrak z(\mathfrak g)=\{X\in\mathfrak g:[X,Y]=0\text{ for all }Y\in\mathfrak g\}.
$$

That this sum is again solvable, and is therefore the unique largest
solvable ideal of $\mathfrak g$, is
recorded with the other properties of this notion;

attrs.title: Solvable radical and centre of a Lie algebra

objects.body:
Let $j:U_0\hookrightarrow C_0$ be a dense open immersion between
separated finite-type
$k_0$-schemes, with $C_0$ a smooth curve. For a lisse
$\Qlb$-sheaf $\mathcal F$ on $U_0$ (in the lisse convention of
[def-weil-pbc-constructible-complexes]), the
*sheaf-theoretic middle extension* is $j_*\mathcal F$, where
$j_*$ is the ordinary direct image in the coefficient category of
[def-weil-pbc-qbar-category]. Thus $(j_*\mathcal F)[1]$
means the ordinary sheaf direct image followed by a cohomological
shift. The derived direct image is written $Rj_*\mathcal F$;
its higher cohomology sheaves must be retained in derived adjunction
and Verdier-duality formulas.

*Recorded in advance* from chapter *Boundary weights, constant twists, and real envelopes* of the source.

The tuple consisting of $\rho$, the geometric group
$H_{\mathrm{geom}}$, the locally finite-type extension
$G_{\mathrm{arith}}(\rho)$, and the degree components $G^{[m]}$ is
called the *monodromy data* of the lisse Weil sheaf. The term
``arithmetic monodromy group'' below always means this degree-graded
extension, with grading as in [lem-wf-degree-components-grading]; its
image in $\operatorname{GL}(V)$ has the Zariski closures
described in [lem-wf-degree-component-image].

Let $\mathcal F$ be a lisse Weil sheaf punctually $\iota$-pure of
weight $w$ on a separated finite-type $k_0$-scheme, and fix
$\iota:\Qlb\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbf C$ as in
[def-weil-punctual-weights]. Using $\iota$, define

$$
b=\iota^{-1}\bigl(q^{-w/2}\bigr)\in\Qlb^\times,
\qquad
\mathcal F^0=\mathcal F\otimes\mathcal B_b,
$$

(where $\mathcal B_b$ is the
constant Weil twist of
[def-wf-constant-weil-twist]), and put

$$
\operatorname{Env}_\iota(\mathcal F;b)=\mathcal F^0\oplus
\bigl(\mathcal F^0\bigr)^\vee.
$$

This direct sum is the *normalized real envelope* associated with
$b$.

A finite-dimensional Lie algebra in characteristic zero is
*semisimple* if it has no nonzero solvable ideal (in the sense of
[def-wf-lie-algebra]).

An algebraic-group module is *semisimple* if it is a direct sum of
simple modules.

An algebraic-group module
is *simple* if it is nonzero and has no nonzero proper stable
subspace.

On the pro-etale site put

$$
\mathbf Z_\ell(1)=\varprojlim_n\mu_{\ell^n},\qquad
E(1)=\mathbf Z_\ell(1)\otimes_{\mathbf Z_\ell}E,
$$

with transition the $\ell$-th power map.
Put $E(0)=E_X$, $E(m)=E(1)^{\otimes^L_E m}$ for $m>0$, and
$E(-m)=R\operatorname{Hom}_E(E(m),E_X)$ for $m>0$, with the induced
tensor and internal-Hom arrows. The *Tate twist* functor is

$$
(-)(m)=-\otimes^L_E E(m):\mathrm{WeilD}(X_0,E)
\longrightarrow\mathrm{WeilD}(X_0,E).
$$

On $D(X,E)$ the derived tensor product $-\otimes^L_E-$ is computed
from a $K$-flat replacement of its first argument. For Weil complexes
$(K,\varphi_K)$, $(L,\varphi_L)$ the tensor Frobenius is
$\varphi_K\otimes\varphi_L$.

*Recorded in advance* from chapter *Weight foundations and monodromy groups* of the source.

Let $E/\mathbf Q_\ell$ be finite and let $X_0$ be a
separated scheme of finite type
over $\mathbf F_q$, with $X=X_0\otimes_{\mathbf F_q}\overline{\mathbf F}_q$.
A *Weil complex* $(K,\varphi_K)$ consists of
$K\in D^b_c(X,E)$ (the categories of
[def-weil-pbc-bounded-constructible-complete]) and an isomorphism
$\varphi_K:\Phi_X^*K\cong K$, where $\Phi_X$ is the geometric
Frobenius of [def-tw-frobenius-action]; morphisms are morphisms
of $K$ commuting with the $\varphi$'s. The *Weil category*
$\mathrm{WeilD}(X_0,E)$ has as objects the Weil complexes; its strict
version uses the same objects and all commuting morphisms. The
$\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$-version is the filtered colimit over the
finite subfields $E$ of its finite-stage analogue (the
$2$-colimit of
[def-weil-pbc-qbar-category]).

*Recorded in advance* from chapter *Weight foundations and monodromy groups* of the source.

For a geometrically connected separated finite-type $k_0$-scheme
$X_0$ with $X=X_0\times_{k_0}k$, the *Weil group*
$W(X_0)$ appearing in the Weil fundamental representation of
[def-wf-fundamental-representation] is the inverse image of the infinite cyclic subgroup
generated by the geometric Frobenius $\Phi_X$ of
[def-tw-frobenius-action] inside the arithmetic
fundamental group, and the
*degree map* is the resulting projection
$\deg:W(X_0)\to\mathbf Z$, which records the exponent of $\Phi_X$.

Fix the finite-field datum
$(p,a,q,k_0,k)$, where $q=p^a$, and a prime $\ell\neq p$; write
$\Ql=\mathbf Q_\ell$ and choose an algebraic closure $\Qlb$ of $\Ql$.
A *Frobenius module* is a pair $(V,F)$ consisting of a
finite-dimensional $\Qlb$-vector space $V$ and a $\Qlb$-linear
automorphism $F:V\to V$, in the sense of the
finite-dimensional
Frobenius-module convention of the framework chapter. For such a pair, define its
*trace series* and its *determinant*

$$
\operatorname{tr}_F(T)
=\sum_{n\geq1}\Tr(F^n\mid V)\frac{T^n}{n}
\in T\Qlb[[T]],
\qquad
P_{(V,F)}(T)=\det(1-TF\mid V)\in\Qlb[T].
$$

The polynomial $P_{(V,F)}(T)$ has constant coefficient $1$ and degree
$\dim_{\Qlb}V$ (its leading coefficient is $(-1)^{\dim V}\det F\neq0$).

For a *finite graded family* of Frobenius modules
$(V_i,F_i)_{i\in I}$, indexed by a finite subset $I\subset\mathbf Z$, the
*alternating trace series* of the family is

$$
\operatorname{str}_F(T)
=\sum_{n\geq1}\left(\sum_{i\in I}(-1)^i
\Tr\bigl(F_i^n\mid V_i\bigr)\right)\frac{T^n}{n}
=\sum_{i\in I}(-1)^i\operatorname{tr}_{F_i}(T)
\in T\Qlb[[T]].
$$

No semisimplicity of $F$ (or of the $F_i$) is assumed anywhere.

In the geometric situation, let $X_0/k_0$ be
smooth, proper, geometrically
connected of pure dimension $d\in\mathbf Z_{\geq0}$, put
$X=X_0\times_{k_0}k$, let $(\Qlb)_X$ be the constant
Weil sheaf, and let $F$ be the
global geometric Frobenius
on $H^i(X,\Qlb)$ in the geometric-Frobenius
convention; for every $0\leq i\leq2d$ the pair
$(H^i(X,\Qlb),F|_{H^i})$ is a Frobenius module, the trace series of the
pair being the degree-$i$ trace series obtained from the
smooth-proper
cohomological family by scalar extension. For the finite graded family
$(H^i(X,\Qlb),F|_{H^i})_{0\leq i\leq2d}$, with $I=\{0,\ldots,2d\}$, the
alternating trace series above is

$$
\operatorname{str}_F(T)
=\sum_{n\geq1}\left(\sum_{i=0}^{2d}(-1)^i
\Tr\bigl(F^n\mid H^i(X,\Qlb)\bigr)\right)\frac{T^n}{n}.
$$

Let $A$ be a domain, $B$ a finitely generated commutative
$A$-algebra, and $0\neq s\in A$. Write
$A_s=A[1/s]$, $B_s=B\otimes_A A_s$, and
$D(s)=\operatorname{Spec}A_s$.
For $d\geq0$ and a tuple $t=(t_1,\ldots,t_d)\in B_s^d$, define
the $D(s)$-morphism

$$
\nu_t:\operatorname{Spec}B_s\longrightarrow
\mathbf A^d_{D(s)}
$$

by the algebra homomorphism $A_s[T_1,\ldots,T_d]\to B_s$,
$T_i\mapsto t_i$. Here affine space has the meaning of
relative affine space; the map is
finite precisely when
$B_s$ is a finitely generated module over that polynomial ring.
No finiteness is included in the choice of $t$.

attrs.title: Coordinates on a principal open of an affine base

objects.body:
Effective Cartier divisors on a smooth curve need not be reduced:
on $\mathbf A^1_k=\Spec k[t]$ the closed subscheme
$V(t^2)=\Spec k[t]/(t^2)$ is defined by the non-zero-divisor
$t^2$, hence is an effective Cartier divisor – the divisor
$2[0]$ in the description of
[lem-sc-cartier-divisor-points] – and it is not reduced.
Thus the reduced-structure description of effective Cartier
divisors is false in general; on a smooth curve it is exactly the
multiplicity-one case $n_P=1$ of
[lem-sc-cartier-divisor-points].

In ordinary derived
categories, even full faithfulness of the comparison functors and
agreement of the left adjoints on their images do not suffice to make
the right-adjoint comparison invertible.

## Proof

Let $k$ be a field and write $D(k)$ for the ordinary derived
category, in the sense of [def-weil-pbc-derived-categories], of
$k$-vector spaces. Take the etale-side source and target both to
be $D(k)$, with $F_{\mathrm{et}}=G_{\mathrm{et}}=\mathrm{id}$.
Take the other source to be $D(k)\times D(k)$, its target to be
$D(k)$, and set

$$
v_X(M)=(M,0),\quad v_Y=\mathrm{id},\quad
F_{\mathrm{proet}}(M,N)=M\oplus N.
$$

Both comparison functors are fully faithful and
$F_{\mathrm{proet}}v_X=\mathrm{id}$. But
$G_{\mathrm{proet}}(K)=(K,K)$, as follows by applying the Hom
universal property of a finite direct sum. The comparison is
$(K,0)\to(K,K)$; it fails to be an isomorphism for every nonzero
$K$. This is an abstract counterexample to the proposed inference,
not a counterexample concerning schemes.

attrs.title: Full faithfulness does not identify ambient right adjoints

objects.body:
The comparison $Lg'^*Rf^{\times}\to Rf'^{\times}Lg^*$ of
[prop-exc-ambient-dual-base-change] is *not* equivalent to the
excision comparison $Rf_!(g'_!\to g'_*)$ for an open immersion $g$:
the former can be an isomorphism while the latter is not.

## Proof

Take $f=\operatorname{id}_Y$ on a smooth curve $Y$, and let
$g:Y'\hookrightarrow Y$ be the complement of a closed point, so that
$X=Y$, $X'=Y'$, $g'=g$ and $f'=\operatorname{id}_{Y'}$. The
identity functor has right adjoint itself, so both sides of
$Lg'^*Rf^{\times}\to Rf'^{\times}Lg^*$ are $Lg^*$ and the comparison
is the identity, an isomorphism. On the other hand
$Rf_!(g'_!\to g'_*)$ is $g_!\to g_*$, and the
[def-weil-extension-by-zero] comparison is not an isomorphism: at
the closed point the stalk of $g_*\Lambda_{Y'}$ is
$\Lambda$ by the [def-weil-pbc-direct-image] description of
direct images, while $g_!\Lambda_{Y'}$ has zero stalk there. Hence the
two statements are not equivalent.

attrs.title: The excision comparison is not the base-change comparison

objects.body:
Let $k$ be an algebraic closure of a finite field of characteristic
$p$, let $T=\mathbf A^1_k$, a
smooth curve, and let $i:\{0\}\hookrightarrow T$.
For nonzero $A=A_{E,n}$ with $\ell\neq p$, the
cohomology sheaf
$\mathcal H^2(Ri^!A_T)$ is nonzero. Thus no bound
$Ri^!D^{[a,b]}\subseteq D^{[a-c,b]}$ is possible for this map.
The support triangle uses the
derived direct image of the
complement.

## Proof

Let $j= T\setminus\{0\}\hookrightarrow T$.
The long exact sequence of the triangle of
[lem-exc-closed-support-triangle], for the right adjoint $Ri^!$
of [lem-exc-closed-ambient], gives
$i_*\mathcal H^2(Ri^!A_T)=R^1j_*A_U$, since $A_T$
has no positive cohomology. By
[prop-weil-pbc-strict-henselization-stalk-formula], the stalk
of its right side at zero is the first Galois cohomology of the
fraction field of the strict local ring. In the two-term calculation
of [lem-exc-dvr-galois], the constant module has trivial action,
so this group is the cokernel of $A\xrightarrow{0}A$, namely
$A\neq0$. This proof of nonvanishing uses no smooth-purity
formula.

attrs.title: Positive cohomology of a closed exceptional image

objects.body:
Fix the finite-field datum
$p,a,q,k_0,k$, where $q=p^a$, and choose a prime $\ell\neq p$. Write
$\Ql=\mathbf Q_\ell$. Put
$Y_0=\mathbf A^1_{k_0}$, and set $Y=Y_0\times_{k_0}k$. The
compact-support cohomology
construction gives
$H_c^2(Y,\Ql)\cong\Ql(-1)$ and no other compactly supported cohomology.
The Tate-twist convention
makes geometric Frobenius act by $q$, so, for
every integer $n\geq1$, the trace expression is
$\#Y_0(\mathbf F_{q^n})=q^n$ and
$Z(Y_0,T)=(1-qT)^{-1}$.

For the finite-field datum $p,a,q,k_0,k$, where $q=p^a$, fix an indeterminate
$T$ and put $Y_0=\Spec\Fq$. The point-count and zeta definitions
[def-weil-point-counts-zeta] give $N_n(Y_0)=1$, $Z(Y_0,T)=(1-T)^{-1}$, and
one closed point of degree one; the corresponding closed-point product is

$$
 Z(Y_0,T)=(1-T)^{-1}.
$$

Fix the finite-field datum
$p,a,q,k_0,k$, where $q=p^a$, and choose a prime $\ell\neq p$. Write
$\Ql=\mathbf Q_\ell$. Put
$Y_0=\mathbf G_{m,k_0}$, and set $Y=Y_0\times_{k_0}k$. One has
$H_c^1(Y,\Ql)\cong\Ql$ and $H_c^2(Y,\Ql)\cong\Ql(-1)$. The
geometric Frobenius
has eigenvalues $1$ and $q$, respectively, under the
compact-support cohomology
and Tate-twist
conventions.
Thus, for every integer $n\geq1$,
$\#Y_0(\mathbf F_{q^n})=q^n-1$ and
$Z(Y_0,T)=(1-T)/(1-qT)$.

Let $q$ be a prime power, let $T$ be an indeterminate, and set
$X_0=\mathbf P^1_{\Fq}$. Its degree-zero and degree-two factors are
$P_0(T)=1-T$, $P_2(T)=1-qT$, and $b_0=b_2=1$. For every integer
$n\geq1$, the point-count and zeta
normalization gives $\#X_0(\mathbf F_{q^n})=1+q^n$, and therefore

$$
Z(X_0,T)=((1-T)(1-qT))^{-1}.
$$

The Lean statement
(`nagataCompactification_of_locallyOfFinitePresentation`) asserts the
existence of a compactification for an arbitrary separated, quasi-compact
morphism of finite presentation over a quasi-compact quasi-separated base,
rather than for the finite-presentation envelope $X_f^{\mathrm{fp}}\to S$
specifically, and the intermediate choice-definitions of this section
([def-nagata-final-descended-model],
[def-nagata-final-noetherian-compactification],
[def-nagata-final-basechanged-compactification] and their spec lemmas)
are collapsed into its proof and are not separately formalized.

Let $X$ be of finite type over $k$ and let $F$ be a
constructible
$\Lambda$-sheaf on $X_{{\mathrm{et}}}$. Then there is an open
subscheme $U\hookrightarrow X$ with
$\dim(X\setminus U)<\dim X$ on which the restriction $F|_U$ is
lisse.

## Proof

If $X$ is empty, take $U=X$.
Otherwise let $C_1,\ldots,C_t$ be all its irreducible components,
using [lem-weil-pbc-noetherian-finite-components].
For each component of maximal dimension, first remove all other
components. This gives an irreducible open $O_i$ of $X$
containing its generic point $\eta_i$. By the finite partition
in [def-weil-pbc-constructible-complexes], the stratum containing
$\eta_i$ contains a nonempty open $V_i\subset O_i$.
The restriction to $V_i$ is finite locally constant.
The $V_i$ are disjoint opens of $X$, so their finite union $U$
is open and $F|_U$ is finite locally constant.
The closed complement meets every maximal-dimensional component in
a proper closed subset. For finite-type schemes over a field such
a subset has strictly smaller dimension, by the dimension formula
for finitely generated algebras. The other components already have
smaller dimension. Hence $\dim(X\setminus U)<\dim X$.

attrs.title: A lisse locus for a constructible sheaf

objects.body:
Let $X$ be of finite type over a field, let $\Lambda$ be
a finite commutative ring, and let $L$ be a
finite locally
constant $\Lambda$-module sheaf. There is a
finite etale
surjective map $p:P\to X$ such that $p^*L$ is constant
on each connected component of $P$, with a finite
$\Lambda$-module fibre. If $X$ is connected, one common
finite module can be used on all of $P$.

## Proof

A Noetherian scheme has finitely many connected components,
which are open and closed. We may therefore work on a
connected component of $X$. Let $M$ be a geometric
fibre of $L$, finite by
[def-weil-pbc-constructible-complexes]. Apply
[thm-galois-lc-etale], [thm-galois-fundamental] to its
underlying finite locally constant set sheaf and retain
the addition and scalar-multiplication maps. These maps
are preserved by the equivalence, so the resulting action
on $M$ is $\Lambda$-linear. Its kernel in the
profinite fundamental group is open: it is the intersection
of the stabilizers of the finitely many elements of $M$.
The finite cover corresponding to this kernel exists by
[cor-galois-open-subgroups]. On that cover the action
is trivial, so the pulled-back module sheaf is
$\underline M$. This also shows surjectivity of the cover;
its fibres are the nonempty finite coset set.
Take the disjoint union of the covers on the finitely many
connected components. This is finite etale in the sense of
[def-weil-pbc-scheme-conventions], hence of finite type
over the ground field. No freeness assertion about $M$
is used; for instance $\mathbf Z/\ell$ is a finite
$\mathbf Z/\ell^2$-module that is not free.

attrs.title: Finite etale trivialization of a lisse sheaf

objects.body:
Let $k'$ be algebraically closed, let $X$ be a
finite-type $k'$-scheme
of dimension at most $d$, and let $F$ be a
constructible
$\Lambda$-sheaf, with finite coefficients as in
[sbc-def-coefficient-conventions].
Then $H^q(X_{\rm et},F)=0$ for $q>2d$, with cohomology
as in [def-weil-pbc-etale-cohomology].

## Proof

The coefficient ring of [sbc-def-coefficient-conventions]
is killed by a positive integer, so $F$ is torsion.
The absolute Galois group of $k'$ is trivial; the field
dictionary of [lem-exc-field-discrete-modules] therefore
gives torsion cohomological dimension zero for $k'$.
Apply [thm-sc-finite-type-torsion-cd] with $c=0$.
It proves the stronger assertion for all torsion etale sheaves.
Its proof uses Zariski Leray and the affine ordinary
cohomological-dimension theorem; no compact-support
identification or affine compact-support bound is involved.

attrs.title: Cohomological dimension over an algebraically closed field

objects.body:
Let $X$ be a Noetherian
scheme and let $F$ be an
abelian etale sheaf on $X$
with finite geometric stalks.
For $n\geq1$ put $C_n=\{x\in X:|F_{\bar x}|=n\}$.
Then $F$ is constructible
if and only if every $C_n$ is a constructible subset of $X$.
For an abelian sheaf, constructibility here means a finite locally
closed partition with finite locally constant restrictions.

## Proof

If $F$ is constructible, refine its finite partition and its finite
etale trivializations so that stalk cardinality is constant on each
part. Each $C_n$ is a finite union of these parts, by
[def-weil-pbc-constructible-complexes].

Conversely use Noetherian induction on closed subsets of $X$.
Pullback to a closed subset preserves stalks by
[prop-weil-pbc-geometric-stalks-exact]; the new level sets are
intersections with $C_n$, hence are constructible.
It suffices to find a nonempty open where $F$ is finite locally
constant. Choose an irreducible component with generic point $\eta$.
Remove the other finitely many components, using
[lem-weil-pbc-noetherian-finite-components], to obtain a nonempty
irreducible open $X_0$. Put $M=F_{\bar\eta}$ and $m=|M|$.
The constructible subset $C_m\cap X_0$ contains $\eta$, hence
contains a nonempty open $U$ of $X_0$: among its finitely many
locally closed pieces one contains $\eta$, and that piece's closed
factor must be all of $X_0$.

A finite abelian group has finitely many generators and relations.
By [def-weil-pbc-geometric-stalks], lift its generators to
sections on one pointed affine etale neighbourhood $V\to U$ of
$\bar\eta$. The relations have zero germs; finitely many further
refinements make all of them zero as sections. Thus we obtain
$\varphi:\underline M_V\to F|_V$ inducing the identity on $M$.
The chosen point over $\eta$ is generic in a component of $V$:
an etale morphism is flat with zero-dimensional fibres, so a point
over a generic point is itself generic. Remove the other components
to make $V$ irreducible, retaining this point.

For $a\ne0$ in $M$, the zero-germ locus of $\varphi(a)$ is
open in $V$. A zero germ is represented by the zero section on an
etale neighbourhood; the images of these neighbourhoods are open by
[lem-weil-pbc-flat-lfp-open], and their union is that locus.
It omits the generic point because $\varphi_{\bar\eta}$ is injective.
An open subset of irreducible $V$ omitting its generic point is
empty. Consequently $\varphi$ is injective at every geometric
stalk. Both sides have $m$ elements at each stalk, so it is an
isomorphism by [lemma-weil-pbc-geometric-stalk-conservative].
The image $W$ of $V\to X$ is nonempty and open by
[lem-weil-pbc-flat-lfp-open], and the etale cover $V\to W$
trivializes $F|_W$. Induction supplies a finite partition on
$X\setminus W$; adjoining $W$ proves constructibility.
This also proves finiteness of the image of $x\mapsto|F_{\bar x}|$;
it was not inferred from an infinite union of constructible subsets.
The classical statement is
[SGA 4,
Exposition IX, Proposition 2.13(iii)](https://grothendiecksga.com/read/sga4/en/IX-2.html).

attrs.title: Constructibility from the cardinalities of finite stalks

objects.body:
Let $f:X\to S$ be a finite
morphism with $S$ of finite type over $k$, and let $F$ be a
constructible
$\Lambda$-sheaf on $X_{{\mathrm{et}}}$ (the ring $\Lambda$ of
[sbc-def-coefficient-conventions]). Then the higher direct
images $R^qf_*F$ of [def-weil-pbc-direct-image] are
constructible on
$S_{{\mathrm{et}}}$ for every $q\geq0$, and $R^qf_*F=0$ for $q>0$:
the vanishing bound $2\cdot0$ of the zero relative dimension.

## Proof

Apply [lem-fin-finite-morphism], which proves both
constructibility of $f_*F$ and exactness of finite direct image.
It uses the finite-stalk formula and the earlier finite-image
constructibility proof, with no cardinality or general finiteness input.

In the six-functor datum of
[def-fix-six-functor-datum], assume that $f$ and the structure
morphisms $a_X$, $a_Y$ are
exceptionally
admissible, and put

$$
\omega_{Y,\Lambda}=Ra_Y^!\Lambda,\qquad
\omega_{X,\Lambda}=Ra_X^!\Lambda,\qquad
D_Y(-)=R\mathcal Hom_{\Lambda}(-,\omega_{Y,\Lambda}),\qquad
D_X(-)=R\mathcal Hom_{\Lambda}(-,\omega_{X,\Lambda}).
$$

For every $M\in D^b_{ctf}(X,\Lambda)$ there is a canonical
isomorphism

$$
D_Y(Rf_!M)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }Rf_*D_X(M),
$$

natural in $M$, compatible with finite reduction, scalar extension,
and shifts.

## Proof

Step 1: the relation $Rf^!\omega_{Y,\Lambda}\cong\omega_{X,\Lambda}$.
The composition law $R(a_Y\circ f)_!\cong R(a_Y)_!Rf_!$ of
[thm-sf-comp-composition] and the adjunctions of
[fix-prop-adjunctions] give, by the mate calculus for a
composite adjunction (the pasted units and counits of
[fix-prop-adjunctions]), the canonical isomorphism

$$
Rf^!\omega_{Y,\Lambda}=Rf^!Ra_Y^!\Lambda
\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }Ra_X^!\Lambda=\omega_{X,\Lambda}.
$$

Step 2: the exchange. Applying [fix-lem-tensor-adjunction]
with $N=\omega_{Y,\Lambda}$ (an object of $D^b_{ctf}(Y,\Lambda)$
by the finite-Tor preservation of
[def-weil-exceptional-inverse-image]) gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
D_Y(Rf_!M)
&=R\mathcal Hom_Y(Rf_!M,\omega_{Y,\Lambda})\\
&\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }Rf_*R\mathcal Hom_X(M,f^!\omega_{Y,\Lambda})\\
&\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }Rf_*R\mathcal Hom_X(M,\omega_{X,\Lambda})
=Rf_*D_X(M),
\end{aligned}
$$

the first isomorphism being the one of
[fix-lem-tensor-adjunction], the second the transport along
step 1. Step 3: the compatibilities. Naturality in $M$ and the
compatibility with finite reduction, scalar extension, and shifts are
those of [fix-lem-tensor-adjunction] and of step 1.

In the six-functor datum of
[def-fix-six-functor-datum], let

$$
\begin{array}{ccc}
X'&\xrightarrow{g'}&X\\
f'\downarrow&&\downarrow f\\
Y'&\xrightarrow{g}&Y
\end{array}
$$

be a cartesian square of
finite-type $k$-schemes
whose four arrows are
separated and of finite
type, and let $K\in D^b_c(X,\Lambda)$, with $K'=Lg'^*K$. The
exchange transformations

$$
\operatorname{Ex}_*(K):Lg^*Rf_*K\longrightarrow Rf'_*K',
\qquad
\operatorname{Ex}_!(K):Lg^*Rf_!K\longrightarrow Rf'_!K',
$$

of [def-exchange-projection] satisfy:

1. both are natural in $K$, in the morphisms of the square, and
in the coefficient ring; $\operatorname{Ex}_!$ agrees with the
compact-support exchange map of [def-cbc-exchange-map] at every
finite level and with its transports of
[thm-cbc-finite-extension] and [thm-cbc-qbar] at the
rational and algebraically closed levels;
1. both are the identity for an identity square, and for
vertically or horizontally pasted cartesian squares the exchange
transformation of the outer rectangle is the composite of the
exchange transformations of the two inner squares after inserting
the canonical associativity isomorphisms; $\operatorname{Ex}_*$
obeys the identity and pasting equations of
[lem-weil-pbc-exchange-identity-pasting] and of
[sbc-lem-identity-and-base-change-composition],
$\operatorname{Ex}_!$ those of [thm-cbc-finite-torsion];
1. for smooth $g$,
$\operatorname{Ex}_*$ is the smooth-base-change exchange morphism of
[sbc-thm-bounded-below-derived-smooth-base-change], and it is an
isomorphism;
1. $\operatorname{Ex}_!$ is independent of the chosen
compactification and compatible with the refinement comparison
isomorphisms of [prop-compactification-coherence-detailed] and with the
composition law of [thm-sf-comp-composition].

## Proof

Step 1: construction. By [def-exchange-projection],
$\operatorname{Ex}_*$ is the adjoint of the composite of the
canonical identification $Lf'^*Lg^*\cong Lg'^*Lf^*$ of the
cartesian square ([def-weil-pbc-cartesian-square]) with the
counit of $Lf^*\dashv Rf_*$ of [def-weil-derived-direct-image],
and $\operatorname{Ex}_!$ is represented by $\operatorname{Ex}_*$
for a proper compactification $\bar f$, followed by the
extension-by-zero identification
$L\bar g'^*j_!\cong j'_!Lg'^*$ of [def-exchange-projection]; at
a finite coefficient level the latter is the map of
[def-cbc-exchange-map], whose definition is the same composite.
Step 2: naturality. Each ingredient of these composites is a natural
transformation: the identification of the cartesian square is natural
in the square and the coefficient ring
([def-weil-pbc-cartesian-square]), the counit is natural by
[def-weil-derived-pullback-tensor-hom] and
[def-weil-derived-direct-image], and the extension-by-zero
identification is natural by [def-cbc-exchange-map]; the
transports of [thm-cbc-finite-extension] and
[thm-cbc-qbar] are the coefficient extensions of the same maps.
Step 3: identity and pasting. The identity and pasting equations
for $\operatorname{Ex}_*$ are the mate versions of the identity
and pasting laws of the identification of the cartesian square,
recorded in [lem-weil-pbc-exchange-identity-pasting] (finite
etale coefficients) and in
[sbc-lem-identity-and-base-change-composition] (derived level,
for successive base changes); the identity and horizontal and
vertical pasting for $\operatorname{Ex}_!$ are the corresponding
properties of its two ingredients, stated in
[thm-cbc-finite-torsion], together with
[lem-weil-pbc-exchange-identity-pasting] for the proper factor.
Step 4: smooth base
change. For smooth $g$, $\operatorname{Ex}_*$ is the derived
exchange morphism of [sbc-def-base-change-map] read on the same
square, and it is an isomorphism by
[sbc-thm-overline-mathbf-q-ell-coefficient-smooth-base-ch] at
the algebraically closed rational level and by the corresponding
finite-level statement of [sbc-thm-bounded-below-derived-smooth-base-change]
at the other levels. Step 5: independence. The comparison
isomorphisms of [prop-compactification-coherence-detailed] identify the
two compactification candidates of $\operatorname{Ex}_!$ and are
compatible with the composition law of
[thm-sf-comp-composition] (the proper-composition
isomorphism and the extension-by-zero identification), so
$\operatorname{Ex}_!$ does not depend on the compactification.

attrs.title: Exchange functoriality: naturality, identities, and pasting

objects.body:
Let $\Lambda=A_{E,n}$, let $M\in D^b_{ctf}(Y,\Lambda)$ be a
bounded constructible
complex of finite Tor amplitude
on the coefficient site,
and let $\bar y\to Y$ be a
geometric point.
Then $M_{\bar y}\in D(\Lambda)$ is quasi-isomorphic to a bounded
complex of finite free $\Lambda$-modules. The same conclusion
holds on the small etale site with the corresponding constructibility
and derived-tensor
Tor-amplitude conditions.
Separately, for a bounded constructible complex at a
field coefficient stage
$E$, or in the
common-stage
$\Qlb$-category, its geometric stalk is a bounded complex of
finite-dimensional vector spaces over that field and is perfect.

## Proof

Put $C=M_{\bar y}$, using [def-weil-pbc-geometric-stalks].
Constructibility in [def-weil-finite-torsion-constructibility]
makes each $H^r(C)$ finite over $\Lambda$, and only finitely
many are nonzero. Choose $[a,b]$ as in
[def-weil-finite-tor-amplitude]. For an arbitrary
$\Lambda$-module $N$, use its constant sheaf $\underline N$
on $Y$. The exact stalk functor commutes with the
[def-weil-derived-tensor] derived tensor product, so

$$
H^r(C\otimes_\Lambda^L N)
=\mathcal H^r(M\otimes_\Lambda^L\underline N)_{\bar y}=0
\qquad(r\notin[a,b]).
$$

Taking $N=\Lambda$ also gives $H^r(C)=0$ outside $[a,b]$.

The ring $\Lambda=\mathcal O_E/\varpi_E^n$ is Noetherian and local.
Construct a bounded-above finite-free resolution $P^\bullet\to C$
with $P^r=0$ for $r>b$. The construction proceeds downwards:
choose finitely many generators of the highest cohomology, lift
them to cycles, and map a finite free module in that degree to a
representative of $C$. The cone has zero cohomology in that degree
and finitely generated cohomology in lower degrees; Noetherianity
ensures finite generation of the new kernels. Repeating this step
constructs the resolution, which stabilizes in each fixed degree.
Being bounded above and free, $P^\bullet$ is K-flat.

Put $Q=\operatorname{coker}(P^{a-1}\xrightarrow{d^{a-1}}P^a)$.
Since $H^r(P^\bullet)=0$ for $r<a$, the augmented sequence

$$
\cdots\longrightarrow P^{a-2}\longrightarrow P^{a-1}
\longrightarrow P^a\longrightarrow Q\longrightarrow0
$$

is a free resolution of $Q$. Hence, for every $\Lambda$-module
$N$, with no finiteness restriction,

$$
\operatorname{Tor}^{\Lambda}_1(Q,N)
=
\frac{\ker(P^{a-1}\otimes N\longrightarrow P^a\otimes N)}
{\operatorname{im}(P^{a-2}\otimes N\longrightarrow P^{a-1}\otimes N)}
=H^{a-1}(P^\bullet\otimes_\Lambda N)=0.
$$

Thus $Q$ is flat. It is finitely presented, as a cokernel of
finite free modules, so is projective and therefore finite free
over the local ring $\Lambda$. The differential $d^a$ factors
through $Q$, and the quotient map to

$$
0\longrightarrow Q\longrightarrow P^{a+1}
\longrightarrow\cdots\longrightarrow P^b\longrightarrow0
$$

with $Q$ in degree $a$ is a quasi-isomorphism.
This proves the finite-coefficient assertion on either site.

At a field coefficient $F$, the constructible stalk is instead a
bounded complex with finite-dimensional cohomology over $F$.
Splitting cycles and boundaries as vector subspaces gives
$\bigoplus_r H^r(C)[-r]\xrightarrow{\sim}C$, with a finite direct
sum, and proves perfectness directly at the rational stage of
[def-weil-rationalization-karoubi].
For $\Qlb$, choose a finite field of definition from
[def-weil-algebraically-closed-coefficients] and extend this
finite-dimensional complex to $\Qlb$.

attrs.title: Geometric-stalk perfectness at finite and field coefficients

objects.body:
In the six-functor datum of
[def-fix-six-functor-datum], let $f$ be
exceptionally
admissible, and let $M\in D^b_{ctf}(X,\Lambda)$ and
$N\in D^b_{ctf}(Y,\Lambda)$. There is a canonical isomorphism

$$
Rf_*R\mathcal Hom_X\bigl(M,f^!N\bigr)
\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }
R\mathcal Hom_Y\bigl(Rf_!M,N\bigr),
$$

natural in $M$ and $N$, compatible with finite reduction, scalar
extension, and shifts.

## Proof

Step 1: the construction. For every
$L\in D^b_{ctf}(Y,\Lambda)$, the derived tensor–internal-Hom
adjunction of [def-weil-derived-pullback-tensor-hom] and the
adjunction of [fix-prop-adjunctions] give the chain

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Hom_Y\bigl(L,R\mathcal Hom_Y(Rf_!M,N)\bigr)
&\cong\Hom_Y(Rf_!M\otimes^L_{\Lambda}L,N)\\
&\cong\Hom_Y\bigl(Rf_!(M\otimes^L_{\Lambda}Lf^*L),N\bigr)\\
&\cong\Hom_X\bigl(M\otimes^L_{\Lambda}Lf^*L,f^!N\bigr)\\
&\cong\Hom_X\bigl(Lf^*L,R\mathcal Hom_X(M,f^!N)\bigr)\\
&\cong\Hom_Y\bigl(L,Rf_*R\mathcal Hom_X(M,f^!N)\bigr),
\end{aligned}
$$

where the second isomorphism is the inverse of the projection formula
of [fix-prop-projection-formula] (applicable since $M$ and
$L$ lie in the finite-Tor subcategories), and the first, third, and
fourth are the tensor–internal-Hom adjunction of
[def-weil-derived-pullback-tensor-hom] with the adjunction
$Rf_!\dashv Rf^!$ of [fix-prop-adjunctions], the last being
the adjunction $Lf^*\dashv Rf_*$ of
[fix-prop-adjunctions]. Step 2: detection. The adjunction chain
defines a canonical map of the two ambient derived objects.
At a finite etale coefficient stage, take
$L=e_!A[r]$, where $e:V\to Y$ is a quasi-compact etale object
of the site and $r\in\mathbf Z$. Such an extension by zero is
constructible and flat, so it is in the finite-Tor domain used in
step 1. The resulting Hom groups are the cohomology of the two
objects on $V$. The cone therefore has zero cohomology on every
such $V$, and hence has zero geometric stalks. Conservativity in
[lemma-weil-pbc-geometric-stalk-conservative] proves the map is
an isomorphism without first assuming that either output belongs to
the finite-Tor subcategory. The site equivalence on the stipulated
coefficient categories in [thm-weil-pbc-site-comparison] and
the coefficient comparisons of the four ingredients give the stated
realizations and field stages. Naturality and the comparison squares
under reduction follow by transposing them to the same tensor and
counit composites. This asserts compatibility of the specified maps;
it does not supply a separate internal-Hom reduction isomorphism
outside the domains where that comparison has been proved.

In the six-functor datum of
[def-fix-six-functor-datum]:

1. the derived pullback and the derived direct image form an
adjoint pair
$$
Lf^*\dashv Rf_*
$$
on $D^b_c(Y,\Lambda)$ and $D^b_c(X,\Lambda)$, with unit
$\eta_f:\operatorname{id}\to Rf_*Lf^*$ and counit
$\varepsilon_f:Lf^*Rf_*\to\operatorname{id}$, satisfying the
triangle identities
$$
(Rf_*\varepsilon_f)\circ(\eta_fRf_*)=\operatorname{id}_{Rf_*},
\qquad
(\varepsilon_fLf^*)\circ(Lf^*\eta_f)=\operatorname{id}_{Lf^*};
$$
1. if $f$ is
exceptionally
admissible, the compact-support direct image and the exceptional
inverse image form an adjoint pair
$$
Rf_!\dashv Rf^!
$$
on $D^b_c(X,\Lambda)$ and $D^b_c(Y,\Lambda)$, with unit
$\nu_f:\operatorname{id}\to Rf^!Rf_!$ and counit
$\mu_f:Rf_!Rf^!\to\operatorname{id}$ satisfying the two triangle
identities; the units and counits agree for the refinement
comparisons, and the adjunction restricts to an adjunction
$$
Rf_!:D^b_{ctf}(X,\Lambda)\rightleftarrows
D^b_{ctf}(Y,\Lambda):Rf^!;
$$
1. for composable separated finite-type morphisms
$X\xrightarrow{f}Y\xrightarrow{g}Z$, the unit of
$L(gf)^*\dashv R(gf)_*$ is the composite
$Lf^*\eta_gLf^*\circ\eta_f$ and the counit is the composite of the
counits; for the exceptional pair the unit and counit of
$R(gf)_!\dashv R(gf)^!$ are the pasted units and counits of
$Rf_!\dashv Rf^!$ and $Rg_!\dashv Rg^!$ under the composition
law of [thm-sf-comp-composition], i.e. the mate of
the composition isomorphism;
1. the adjunction is compatible with the exchange
transformations: the transpose of $\operatorname{Ex}_!$ is
the corresponding exceptional-inverse-image identification, and
$\operatorname{Ex}_*$ is the transpose of the base-change
composite of [def-exchange-projection].

## Proof

Step 1: the derived adjunction $(Lf^*,Rf_*)$. The sheaf-level
adjunction of inverse image and direct image, its derived form
$Lf^*\dashv Rf_*$ on the categories of
[def-weil-pbc-derived-categories], and its unit and counit
$\eta_f,\varepsilon_f$ are [def-weil-pbc-inverse-image] of
the ambient-foundations chapter (finite etale level; the pro-etale level is the site
transport of the same datum, the operations being those of
[def-weil-derived-pullback-tensor-hom] and
[def-weil-derived-direct-image]); the triangle identities hold
for the derived adjunction because the derived unit and counit are
the images of the sheaf-level ones under K-injective and K-flat
replacement of [def-weil-pbc-kinjective-resolutions], the
resolution-independence of
[lem-weil-derived-tensor-resolution-independent], and the sheaf-level
triangle identities are preserved by the derived functors. Step 2:
the exceptional adjunction $(Rf_!,Rf^!)$. The natural adjunction
isomorphisms $\Hom_Y(Rf_!K,L)\cong\Hom_X(K,Rf^!L)$ characterize
$Rf^!$ by [def-weil-exceptional-inverse-image], so the
adjunction $Rf_!\dashv Rf^!$, its unit and counit, and the
triangle identities are the datum of
[def-weil-exceptional-adjoint-admissibility]; the agreement of
the units and the counits with the refinement comparisons is
condition (1) of that definition, and the restriction to the
finite-Tor subcategories is condition (3) of the same definition.
Step 3: composition. The composite adjunction of step 1 is the
paste of the component adjunctions (the unit of the composite is the
composite of the units, the counit the composite of the counits, and
the triangle identities of the composite are the composites of the
triangle identities of the components, through the composition
isomorphisms $R(gf)_*\cong Rg_*Rf_*$ of
[lem-weil-derived-direct-image-composition], which are natural, unital
and associative); for the
exceptional pair, the mate of the composition isomorphism of
[thm-sf-comp-composition] (with its transports of
[def-weil-integral-rational-qbar-compact-support]) gives an
isomorphism $(g\circ f)^!\cong f^!g^!$, the pasted units and
counits are the mates of this isomorphism through the two component
adjunctions, and the triangle identities are the composite versions
of the component ones. Step 4: exchange compatibility. The
transpose of $\operatorname{Ex}_!$ is obtained by the mate
calculus of [def-exchange-projection]: the exchange
transformation is defined as the transpose of the compatibility of
the pullbacks with the counit, and the same holds for
$\operatorname{Ex}_*$; the compatibility of these transposes with
the composition law is [fix-lem-exchanges].

The operations in [def-fix-six-functor-datum] and their proved
comparison maps satisfy identity, composition, exchange and projection
coherence. The elementary coefficient comparisons of
[lem-fix-operation-reduction] extend to general constructible
finite-Tor internal Hom by [thm-coef-finite-hom], to integral
internal Hom by [lem-coef-integral-hom-reduction], and to finite
coefficient-field extensions by [lem-coef-integral-finite-extension].
Exceptional comparisons on these constructible domains are
[lem-coef-finite-exceptional], [prop-coef-integral-exceptional-adjoint], [lem-coef-rational-operations]. Smooth orientation and the site-perfect Poincare pairing have
the additional compatibilities of
[thm-pur-finite-reduction-of-purity], [thm-pod-finite-reduction].
At field coefficients these maps are Weil-equivariant, with the purity
compatibilities of [prop-pur-weil-equivariance-compatibilities].

## Proof

The identity and pasting equations are [fix-lem-exchanges].
The projection diamonds and associativity are
[fix-prop-projection-formula]; taking adjoint mates gives the
corresponding equations for [fix-cor-verdier-exchange].
The maps used here are tensor reassociation, evaluation, and adjunction
units and counits, whose coefficient comparisons are proved in
[lem-fix-operation-reduction]. The general Hom comparisons
[thm-coef-finite-hom], [lem-coef-integral-hom-reduction], [lem-coef-integral-finite-extension]
are defined by the same evaluation maps. The exceptional comparisons
[lem-coef-finite-exceptional], [prop-coef-integral-exceptional-adjoint], [lem-coef-rational-operations]
preserve units and counits, so their mates satisfy the same equations.
Their Weil structures are [lem-fix-weil-operations], with
general duality equivariance given by [cor-coef-verdier-weil-equivariance]. The geometric orientation is supplied
separately by [thm-pur-finite-reduction-of-purity] and
[prop-pur-weil-equivariance-compatibilities]; composing it with
evaluation gives the pairing comparison [thm-pod-finite-reduction].
Thus coherence is inherited from the individual maps on the stated
domains, without an additional preservation or biduality assertion.

In the six-functor datum of
[def-fix-six-functor-datum], let $f:X\to Y$ be
separated of finite
type, let $K\in D^b_c(X,\Lambda)$ and
$L\in D^b_{ctf}(Y,\Lambda)$, using the
finite-Tor subcategory.
The
projection transformation, built from the
derived tensor and pullback
and the compact-support direct image of
[def-compact-support-direct-image-detailed],
is then an isomorphism at every coefficient stage:

$$
\operatorname{PF}_{f,K,L}:Rf_!K\otimes^L_{\Lambda}L
\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }Rf_!\bigl(K\otimes^L_{\Lambda}Lf^*L\bigr),
$$

natural in $K$ and $L$, compatible with the composition law of
[thm-sf-comp-composition] (associativity pentagon), with the compactification comparisons, with
finite reduction on the stated finite-Tor domains and scalar extension,
and with the identification
$Rf_!\cong Rf_*$ for proper $f$; at the rational and algebraically
closed stages the isomorphism restricts to the Weil categories of
[def-wf-tensor-product]. A projection formula for the
derived direct image is asserted
only in the proper case, where it is this same statement via
$Rf_!\cong Rf_*$.

## Proof

The geometric-fiber argument of
[lem-weil-finite-compact-projection-formula] proves the finite
coefficient formula. The compatibility of the specified maps under
successive coefficient reductions is [prop-sf-pf-reduction].
Thus [thm-sf-pf-adic] reconstructs the integral map, and
[thm-sf-pf-field] transports it to the field stages.
The site comparison of [thm-sf-pf-proetale] gives the stated
pro-etale realization. The composition, refinement, exchange and
proper-coincidence identities are [prop-sf-pf-coherence].
Its equivariance for Weil complexes is the equivariance of the
projection transformation in [lem-fix-weil-operations].
Every step constructs or compares the same projection map; none
uses smooth purity or Verdier duality.

attrs.title: Compact-support projection formula at all coefficient stages

objects.body:
In the setting of [d-relative-frob], for every $m\geq1$ the map
$r_m:X\to X'_m$ is finite and a universal homeomorphism
([def-weil-scheme-morphism-properties]).

## Proof

Put $Q=q^m$. By [d-relative-frob], $r_m$ is the base change along
$k_0\to k$ of the relative $Q$-power Frobenius
$F_{X_0/Y_0}:X_0\to X_0^{(Q)}$. Finite morphisms and universal
homeomorphisms are stable under base change, so it suffices to prove
that $F_{X_0/Y_0}$ is finite and a universal homeomorphism. Write
$\pi:X_0^{(Q)}\to X_0$ for the second projection, the base change of
$F_{Y_0}$ along $f_0$; then $\pi\circ F_{X_0/Y_0}=F_{X_0}$.

*Step 1: finiteness.* Since $\pi\circ F_{X_0/Y_0}=F_{X_0}$ is the
identity on underlying spaces, for affine opens
$\operatorname{Spec}R\subseteq Y_0$ and
$\operatorname{Spec}S\subseteq f_0^{-1}(\operatorname{Spec}R)$ the
inverse image under $F_{X_0/Y_0}$ of the affine open
$\operatorname{Spec}(R\otimes_{F,R}S)\subseteq X_0^{(Q)}$ is
$\operatorname{Spec}S$, and such opens cover $X_0^{(Q)}$. Finiteness is
local on the target, so it suffices that the ring map
$R\otimes_{F,R}S\to S$, $r'\otimes s\mapsto f_0^\#(r')s^Q$, of
[d-relative-frob] is finite. Choose generators $s_1,\ldots,s_n$ of the
finitely generated $R$-algebra $S$. Its image contains $f_0^\#(R)$ and
all $Q$-th powers. Every element of $S$ is an $f_0^\#(R)$-linear
combination of monomials $s^e=\prod_is_i^{e_i}$, and writing
$e_i=Qa_i+b_i$ with $0\leq b_i<Q$ gives $s^e=(s^a)^Q\,s^b$. Hence the
$Q^n$ monomials $s^b$ with $0\leq b_i<Q$ generate $S$ as a module over
the image, and the ring map is finite.

*Step 2: absolute Frobenius.* For an $\mathbf F_p$-scheme $T$, the
absolute $Q$-power Frobenius $F_T$ is the identity on the underlying
space, hence bijective; it is integral, since every local section $b$
is a root of $t^Q-b^Q$ whose coefficient $b^Q$ lies in the image; and
on residue fields it induces $\kappa\to\kappa$, $a\mapsto a^Q$, a
purely inseparable extension. Thus $F_T$ is radicial, that is,
universally injective, and being integral, universally injective and
surjective it is a universal homeomorphism
([Stacks, Tag 04DF](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/04DF)). In
particular $F_{Y_0}$ is one, and so is its base change $\pi$.

*Step 3: universal homeomorphism.* The morphism $F_{X_0/Y_0}$ is
integral by Step 1. It is surjective: for $x'\in X_0^{(Q)}$ choose $x$
with $F_{X_0}(x)=\pi(x')$ (Step 2); then
$\pi(F_{X_0/Y_0}(x))=\pi(x')$, and $\pi$ is injective, so
$F_{X_0/Y_0}(x)=x'$. It is universally injective: a morphism is
universally injective if and only if it is injective on $K$-valued
points for every field $K$, and on $K$-points
$\pi\circ F_{X_0/Y_0}=F_{X_0}$ is injective by Step 2, so
$F_{X_0/Y_0}$ is injective on $K$-points. By
[Stacks, Tag 04DF](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/04DF) again,
$F_{X_0/Y_0}$ is a universal homeomorphism. With Step 1 and the
reduction at the beginning, $r_m$ is a finite universal homeomorphism.

For a finite universal homeomorphism $r:X\to Y$,
pullback is an equivalence
$r^*:D^b_{ctf}(Y,A)\simeq D^b_{ctf}(X,A)$ (the categories of
[def-trf-coefficient-conventions]), with inverse $Rr_*=Rr_!$ and
invertible unit and counit. This includes reduction.

## Proof

Base change $V\mapsto V\times_YX$ is an equivalence of the small étale
categories, natural in the scheme and compatible with identities and
composites, and it preserves and reflects jointly surjective families,
because the underlying map of $r$ and of every base change of $r$ is a
homeomorphism. Its inverse functors are $r^{-1}$ and $r_*$, so the two
categories of étale sheaves are equivalent, with $r^{-1}$ exact and
$r_*$ its quasi-inverse. Exactness carries an injective resolution to an
injective resolution, which gives the compatibility with cohomology and
hence the statement on derived categories. Constructibility and finite
Tor amplitude are preserved on both sides, so the equivalence restricts to
$D^b_{ctf}$; $Rr_*=Rr_!$ because $r$ is finite, hence proper, by
[prop-functor-package]. A reduction is a finite universal homeomorphism, so the
reduction clause is a special case.

Uses: [def-trf-coefficient-conventions], [prop-functor-package]

Every smooth curve which is geometrically a connected curve has a nonempty dense affine
open whose complement is finite over the base field.

## Proof

Let $C_0$ be a smooth curve over $k_0$ which is geometrically a
connected curve. By
[lem-sc-compactification] there is a proper smooth curve
$\overline C$ and a dense open immersion $C_0\hookrightarrow\overline C$
with finite complement $S=\overline C\setminus C_0$. If
$S\neq\emptyset$, choose any closed point $s\in S$ and another
closed point $t\in\overline C\setminus\{s\}$ (a positive-dimensional
scheme of finite type over a finite field has infinitely many closed
points); put $V_0:=\overline C\setminus(S\cup\{t\})$, which is a dense
open of $C_0$ with nonempty complement in $\overline C$, hence
affine by [lem-sc-affine-open-proper] (its complement in the
proper smooth curve is a nonempty finite set). If $S=\emptyset$, i.e. $C_0=\overline C$ is proper, any closed point $s'\in C_0$ gives
$V_0:=C_0\setminus\{s'\}$ a dense open, again nonempty-complemented
and hence affine by the same lemma. In both cases $V_0$ is a
nonempty dense affine open of $C_0$ with finite complement.

attrs.title: Affine core of a smooth curve

objects.body:
Let $U_0$ be a smooth geometrically connected affine curve and let
$\mathcal F$ be a lisse Weil sheaf
on $U_0$. Then, in the
compactly supported
cohomology of [def-weil-ordinary-compact-cohomology],
$H_c^0(U,\mathcal F)=0$.

## Proof

A class in $H_c^0$ is a global section of $\mathcal F$ whose support
is proper over the base field. By lissity in
[def-weil-pbc-constructible-complexes], a global section of
$\mathcal F$ is locally constant, so on the connected curve it is
determined by its value at one geometric point: a section vanishing at
one point is zero; consequently the support of a nonzero global lisse
section is all of $U$, which is not proper. Hence only the zero
section has compact support, and $H_c^0=0$.

attrs.title: Vanishing of $H_c^0$ on a nonproper curve

objects.body:
Let $U_0$ be a smooth geometrically connected affine curve, let
$U=U_0\times_{k_0}k$, and let $\mathcal F$ be a lisse Weil sheaf on
$U_0$ with local generic fiber $V=\mathcal F_{\bar\eta}$ (a
geometric generic stalk of [def-wf-fundamental-representation]).
In the compactly
supported cohomology of
[def-weil-ordinary-compact-cohomology] there is a canonical
Frobenius-equivariant isomorphism

$$
H_c^2(U,\mathcal F)\;\simeq\;V_{\pi_1(U)}(-1),
$$

where the coinvariants are formed for the geometric monodromy action of
[def-wf-monodromy-data] and $(-1)$ is the
Tate twist $(-1)$.

## Proof

We work through a smooth compactification (global Verdier duality
would also apply directly on $U$, which need not be proper, but the
argument below only needs it on $\bar C$). By [lem-wf-curve-normal-smooth-compactification]
there are a smooth projective geometrically connected curve $\bar C_0$
over $k_0$ and a dense open immersion $j_0:U_0\hookrightarrow\bar C_0$
with finite boundary; put $\bar C=\bar C_0\times_{k_0}k$, let
$j:U\hookrightarrow\bar C$ be the base change of $j_0$, and let
$a_U=a_{\bar C}\circ j$ be the structure morphisms. Then $\bar C_0$
satisfies the hypotheses of the Poincare duality conventions of
[def-pod-conventions] with $d=1$, and we use its canonical orientation
$\eta_{\bar C}:\omega_{\bar C}\xrightarrow{\sim}E_{\bar C}(1)[2]$.

*Step 1 (compact support through $\bar C$).* For the open immersion
$j$ the identity of $\bar C$ is a compactification, so the compact-support
direct image of [def-compact-support-direct-image-detailed] is
$Rj_!=j_!$, the extension by zero of [def-weil-extension-by-zero]. The
composition law for compact-support direct images ([fix-lem-exchanges])
gives $Ra_{U!}\mathcal F\simeq Ra_{\bar C!}\,j_!\mathcal F$, hence, by
[def-weil-ordinary-compact-cohomology],

$$
R\Gamma_c(U,\mathcal F)\simeq R\Gamma_c(\bar C,j_!\mathcal F),
$$

where $j_!\mathcal F$ is a constructible (not lisse) sheaf on the proper
curve $\bar C$.

*Step 2 (duality on $\bar C$).* Apply [thm-pod-global-verdier-duality]
on the proper $\bar C$ to $K=j_!\mathcal F$, which that theorem allows
since it is stated for every $K\in D^b_{ctf}(\bar C,\Lambda)$:

$$
R\Gamma_c(\bar C,j_!\mathcal F)^\vee\simeq
R\Gamma\bigl(\bar C,\mathbb D_{\bar C}(j_!\mathcal F)\bigr).
$$

The Verdier-duality exchange [fix-cor-verdier-exchange] for $f=j$ gives
$\mathbb D_{\bar C}(j_!\mathcal F)\simeq Rj_*\mathbb D_U\mathcal F$
with $\mathbb D_U=R\mathcal Hom(-,\omega_U)$ and
$\omega_U\simeq Rj^!\omega_{\bar C}$ (step 1 of its proof). For an open
immersion the right adjoint of $j_!$ is $j^*$
([prop-exc-open-adjoint]), so $\omega_U\simeq j^*\omega_{\bar C}$, and
$j^*\eta_{\bar C}$ gives $\omega_U\simeq E_U(1)[2]$. As $\mathcal F$ is
lisse, $R\mathcal Hom(\mathcal F,E_U)=\mathcal F^\vee$, so
$\mathbb D_U\mathcal F\simeq\mathcal F^\vee(1)[2]$. Finally
$Ra_{\bar C*}Rj_*\simeq Ra_{U*}$ by the composition isomorphism
[lem-weil-derived-direct-image-composition] for $a_U=a_{\bar C}\circ j$,
which applies because $Rj_*\mathbb D_U\mathcal F\simeq
\mathbb D_{\bar C}(j_!\mathcal F)$ is constructible. Hence

$$
R\Gamma_c(U,\mathcal F)^\vee\simeq
R\Gamma\bigl(U,\mathcal F^\vee(1)\bigr)[2].
$$

*Step 3 (degree $-2$).* Taking $H^{-2}$ (over the field $E$ or $\Qlb$
dualizing commutes with cohomology) gives
$H_c^2(U,\mathcal F)^\vee\simeq H^0(U,\mathcal F^\vee(1))$. Global
sections of a lisse sheaf are the invariants of the geometric
representation of [def-wf-fundamental-representation] [p-real-sections],
so $H^0(U,\mathcal F^\vee(1))=(V^\vee(1))^{\pi_1(U)}$, the geometric
monodromy action being that of [def-wf-monodromy-data]. Dualizing turns
invariants of $V^\vee$ into coinvariants of $V$, and turns the twist
$(1)$ into $(-1)$, which gives the displayed isomorphism. All maps above
are canonical and $\bar C$, $j$, $\eta_{\bar C}$ are base changed from
$k_0$, so the isomorphism commutes with the Frobenius operators induced
by the Weil structures, with the twist normalized as in
[def-wf-tate-twist].

attrs.title: Description of $H_c^2$ on an affine curve

objects.body:
Let $U_0$ be a smooth geometrically connected affine curve and let
$\mathcal F$ be a lisse Weil sheaf on $U_0$ which is punctually
$\iota$-pure of weight $w$. Then $H_c^2(U,\mathcal F)$, with its
Frobenius, is $\iota$-pure of weight $w+2$ in the sense of
[def-weil-frobenius-module-weights] (the zero module being pure of
every weight).

## Proof

By [lem-a1-affine-hc2] there is a canonical Frobenius-equivariant
isomorphism $H_c^2(U,\mathcal F)\simeq W(-1)$, where
$W=V_{\pi_1(U)}$ is the coinvariant quotient of the geometric generic
stalk $V=\mathcal F_{\bar\eta}$ under the geometric fundamental group.

*The coinvariants are pure of weight $w$.* The curve $U_0$ is smooth
and geometrically connected, in particular nonempty, so
[lem-a1-geometric-coinvariants-pure] shows that $W$ with its induced
Frobenius $F_W$, the Frobenius of the coinvariants in
[lem-a1-affine-hc2], is $\iota$-pure of weight $w$.

*The twist.* By [lem-wf-tate-twist-frobenius] the geometric Frobenius
acts on the twist $\Qlb(-1)$ by multiplication by $q$, so the Frobenius
of $W(-1)$ is $qF_W$, whose eigenvalues $q\lambda$ have
$\iota$-modulus $q\cdot q^{w/2}=q^{(w+2)/2}$. Hence
$H_c^2(U,\mathcal F)\simeq W(-1)$ is $\iota$-pure of weight $w+2$.

attrs.title: Purity of $H_c^2$ on an affine curve

objects.body:
Let $\psi=\Psi\circ\operatorname{Tr}$ be the additive character of
[def-fd-additive-character], with $\Psi:\mathbf F_p\to\Qlb^\times$ the fixed
nontrivial character, let $k_1\subseteq k$ be a finite
field, and let $a\in k_1^\times$. Let
$\mathcal L_{\psi(ax)}:=\mathcal L_{\psi,ax}$ be the Artin–Schreier
sheaf of [def-fd-artin-schreier-sheaf] on
$\mathbf A^1_{k_1}=\operatorname{Spec}k_1[x]$ for $f=ax$; explicitly, it is the
$\Psi$-isotypic part

$$
\mathcal L_{\psi(ax)}=e_\Psi\cdot\pi_*\Qlb,\qquad
e_\Psi=\frac1p\sum_{c\in\mathbf F_p}\Psi(-c)\,\sigma_c,
$$

for the Artin–Schreier cover
$\pi:Y=\operatorname{Spec}k_1[x][u]/(u^p-u-ax)\to\mathbf A^1_{k_1}$
with $\mathbf F_p$-action $\sigma_c:u\mapsto u+c$. Then
$\mathcal L_{\psi(ax)}$ is lisse of rank one and ramified at infinity
in the sense of [rem-dl-a1-conventions]: the inertia group $I_\infty$
at $\infty\in\mathbf P^1_k$ acts on its geometric generic stalk through
a character of exact order $p$.

## Proof

By [lem-fd-as-cover], $\pi$ is finite etale of degree $p$ with
automorphism group $\mathbf F_p$ acting by $\sigma_c$, and by
[lem-fd-as-characters] its $\Psi$-isotypic part is lisse of rank one.

Let $R$ be the strict henselization of $\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^1_k,\infty}$,
with residue field $k$, uniformizer $t=1/x$ and fraction field $K$;
let $\overline K$ be an algebraic closure. Since $k$ is algebraically
closed, the inertia group of [d-real-boundary] at $\infty$ is
$I_\infty=\operatorname{Gal}(\overline K/K)$, acting on the geometric
generic stalk at $\operatorname{Spec}\overline K\to\mathbf A^1$.

*The stalk.* Over $\operatorname{Spec}\overline K$ the fibre of $\pi$ is
the set $\mathcal R$ of roots of $u^p-u=a/t$ in $\overline K$; it has
$p$ elements (the derivative is $-1$) and is a torsor under
$\mathbf F_p$ by translation. By [lemma-weil-pbc-finite-stalk-formula],
$(\pi_*\Qlb)_{\bar\eta}$ is the space of functions
$\mathcal R\to\Qlb$, with $\sigma_c$ and $g\in I_\infty$ acting
through their actions on $\mathcal R$. Fix $u_0\in\mathcal R$ and write
$g(u_0)=u_0+\kappa(g)$ with $\kappa(g)\in\mathbf F_p$. Since $g$ fixes
$\mathbf F_p$, $g(u_0+c)=u_0+c+\kappa(g)$, so $g$ acts on $\mathcal R$
as the translation by $\kappa(g)$, and $\kappa$ is a homomorphism.
Hence $g$ acts on $(\pi_*\Qlb)_{\bar\eta}$ as $\sigma_{\pm\kappa(g)}$
(the sign is fixed by the convention for the induced action on
functions). From $\sigma_be_\Psi=\Psi(b)e_\Psi$ it follows that $g$
acts on the line $(\mathcal L_{\psi(ax)})_{\bar\eta}$ by the scalar
$\Psi(\pm\kappa(g))$.
