*The cover is totally ramified.* Put $L=K(u_0)$, so $[L:K]\leq p$.
Since $K$ is henselian, its valuation extends uniquely to $L$; let
$v_L$ be the extension normalized with value group $\mathbf Z$, and
put $e=v_L(t)\geq1$, so $e\leq[L:K]$. As $a$ is a unit,
$v_L(a/t)=-e<0$. If $v_L(u_0)\geq0$ then $v_L(u_0^p-u_0)\geq0$, a
contradiction; so $v_L(u_0)<0$, whence $v_L(u_0^p)<v_L(u_0)$ and
$p\,v_L(u_0)=v_L(u_0^p-u_0)=-e$. Thus $p\mid e$, and
$e\leq[L:K]\leq p$ forces $e=[L:K]=p$. In particular
$u_0\notin K$, so some $g\in I_\infty$ moves $u_0$, and $\kappa$ is
surjective onto $\mathbf F_p$.

*Conclusion.* The nontrivial character $\Psi$ of the group
$\mathbf F_p$ of prime order is injective, so
$g\mapsto\Psi(\pm\kappa(g))$ is a character of $I_\infty$ of exact
order $p$. Inertia at infinity therefore acts nontrivially on the
geometric generic stalk: $\mathcal L_{\psi(ax)}$ is ramified at
infinity.

attrs.title: Linear Artin–Schreier sheaves are ramified at infinity

objects.body:
Let $j:U_0\hookrightarrow\mathbf A^1_{k_0}$ be a dense open immersion
and let $\mathcal M$ be a nonzero irreducible lisse Weil sheaf on
$U_0$.

1. If $\mathcal M$ is constituent-nonexceptional in the sense of
[def-a1-constituent-nonexceptional], then its middle extension
$j_*\mathcal M$ is Fourier-nonexceptional in the sense of
[def-fd-nonexceptional].
2. If moreover the geometric fundamental representation of
$\mathcal M$ is irreducible, the converse holds: the two notions then
coincide.

## Proof

First translate [def-fd-nonexceptional] into a condition on $U$.
Over $k$, the middle extension of [def-wf-middle-extension]
satisfies $j^*j_*\mathcal M=\mathcal M$. Conversely, if $\mathcal L$ is a
lisse sheaf on $\mathbf A^1_k$ (a constant sheaf, or some
$\mathcal L_{\psi(ax)}$), then $j_*(\mathcal L|_U)=\mathcal L$, because
the stalks of the ordinary direct image at the missing points are the
inertia invariants, and inertia acts trivially on a sheaf that is lisse
there. Geometrically, a constant Weil twist of
[def-wf-constant-weil-twist] becomes the constant sheaf. Hence
$j_*\mathcal M$ is Fourier-exceptional exactly when
$\mathcal M_{\bar k}$ is a constant sheaf or is isomorphic to
$\mathcal L_{\psi(ax)}|_U$ for some $a$.

(1) Suppose $j_*\mathcal M$ is Fourier-exceptional. If
$\mathcal M_{\bar k}$ is constant, it is nonzero, and every geometric
irreducible constituent is the trivial rank-one sheaf
$\mathcal L_{\psi(0\cdot x)}|_U$. If
$\mathcal M_{\bar k}\cong\mathcal L_{\psi(ax)}|_U$, this rank-one sheaf
is its only geometric constituent. In both cases $\mathcal M$ is not
constituent-nonexceptional.

(2) If the geometric fundamental representation $V$ is irreducible,
then $V$ is the only geometric irreducible constituent. If it is
isomorphic to $\mathcal L_{\psi(ax)}|_U$, then
$\mathcal M_{\bar k}\cong\mathcal L_{\psi(ax)}|_U$. For $a=0$ this sheaf
is constant, and for $a\ne0$ it is an Artin–Schreier restriction. In
either case $j_*\mathcal M$ is Fourier-exceptional by the translation
above.

Without geometric irreducibility, the converse of (1) is not asserted.
Fourier-nonexceptionality looks at the whole geometric sheaf, while
constituent-nonexceptionality looks at each geometric constituent.

If $C_0$ is a smooth affine curve and $\mathcal F$ is lisse and
punctually $\iota$-pure of weight $w$, then
$H_c^2(C,\mathcal F)$ has weights at most $w+2$.

## Proof

The coinvariant description [lem-a1-affine-hc2] realizes the group
as a quotient of the local generic fiber $V=\mathcal F_{\bar\eta}$
followed by the twist $(-1)$. The quotient does not increase weights
by [lem-a1-subquotient-extension-bounds] (every eigenvalue of a
quotient is an eigenvalue of the pure module $V$ of weight $w$), and
the twist $(-1)$ in [lem-tw-tate-twist-weight-shift] raises
weights by two, giving weights at most $w+2$.

attrs.title: Top compact-support bound on a curve

objects.body:
Let $\mathcal E$ be either a rank-one constant
Weil sheaf or its tensor product
with an Artin–Schreier sheaf
$\mathcal L_{\psi,ax}$ for some $a\in k_0^\times$. If $\mathcal E$
is punctually $\iota$-pure of weight $w$ on a dense open
$U_0\hookrightarrow\mathbf A^1_{k_0}$, then the compactly supported
cohomology groups $H_c^i(U,\mathcal E)$ have weights at most $w+i$
for every $i$.

## Proof

Let $j:U_0\hookrightarrow\mathbf A^1_{k_0}$ be the given dense open
immersion with finite closed complement $i:Z\hookrightarrow\mathbf A^1$,
and let $\mathcal E_0$ be the lisse extension of $\mathcal E$ to the
line: $\mathcal E_0=\mathcal B_b\otimes\mathcal L_{\psi,ax}$ (a rank-one
lisse $\Qlb$-sheaf on $\mathbf A^1_{k_0}$, since both factors are
lisse there — the linear phase $ax$ has no pole on the line —
with the constant [def-wf-constant-weil-twist] of the Weil twist
$\mathcal B_b$ and
the convention $\mathcal L_{\psi,0}=1$), so that
$j_*\mathcal E=\mathcal E_0$ and $i^*j_*\mathcal E= i^*\mathcal E_0$.

Step 1 (the cohomology of the line). The compactly supported cohomology
of $\mathcal E_0$ on the affine line is concentrated in degree $2$
for $a=0$ and vanishes altogether for $a\neq0$. Both cases use the
degreewise Poincare duality [thm-pod-degreewise-perfectness-over-a-field]
of the Poincare-duality chapter for the smooth, separated (not proper)
curve $\mathbf A^1_{k_0}$, of dimension $d=1$, at the field stage
$\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$: the lisse rank-one sheaf $\mathcal E_0$ is
perfect ([def-pod-perfect-complex-on-x]), so
$H_c^i(\mathbf A^1,\mathcal E_0)^\vee\cong
H^{2-i}(\mathbf A^1,\mathcal E_0^\vee(1))$. For $a\neq0$, the coefficient
dual is $\mathcal E_0^\vee=\mathcal B_b^{-1}\otimes\mathcal L_{\psi,-ax}$
([lem-fd-as-lisse]); over $\mathbf A^1_k$ the constant factor
$\mathcal B_b^{-1}$ is geometrically trivial (it only rescales the
Frobenius eigenvalues by a constant, [lem-wf-constant-twist-weight]),
so the ordinary cohomology of $\mathcal E_0^\vee$ is that of
$\mathcal L_{\psi,-ax}$ and vanishes by
[lem-fd-cohomology-affine-line-character], $-a\neq0$; hence all
$H_c^i(\mathbf A^1,\mathcal E_0)$ vanish. For $a=0$,
$j_*\mathcal E=\mathcal E_0= \mathcal B_b$ is lisse and constant;
for the constant sheaf, $H^j(\mathbf A^1,\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell)$ is
$\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ for $j=0$ and zero otherwise
([lem-fd-affine-line-constant-cohomology]), so the duality leaves only
$H^2_c(\mathbf A^1,\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell)$, one-dimensional, and the
Frobenius similitude of [cor-pod-untwisted-similitude],
$\langle Fx,Fy\rangle_2=q\langle x,y\rangle_2$ with $y=1\in H^0$ fixed by
$F$, shows that $F$ acts on it by $q$:
$R\Gamma_c(\mathbf A^1,\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell)\cong
\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell(-1)[-2]$. Tensoring with the constant twist gives
$H_c^0=H_c^1=0$ and $H_c^2=\mathcal B_b(-1)$ with weights
$w+2$ by the weight-shift and constant-twist rules. Hence, in all
cases, $H_c^i(\mathbf A^1,\mathcal E_0)=0$ for $i\neq0,2$ and
$H_c^2(\mathbf A^1,\mathcal E_0)$ has weights at most $w+2$.

Step 2 (the boundary). The boundary sheaf $B=i^*\mathcal E_0$ is
supported on the finite set $Z$ and has weights at most $w$: at a
point $z\in Z$ the stalk is the stalk of the lisse rank-one
$\mathcal E_0$, whose Frobenius eigenvalue has modulus
$q_z^{w/2}$ (the twist-scaled root of unity, weights by
[lem-fd-as-purity] and [lem-wf-constant-twist-weight]). By
the finite-boundary computation [lem-a1-finite-boundary-cohomology],
$H_c^r(Z,B)=0$ for $r\neq0$, and $H_c^0(Z,B)$ has weights at most
$w$ by [lem-a1-finite-boundary-weights].

Step 3 (the localization sequence). The open–closed recollement
triangle of [def-weil-open-closed-recollement] (at $\Qlb$ for Weil sheaves, [prop-sf-open-closed-triangle-all-stages]), applied with
$K=j_*\mathcal E=\mathcal E_0$ and the extension-by-zero functor
[def-weil-extension-by-zero] of the framework chapter, gives the exact
sequence

$$
H_c^0(Z,B)\longrightarrow H_c^1(U,\mathcal E)\longrightarrow
H_c^1(\mathbf A^1,\mathcal E_0)\longrightarrow H_c^1(Z,B)=0,
$$

and $H_c^0(U,\mathcal E)=0$ (it injects into $H_c^0(\mathbf A^1, \mathcal E_0)=0$). Hence $H_c^1(U,\mathcal E)$ is a quotient of the
weight-$w$ group $H_c^0(Z,B)$ and has weights at most $w$ (in
particular at most $w+1$); the group $H_c^2(U,\mathcal E)$ is a
subobject of $H_c^2(\mathbf A^1,\mathcal E_0)$, of weights at most
$w+2$ by the subquotient bound of
[lem-a1-subquotient-extension-bounds]. This is the asserted bound
$w+i$ for $i=0,1,2$; the degrees outside $\{0,1,2\}$ have no
cohomology (the compact-support range of
[lem-zl-affine-curve-range] of this chapter, or directly from the
concentration of the two terms of the triangle).

Let $0\to V'\to V\to V''\to 0$ be an exact sequence of Frobenius
modules. If $V'$ and $V''$ are mixed of weights at most $w$, then
$V$ is mixed of weights at most $w$.

## Proof

Choose the Frobenius-stable filtrations of $V'$ and $V''$ given by
[def-weil-frobenius-module-weights] (of weights at most $w$);
pull back the filtration of $V''$ along the projection
$V\to V''$ and splice it after the filtration of $V'$. The graded
pieces are the graded pieces of $V'$ and the graded pieces of
$V''$, so all their weights are at most $w$; by
[def-weil-frobenius-module-weights] the module $V$ is mixed of
weights at most $w$.

Let $Z_0$ be finite over $k_0$ and let $\mathcal G$ be a
constructible Weil sheaf whose stalks have weights at most $w$. Then
$H_c^r(Z,\mathcal G)=0$ for $r\neq0$.

## Proof

After geometric base change a finite scheme is a finite discrete space:
its cohomology is concentrated in degree zero, and the higher
compact-support groups of [def-weil-ordinary-compact-cohomology]
vanish since the scheme is zero-dimensional.

Let $Z_0$ be finite over $k_0$ and let $\mathcal G$ be a
constructible Weil sheaf whose stalks have weights at most $w$. Then
$H_c^0(Z,\mathcal G)$ has weights at most $w$.

## Proof

Evaluation at geometric points gives, as in the proof of
[lem-a1-finite-boundary-cohomology],

$$
H_c^0(Z,\mathcal G)=\bigoplus_{x\in|Z_0|}\mathcal G_{\bar x}^{
\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{\kappa(x)}/\kappa(x))},
$$

and each summand is an
$F_x$-stable submodule of the stalk $\mathcal G_{\bar x}$, whose
eigenvalues are among the eigenvalues of $F_x$ ([p-linear-filtration]): all of them have
weight at most $w$ by hypothesis, so the submodule is mixed of
weights at most $w$ by [lem-a1-punctual-bound-module-mixed].

attrs.title: Weights of the cohomology of a finite boundary

objects.body:
Let $C_0$ be a smooth geometrically connected curve and let
$\mathcal F$ be a lisse Weil sheaf
on $C_0$ (lisse in the sense of
[def-weil-pbc-constructible-complexes]). Then
$\mathcal F$ has finite length in the category of lisse Weil sheaves:
there is a finite Frobenius-stable filtration

$$
0=\mathcal F_0\subset\mathcal F_1\subset\cdots\subset\mathcal F_m=\mathcal F
$$

with each graded piece $\mathcal F_r/\mathcal F_{r-1}$ irreducible
(with respect to the Weil-sheaf structure).

## Proof

Every nonzero lisse Weil sheaf has a nonzero lisse Weil subsheaf:
if it is not irreducible, it admits a nonzero proper Weil subsheaf, and
a Weil subsheaf of a lisse sheaf on the connected curve with the
induced Frobenius structure. The rank strictly decreases, so induction
on the rank terminates, giving the filtration with irreducible graded
pieces.

attrs.title: Finite length of a lisse Weil sheaf on a curve

objects.body:
For a finite map $g:C_0\to\mathbf A^1_{k_0}$ of separated finite-type
$k_0$-schemes and a lisse Weil sheaf $\mathcal F$ on $C_0$,

$$
H_c^i(C,\mathcal F)\simeq H_c^i(\mathbf A^1,g_*\mathcal F)
$$

for every $i$.

## Proof

A finite morphism is proper, so $Rg_!=Rg_*$ by the properness law of
[prop-functor-package], and $g_*$ is exact by the finite-direct-
image exactness [lemma-weil-pbc-finite-direct-image-exact]: hence

$$
R\Gamma_c(C,\mathcal F)=Ra_{!}Rg_!\mathcal F\simeq Ra_{!}g_*\mathcal F
=R\Gamma_c(\mathbf A^1,g_*\mathcal F)
$$

(the compact-support composition of [prop-functor-package]), and
taking cohomology gives the displayed identification degreewise.

attrs.title: Cohomology under a finite curve map

objects.body:
Let $C_0$ be a smooth affine curve which is geometrically a connected
curve. There is a smooth curve $C'_0$, geometrically a connected curve, containing $C_0$ as a
dense open with finite complement, and a finite generically etale
morphism $g:C'_0\to\mathbf A^1_{k_0}$.

## Proof

Take the smooth projective completion $\overline C$ of
[lem-sc-compactification], and choose a closed point
$s\in\overline C\setminus C_0$. Such a point exists because a
positive-dimensional proper curve is not affine.
It is an effective Cartier divisor by [lem-sc-point-cartier];
write $d_s=[\kappa(s):k_0]$, without assuming $d_s=1$.
Choose an integer $m$ prime to the characteristic and large enough
that $(m-1)d_s>2g(\overline C)-2$.
Riemann–Roch, [lem-sc-riemann-roch], gives

$$
h^0(\overline C,\mathcal O(ms))-
h^0(\overline C,\mathcal O((m-1)s))=d_s>0.
$$

Choose a function $f$ in the difference. It has its only pole at
$s$, of order exactly $m$.
The sections $1,f$ of $\mathcal O(ms)$ have no common zero:
away from $s$ the first generates, and at $s$ the second generates
because its pole has exactly the allowed order.
They define $h:\overline C\to\mathbf P^1$ with
$h^{-1}(\infty)=\{s\}$.
This map is proper and has finite fibres, so it is finite by
[thm-pqf-finite-iff-proper-finite-fibres].

It is also generically etale. Over the perfect field $k_0$, the
kernel of the differential on the one-variable function field is
$k_0(\overline C)^p$ in characteristic $p$.
A $p$-th power has valuation divisible by $p$ at every point,
whereas $\operatorname{ord}_s(f)=-m$ is not divisible by $p$.
Thus $df\neq0$, which makes the finite function-field extension
$k_0(\overline C)/k_0(f)$ separable.
Set $C'_0=\overline C\setminus\{s\}$.
The restriction $g:C'_0\to\mathbf A^1$ is finite by the base-change
stability in [lem-weil-pbc-finite-pullback-identities],
and it remains generically etale.
Since $s$ lies outside $C_0$, this $C'_0$ contains $C_0$
with finite complement.

attrs.title: Finite map to the affine line

objects.body:
If $g$ is finite etale and $\mathcal F$ is punctually $\iota$-pure
of weight $w$, then $g_*\mathcal F$ is punctually $\iota$-pure of
weight $w$.

## Proof

Fix a closed point $y$ of the target.
By [lemma-weil-pbc-finite-stalk-formula], the geometric stalk of
the direct image is the direct sum over all geometric points above
$\bar y$. A closed point $x$ above $y$, of residue degree
$e=[\kappa(x):\kappa(y)]$, contributes a Frobenius cycle of
$e$ copies of $\mathcal F_{\bar x}$.
The $e$-th power of $F_y$ on each copy is $F_x$.
Consequently every eigenvalue $\lambda$ of $F_y$ on this cycle
satisfies $\lambda^e=\alpha$ for an eigenvalue $\alpha$ of $F_x$.
Purity in [def-weil-punctual-weights] gives

$$
|\iota(\lambda)|^e=|\iota(\alpha)|
=q_x^{w/2}=q_y^{ew/2},
$$

so $|\iota(\lambda)|=q_y^{w/2}$.
All cycles have this property, proving purity of the pushforward.

Let $U_0$ be a nonempty smooth geometrically connected curve over
$k_0=\mathbf F_q$, and let $\mathcal F$ be a lisse Weil sheaf on $U_0$
which is punctually $\iota$-pure of weight $w$. For its geometric
fundamental representation $V$ ([def-wf-fundamental-representation]),
the coinvariant quotient $W=V_{\pi_1(U)}$ — the maximal geometrically
constant quotient of $\mathcal F$ — with its induced Frobenius $F_W$ is
$\iota$-pure of weight $w$ (possibly $W=0$).

## Proof

The geometric subgroup $\pi_1(U)$ of the Weil group of
[def-wf-fundamental-representation] is normal, so the subspace of $V$
spanned by the vectors $gv-v$, $g\in\pi_1(U)$, is stable under the Weil
group and $V\twoheadrightarrow W$ is a quotient Weil representation. On
$W$ the geometric subgroup acts trivially, so the action of any element
of degree one of the Weil group on $W$ is a single operator $F_W$,
independent of the chosen lift; an element of degree $d$ acts by
$F_W^d$.

Choose a closed point $x\in U_0$ (a maximal ideal of the coordinate
ring of a nonempty affine open; its residue field is finite over
$\mathbf F_q$) and put $d=[\kappa(x):\mathbf F_q]$. A local Frobenius
at $x$ is an element of degree $d$ of the Weil group, and under the
identification of $V$ with the stalk $\mathcal F_{\bar x}$ it acts as
the operator $F_x$ of [def-weil-punctual-weights]. Hence
$V\twoheadrightarrow W$ is an $F_x$-equivariant quotient onto
$(W,F_W^d)$. In a basis of $V$ extending a basis of the kernel, the
matrix of $F_x$ is block upper triangular ([p-linear-filtration]), so
every eigenvalue of $F_W^d$ is an eigenvalue of $F_x$ on
$\mathcal F_{\bar x}$, and has $\iota$-modulus
$|\kappa(x)|^{w/2}=q^{dw/2}$ by punctual purity
([def-weil-punctual-weights]). If $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of $F_W$,
then $\lambda^d$ is an eigenvalue of $F_W^d$, so
$|\iota(\lambda)|^d=q^{dw/2}$ and $|\iota(\lambda)|=q^{w/2}$. Thus
$(W,F_W)$ is $\iota$-pure of weight $w$ in the sense of
[def-weil-frobenius-module-weights].

Let $\mathcal F$ be a punctually pure lisse Weil sheaf of weight $w$
on a smooth geometrically connected curve over a finite field.
After a finite constant-field extension, it admits a finite filtration
by Weil subsheaves whose nonzero graded pieces are geometrically
irreducible and punctually pure of weight $w$.

## Proof

By [lem-a1-finite-length], [lem-a1-subquotient-pure], it is enough
to handle an irreducible Weil representation $V$, all resulting
subquotients retaining purity.
Its restriction to the normal geometric subgroup
$\Pi$ of [def-wf-weil-group] is semisimple by
[lem-mg-normal-restriction-semisimple].
A Frobenius lift permutes its finitely many geometric isotypic
components. Choose $m>0$ killing this permutation.
The subgroup generated by $\Pi$ and that Frobenius lift to the
$m$-th power is the Weil group after the constant extension of
degree $m$, by [lem-wf-weil-group-constant-extension].
Restriction to this finite-index normal subgroup is semisimple by
[lem-wf-finite-index-restriction-semisimple].
Every irreducible summand is now geometrically isotypic, say
$S\otimes E$, with $S$ geometrically irreducible and $\Pi$
acting trivially on the multiplicity space $E$.
Choose an intertwiner $T$ on $S$ for the Frobenius conjugation.
Schur's lemma makes the Frobenius operator on $S\otimes E$ equal
to $T\otimes B$ for an invertible operator $B$ on $E$.
Over the algebraically closed coefficient field $B$ has an
eigenline. Its tensor with $S$ is a nonzero Weil-stable subspace;
irreducibility forces $\dim E=1$.
Thus each summand is geometrically irreducible.
Take a common multiple of the finitely many extension degrees for
the original composition factors and refine the original filtration.
Purity of all its pieces follows again from
[lem-a1-subquotient-pure].

attrs.title: Geometrically irreducible constituents after a constant extension

objects.body:
If $\mathcal F$ is lisse on a smooth curve $C_0$ and
$j:U_0\hookrightarrow C_0$ is dense, then the adjunction map

$$
\mathcal F\xrightarrow{\sim}j_*j^*\mathcal F
$$

is an isomorphism.

## Proof

The assertion is clear on $U_0$. At a removed point, lissity on
$C_0$ makes the local inertia action trivial, so the invariant-stalk
formula of [lem-wf-boundary-stalk-invariants] identifies the
target stalk with the original stalk: $(j_*j^*\mathcal F)_{\bar x}= ((j^*\mathcal F)_{\bar\eta})^{I_x}=(\mathcal F_{\bar x})^{I_x}= \mathcal F_{\bar x}$, the last equality because $I_x$ acts trivially
on the stalk of a lisse sheaf. The map is the naturality of the
adjunction at every geometric point, hence an isomorphism.

attrs.title: Recovery from a dense lisse open

objects.body:
In the conventions of [rem-dl-a1-conventions], let
$j:U_0\hookrightarrow C_0$ be a dense open immersion of smooth
curves over $k_0$, let $i:Z_0\hookrightarrow C_0$ be the closed
complement with its reduced structure, and let $F$ be a lisse
$\Qlb$-Weil sheaf on $U_0$, with dual $F^\vee$. Put
$A(F)=i^*Rj_*F$ on $Z$. Then there is a canonical
Frobenius-equivariant isomorphism

$$
\mathbb D_Z A(F)\;\simeq\;A(F^\vee)(1)[1].
$$

Consequently, for every missing closed point $s\in Z_0$, with
geometric point $\bar s$ and local geometric Frobenius $F_s$, there is
a canonical perfect $F_s$-equivariant pairing

$$
(j_*F^\vee)_{\bar s}\otimes(R^1j_*F)_{\bar s}
\longrightarrow\Qlb(-1),
$$

equivalently an isomorphism
$(R^1j_*F)_{\bar s}^\vee\simeq(j_*F^\vee)_{\bar s}(1)$. Here
$j_*$ is the ordinary direct image.

## Proof

Work on the geometric curves with $\Qlb$-coefficients and the Weil
structures of [lem-fix-weil-operations]. The Verdier duals, their
biduality, the exceptional functors $Ri^!$ of
[def-weil-exceptional-inverse-image] with $Ri_!=Ri_*\dashv Ri^!$,
and the identity $Rf^!=\mathbb D_Xf^*\mathbb D_Y$ are those of
[thm-coef-qbar-verdier]. Smooth purity
[thm-pur-rational-and-qbar-purity] for the structure map of $U$
gives $\omega_U\simeq\Qlb(1)[2]$, hence, $F$ being lisse,
$\mathbb D_UF\simeq F^\vee(1)[2]$ (the dual of a lisse sheaf is the
finite-rank coefficient dual; see [def-wf-tate-twist] for the twist).

*Step 1: $\mathbb D_CRj_*\simeq j_!\mathbb D_U$.* The exchange
[fix-cor-verdier-exchange] for $f=j$ gives
$\mathbb D_C(j_!M)\simeq Rj_*\mathbb D_UM$. Put
$M=\mathbb D_UG$ for a constructible $G$ on $U$; biduality on $U$
gives $Rj_*G\simeq\mathbb D_Cj_!\mathbb D_UG$. In particular
$Rj_*G$ is bounded constructible, and applying $\mathbb D_C$ and
biduality on $C$ gives $\mathbb D_CRj_*G\simeq j_!\mathbb D_UG$.

*Step 2: $\mathbb D_Zi^*\simeq Ri^!\mathbb D_C$.* By
[thm-coef-qbar-verdier], $Ri^!=\mathbb D_Zi^*\mathbb D_C$, so
biduality on $C$ gives
$Ri^!\mathbb D_CK\simeq\mathbb D_Zi^*K$ for constructible $K$.

*Step 3: $Ri^!j_!G\simeq i^*Rj_*G[-1]$.* First
$Ri^!Rj_*G=0$: for every $N$ on $Z$,

$$
\operatorname{Hom}(N,Ri^!Rj_*G)
\cong\operatorname{Hom}(i_*N,Rj_*G)
\cong\operatorname{Hom}(j^*i_*N,G)=0,
$$

since $j^*i_*=0$, and Yoneda applies. Next, the open–closed
recollement triangle ([def-weil-open-closed-recollement]), which exists at $\Qlb$ with Weil-equivariant arrows by [prop-sf-open-closed-triangle-all-stages] (at a finite stage it is [lem-cbc-open-closed-recollement]), for $K=Rj_*G$, with
$j^*Rj_*G\simeq G$ by the unit/counit identities of
[prop-weil-open-closed-recollement-adjunctions], reads

$$
j_!G\longrightarrow Rj_*G\longrightarrow i_*i^*Rj_*G
\xrightarrow{+1}.
$$

Apply the exact functor $Ri^!$. The middle term vanishes, and the
closed-immersion unit $Q\xrightarrow{\sim}Ri^!Ri_*Q$ at $\Qlb$,
clause (4) of [prop-sf-localization-all-stages] (from the full faithfulness of
[prop-sf-closed-unit-all-stages]; at a finite stage it is
[prop-sf-closed-immersion-unit]), identifies the third term with
$i^*Rj_*G$. Hence $Ri^!j_!G\simeq i^*Rj_*G[-1]$.

*Step 4: the isomorphism.* Combining the steps with
$G=\mathbb D_UF\simeq F^\vee(1)[2]$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb D_ZA(F)
&\simeq Ri^!\mathbb D_CRj_*F
\simeq Ri^!j_!\mathbb D_UF\\
&\simeq i^*Rj_*(\mathbb D_UF)[-1]
\simeq A(F^\vee)(1)[1].
\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 5: the stalks.* The reduced scheme $Z$ is finite over the
algebraically closed field $k$, hence a finite disjoint union of
copies of $\operatorname{Spec}k$, smooth of dimension zero. Smooth
purity [thm-pur-rational-and-qbar-purity] in dimension zero gives
$\omega_Z=\Qlb$, so on the component $\bar s$ the functor
$\mathbb D_Z$ is $R\operatorname{Hom}_{\Qlb}(-,\Qlb)$ on bounded
complexes of finite-dimensional spaces. By
[lem-pod-cohomology-of-dual-over-field] (at a finite coefficient
field over which the stalk complex is defined, then extended to
$\Qlb$),

$$
H^{-1}\bigl(\mathbb D_ZA(F)\bigr)_{\bar s}
\simeq H^1(A(F)_{\bar s})^\vee=(R^1j_*F)_{\bar s}^\vee.
$$

On the other side,
$H^{-1}\bigl(A(F^\vee)(1)[1]\bigr)_{\bar s}
=H^0\bigl(Rj_*F^\vee\bigr)_{\bar s}(1)=(j_*F^\vee)_{\bar s}(1)$,
because the ordinary direct image is $\mathcal H^0$ of the derived
one. This is the asserted isomorphism; its transpose is the
asserted perfect pairing, the twist $(1)$ on one side becoming
$(-1)$ in the target.

*Frobenius equivariance.* Every map used is built from pullbacks,
direct images, internal Hom, evaluation, adjunction units and counits,
and exchange maps, all Weil-equivariant by
[lem-fix-weil-operations], together with the smooth-purity
orientations, whose equivariance and trace compatibility are
[prop-pur-rational-purity-trace-coherence]. Hence the isomorphism of
Step 4 is one of Weil complexes on $Z_0$, and its stalk at $\bar s$
commutes with $F_s$; the twists carry their prescribed Frobenius
actions.

Let $j:U_0\hookrightarrow C_0$ be a dense open immersion, with $C_0$ a
smooth geometrically connected affine curve over $k_0=\mathbf F_q$, and
let $\mathcal F$ be a lisse Weil sheaf on $U_0$ with generic geometric
representation $V$ ([def-wf-fundamental-representation]). For the
middle extension $j_*\mathcal F$ of [def-wf-middle-extension], in the
compactly supported cohomology of [def-weil-ordinary-compact-cohomology],

$$
H_c^0(C,j_*\mathcal F)=0,\qquad
H_c^2(C,j_*\mathcal F)\simeq V_{\pi_1(U)}(-1)
$$

Frobenius-equivariantly, and $H_c^r(C,j_*\mathcal F)=0$ for
$r\notin\{0,1,2\}$. If $\mathcal F$ is punctually $\iota$-pure of weight
$w$, then $H_c^2(C,j_*\mathcal F)$ is $\iota$-pure of weight $w+2$
(possibly zero).

## Proof

As a dense open subscheme of the irreducible affine curve $C_0$ (and
likewise after base change to $k$), $U_0$ is a smooth geometrically
connected affine curve: the complement $Z_0=C_0\setminus U_0$ is a
finite set of closed points, and the complement of finitely many closed
points in an affine curve is affine. So the results on affine curves
apply to $(U_0,\mathcal F)$.

*Degree zero.* A class in $H_c^0(C,j_*\mathcal F)$ is a global section
$s$ of $j_*\mathcal F$ over $C$ whose support is proper over $k$. By
definition of the ordinary direct image,
$\Gamma(C,j_*\mathcal F)=\Gamma(U,\mathcal F)$, so $s$ corresponds to a
section $s|_U$ of the lisse sheaf $\mathcal F$ on $U$, and $s=0$ if and
only if $s|_U=0$. If $s\neq0$, then $s|_U$ is a nonzero section of a
lisse sheaf on the connected curve $U$, hence has nonzero germ at every
point of $U$ (as in the proof of [lem-a1-affine-hc0]). The support of
$s$ is closed in $C$ and contains $U$, hence is all of $C$, since $U$ is
dense. But $C$ is an affine curve, so it is not proper over $k$. Thus
$s=0$ and $H_c^0(C,j_*\mathcal F)=0$.

*Degree two and the range.* The boundary localization triangle
[prop-a1-curve-boundary-sequence] for $j$, with $i:Z\hookrightarrow C$,

$$
R\Gamma_c(U,\mathcal F)\longrightarrow
R\Gamma_c(C,j_*\mathcal F)\longrightarrow
R\Gamma_c(Z,i^*j_*\mathcal F)\longrightarrow,
$$

has its third term concentrated in degree zero. Its long exact
sequence therefore gives isomorphisms
$H_c^r(U,\mathcal F)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_c^r(C,j_*\mathcal F)$ for all
$r\geq2$ and for all $r<0$. The lisse sheaf $\mathcal F$ is
constructible, so [lem-zl-affine-curve-range] on the affine curve
$U_0$ gives $H_c^r(U,\mathcal F)=0$ for $r\notin\{0,1,2\}$; hence
$H_c^r(C,j_*\mathcal F)=0$ for $r\notin\{0,1,2\}$. For $r=2$, composing
with the canonical Frobenius-equivariant isomorphism of
[lem-a1-affine-hc2] on $U_0$ gives

$$
H_c^2(C,j_*\mathcal F)\;\simeq\;H_c^2(U,\mathcal F)\;\simeq\;
V_{\pi_1(U)}(-1).
$$

The triangle is formed from Weil complexes over $k_0$, so the
isomorphism $H_c^2(U,\mathcal F)\to H_c^2(C,j_*\mathcal F)$ commutes
with the Frobenius operators, and the composite is
Frobenius-equivariant.

*Purity.* Suppose $\mathcal F$ is punctually $\iota$-pure of weight
$w$. By [lem-a1-geometric-coinvariants-pure] the coinvariant quotient
$W=V_{\pi_1(U)}$ with its induced Frobenius $F_W$ is $\iota$-pure of
weight $w$. On the twist $W(-1)$ the Frobenius is $q\,F_W$, by the
stalk formula of [lem-wf-tate-twist-frobenius] for $E(-1)$ over
$k_0=\mathbf F_q$. So every eigenvalue of Frobenius on $W(-1)$ has
$\iota$-modulus $q\cdot q^{w/2}=q^{(w+2)/2}$, and $W(-1)$, hence
$H_c^2(C,j_*\mathcal F)$, is $\iota$-pure of weight $w+2$ in the sense
of [def-weil-frobenius-module-weights]. It may be zero, which happens
exactly when $V$ has no nonzero geometrically constant quotient.

Fix $\iota:\Qlb\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathbf C$ and $w\in\mathbf R$, and let
$Y_0$ be a finite-type $k_0$-scheme. In the abelian category of
constructible $\Qlb$-Weil sheaves on $Y_0$
([def-weil-weil-sheaf-complex], [def-weil-constructible-heart]):

1. every Weil subsheaf and every Weil quotient sheaf of a sheaf that is
   $\iota$-mixed of weights at most $w$ in the sense of
   [def-weil-punctual-weights] is $\iota$-mixed of weights at most $w$;
2. if $0\to\mathcal G'\to\mathcal G\to\mathcal G''\to0$ is an exact
   sequence of constructible Weil sheaves and $\mathcal G'$,
   $\mathcal G''$ are $\iota$-mixed of weights at most $w$, then so is
   $\mathcal G$;
3. in particular, a direct summand of an $\iota$-mixed constructible
   Weil sheaf of weights at most $w$ is $\iota$-mixed of weights at most
   $w$.

The analogous statements hold for Frobenius modules in the sense of
[def-weil-frobenius-module-weights].

## Proof

Since $g_Y$ is an automorphism, $Lg_Y^*=g_Y^*$ is exact on the
constructible heart, so kernels, images and cokernels of morphisms of
Weil sheaves (morphisms commuting with the structure isomorphisms
$\theta$ of [def-weil-weil-sheaf-complex]) inherit Weil structures; thus
constructible Weil sheaves form an abelian category, and a Weil subsheaf
is a subobject $\mathcal H\subset\mathcal G$ with
$\theta(g_Y^*\mathcal H)=\mathcal H$. For every closed point $y$ with
geometric point $\bar y$ above it, the stalk functor
$\mathcal G\mapsto\mathcal G_{\bar y}$ is exact and carries the local
geometric Frobenius $F_y$; hence it sends exact sequences of Weil sheaves
to exact sequences of $F_y$-modules. We use repeatedly: if $V$ is a
finite-dimensional $F_y$-module all of whose eigenvalues have
$\iota$-modulus $q_y^{u/2}$, then every $F_y$-stable subquotient of $V$
has the same property, because in a basis adapted to a stable subspace
the matrix of $F_y$ is block triangular, so the characteristic
polynomials of the sub and of the quotient divide that of $V$.

Let $0=\mathcal G_0\subset\cdots\subset\mathcal G_m=\mathcal G$ be a
filtration by Weil subsheaves as in [def-weil-punctual-weights], whose
quotients $\mathcal Q_i=\mathcal G_i/\mathcal G_{i-1}$ are punctually
$\iota$-pure of weights $u_i\le w$.

*Subsheaves.* Let $\mathcal H\subset\mathcal G$ be a Weil subsheaf and put
$\mathcal H_i=\mathcal H\cap\mathcal G_i$, the kernel of the Weil morphism
$\mathcal H\to\mathcal G/\mathcal G_i$; these are Weil subsheaves in the
constructible heart. The induced map
$\mathcal H_i/\mathcal H_{i-1}\to\mathcal Q_i$ is injective, since its
kernel is $(\mathcal H\cap\mathcal G_{i-1})/\mathcal H_{i-1}=0$. Taking
stalks at $\bar y$, $(\mathcal H_i/\mathcal H_{i-1})_{\bar y}$ is an
$F_y$-stable subspace of $\mathcal Q_{i,\bar y}$, so all its Frobenius
eigenvalues have $\iota$-modulus $q_y^{u_i/2}$: the quotient is
punctually pure of weight $u_i$ (vacuously so if it is zero). Thus
$(\mathcal H_i)$ is a filtration as required by
[def-weil-punctual-weights], with weights $u_i\le w$.

*Quotients.* Let $\pi:\mathcal G\to\mathcal G''$ be an epimorphism of Weil
sheaves and put $\mathcal G''_i=\pi(\mathcal G_i)$, Weil subsheaves with
$\mathcal G''_0=0$ and $\mathcal G''_m=\mathcal G''$. The composite
$\mathcal G_i\to\mathcal G''_i\to\mathcal G''_i/\mathcal G''_{i-1}$ is
surjective and kills $\mathcal G_{i-1}$, so it factors through an
epimorphism $\mathcal Q_i\to\mathcal G''_i/\mathcal G''_{i-1}$. On stalks
this is an $F_y$-equivariant surjection from $\mathcal Q_{i,\bar y}$, so
the eigenvalues of $F_y$ on the quotient have $\iota$-modulus
$q_y^{u_i/2}$, and $(\mathcal G''_i)$ is a mixed filtration with weights
$u_i\le w$. This proves (1).

*Extensions.* In (2), choose mixed filtrations
$0=\mathcal G'_0\subset\cdots\subset\mathcal G'_a=\mathcal G'$ and
$0=\mathcal G''_0\subset\cdots\subset\mathcal G''_b=\mathcal G''$ with
punctually pure quotients of weights at most $w$. Let
$p:\mathcal G\to\mathcal G''$ be the given epimorphism and consider the
filtration of $\mathcal G$ by Weil subsheaves

$$
0=\mathcal G'_0\subset\cdots\subset\mathcal G'_a=\mathcal G'
=p^{-1}(\mathcal G''_0)\subset p^{-1}(\mathcal G''_1)\subset\cdots
\subset p^{-1}(\mathcal G''_b)=\mathcal G,
$$

where $p^{-1}(\mathcal G''_s)=\ker(\mathcal G\to\mathcal G''/\mathcal
G''_s)$. Its first $a$ quotients are those of $\mathcal G'$, and
$p$ induces isomorphisms of Weil sheaves
$p^{-1}(\mathcal G''_s)/p^{-1}(\mathcal G''_{s-1})\cong\mathcal
G''_s/\mathcal G''_{s-1}$. All quotients are therefore punctually pure of
weights at most $w$, which is (2).

*Direct summands.* If $\mathcal G=\mathcal G'\oplus\mathcal G''$ in the
Weil category, then $\mathcal G'$ is a Weil subsheaf of $\mathcal G$, so
(3) is a special case of (1).

For Frobenius modules in the sense of [def-weil-frobenius-module-weights],
stability under stable subquotients (hence direct summands) is
[lem-a1-subquotient-extension-bounds] and stability under extensions is
[lem-a1-extension-bounds]; alternatively, the three arguments above apply
verbatim with sheaves replaced by modules.

attrs.title: Mixedness passes to subobjects, quotients, extensions and direct summands

objects.body:
Let $(V,F)$ be a finite-dimensional $\Qlb$-Frobenius module in the
sense of [def-weil-frobenius-module-weights] such that every
eigenvalue $\alpha$ of $F$ satisfies
$|\iota(\alpha)|\leq q^{w/2}$.
Then $(V,F)$ is $\iota$-mixed of weights at most $w$.

## Proof

Choose a Jordan–Holder filtration of the finite-dimensional module
$(V,F)$. Every nonzero simple Frobenius module is one-dimensional:
after extending scalars (already allowed in $\Qlb$), a simple nonzero
$F$-stable subspace contains an eigenvector, and the span of that
eigenvector is a nonzero stable subspace, hence the whole module. Thus
each graded piece has a single eigenvalue $\lambda$, which is also an
eigenvalue of $F$ by
[lem-a1-spectrum-exact-sequence]; its modulus is at most
$q^{w/2}$. It is therefore $\iota$-pure of weight
$2\log_q|\iota(\lambda)|\le w$ in the sense of
[def-weil-frobenius-module-weights].
Hence the Jordan–Holder filtration exhibits $(V,F)$ as $\iota$-mixed
of weights at most $w$.

attrs.title: Punctual bound suffices for a module bound

objects.body:
Let $C_0$ be a smooth geometrically connected affine curve, let
$C'_0$ be a smooth geometrically connected curve containing $C_0$
as a dense open with finite complement, let
$g:C'_0\to\mathbf A^1_{k_0}$ be a finite generically etale morphism,
let $j:C_0\hookrightarrow C'_0$, and let $\mathcal F$ be lisse and
punctually $\iota$-pure of weight $w$ on $C_0$. Put
$\mathcal K:=g_*j_!\mathcal F$, a constructible $\Qlb$-Weil sheaf on
$\mathbf A^1_{k_0}$. Then

$$
R\Gamma_c(C,\mathcal F)\simeq R\Gamma_c(\mathbf A^1,\mathcal K),
\qquad\text{hence}\qquad
H_c^i(C,\mathcal F)\simeq H_c^i(\mathbf A^1,\mathcal K)\quad(i\in\mathbf Z).
$$

## Proof

By the finite-map transport applied to the sheaf $j_!\mathcal F$
on $C'_0$: the finite morphism $g$ is proper and $g_*$ is exact
(the finite-direct-image exactness
[lemma-weil-pbc-finite-direct-image-exact]), so

$$
R\Gamma_c(C,\mathcal F)=R\Gamma_c\bigl(C'_0,j_!\mathcal F\bigr)
\simeq R\Gamma_c\bigl(\mathbf A^1_{k_0},g_*j_!\mathcal F\bigr)
=R\Gamma_c(\mathbf A^1,\mathcal K),
$$

with the same compact-support composition of [prop-functor-package]
as in [lem-a1-finite-map-cohomology].

attrs.title: Cohomology transport under the finite-map reduction

objects.body:
Let $C_0$ be a smooth geometrically connected affine curve, let
$C'_0$ be a smooth geometrically connected curve containing $C_0$
as a dense open with finite complement, let
$g:C'_0\to\mathbf A^1_{k_0}$ be a finite generically etale morphism,
let $j:C_0\hookrightarrow C'_0$, and let $\mathcal F$ be lisse and
punctually $\iota$-pure of weight $w$ on $C_0$. Put
$\mathcal K:=g_*j_!\mathcal F$ and let $B$ be the branch locus of
$g$. Then the restriction $\mathcal K|_W$ to
$W:=\mathbf A^1_{k_0}\setminus(B\cup g(C'_0\setminus C_0))$
is lisse and punctually $\iota$-pure of weight $w$.

## Proof

On the open
$W:=\mathbf A^1_{k_0}\setminus(B\cup g(C'_0\setminus C_0))$
the morphism $g$ is finite etale, all of its inverse image lies
in $C_0$, and
$\mathcal K|_W=g_*(j_!\mathcal F)|_W$ sheaf-theoretically, so the
lissity and the punctual purity of weight $w$ in the sense of
[def-weil-punctual-weights] follow from
[lem-a1-finite-map-purity].

attrs.title: Lisse purity of the transported complex

objects.body:
For a short exact sequence $0\to V'\to V\to V''\to0$ of finite
Frobenius modules whose maps commute with Frobenius, the spectrum of
$(V,F)$ (the multiset of the images under $\iota$ of the
eigenvalues, [def-weil-frobenius-module-weights]) is the multiset
union of the spectra of $V'$ and $V''$, counted with algebraic
multiplicity.

## Proof

Choose a basis of $V'$ and complete it to a basis of $V$; the Frobenius
matrix of $V$ is upper block triangular with diagonal blocks the
Frobenius matrices of $V'$ and $V''$, in the sense of
[def-weil-frobenius-module-weights]. Hence the characteristic
polynomial satisfies $\chi_V(T)=\chi_{V'}(T)\chi_{V''}(T)$ ([p-linear-filtration]), and taking
orders of vanishing at each root shows the algebraic multiplicities add.

attrs.title: Spectrum of an exact Frobenius sequence

objects.body:
If $(V,F)$ is mixed of weights at most $w$, then every
Frobenius-stable subquotient of $V$ is mixed of weights at most $w$.

## Proof

A finite-dimensional
Frobenius module all of whose Frobenius eigenvalues have $\iota$-modulus
at most $q^{w/2}$ is mixed of weights at most $w$: a Jordan–Holder
filtration of the module has graded pieces with eigenvalues among those ([p-linear-filtration])
of the module, hence pure of weights at most $w$, which is the
filtered criterion of [def-weil-frobenius-module-weights]. Every
eigenvalue of the Frobenius on a submodule or on a quotient is an
eigenvalue of the Frobenius on the ambient module (a quotient's
characteristic polynomial divides that of the ambient endomorphism by
[lem-a1-spectrum-exact-sequence], and a submodule's eigenvalues are
eigenvalues by the same triangular matrix argument), so both are mixed
of weights at most $w$.

Let $X_0$ be a separated
finite-type $k_0$-scheme and let $\mathcal G$ be a lisse
Weil sheaf on $X_0$ (lisse in the sense
of [def-weil-pbc-constructible-complexes]) which is punctually
$\iota$-pure of weight $w\in\mathbf R$ in the sense of
[def-weil-punctual-weights]. Then every irreducible lisse subquotient
$\mathcal S$ of $\mathcal G$ is punctually $\iota$-pure of weight
$w$.

## Proof

Fix a closed point $x$ and let $(V_x,F_x)$ be the stalk Frobenius
module of $\mathcal G$ at $x$, with eigenvalue multiset $S_x$ as in
[def-weil-punctual-weights]. The geometric stalk functor of the
constructible conventions of [def-weil-pbc-constructible-complexes]
is exact, so the stalk module of $\mathcal S$ at $x$ is an
$F_x$-stable subquotient of $(V_x,F_x)$; hence its eigenvalue multiset
is a submultiset of $S_x$, which is the spectrum bookkeeping of
[lem-a1-spectrum-exact-sequence] applied successively to the
subobject and to the quotient. Every eigenvalue of $(V_x,F_x)$ has
$\iota$-modulus $q_x^{w/2}$ by the punctual purity of weight $w$ of
[def-weil-punctual-weights], hence so does every eigenvalue of the
stalk module of $\mathcal S$; the closed point $x$ was arbitrary, so
$\mathcal S$ is punctually $\iota$-pure of weight $w$.

attrs.title: Irreducible lisse subquotients of a pure lisse sheaf are pure of the same weight

objects.body:
Let $\mathcal F$ be a punctually pure lisse Weil sheaf of weight $w$
on a dense open $U_0\subset\mathbf A^1_{k_0}$.
After a finite constant-field extension, there are a dense open
$V_0\subset\mathbf A^1$ and a lisse sheaf $\mathcal E$ on $V_0$
of the same weight, with trivial local inertia at infinity, together
with a Frobenius-equivariant surjection

$$
H_c^1(V,\mathcal E)\twoheadrightarrow H_c^1(U,\mathcal F).
$$

Geometric irreducibility is preserved.

## Proof

Choose a geometric point $s\in U$, defined over a finite extension.
Over a further finite extension choose
$\tau\in\mathrm{PGL}_2$ with $\tau(s)=\infty$.
Set $V_0=\tau(U_0\setminus\{s\})\subset\mathbf A^1$ and let
$\mathcal E$ be the transported restriction.
It extends lisse across infinity, since $\mathcal F$ was lisse at
$s$; hence its inertia there is trivial.
Restriction to a dense open preserves geometric irreducibility:
the fundamental group of that open surjects onto the fundamental
group of the original smooth curve, by
[lem-wf-dense-open-pi1-surjective] (parts (1) and (4)).
The isomorphism $\tau$ and restriction preserve the local
weight condition of [def-weil-punctual-weights].

Open–closed recollement, [def-weil-open-closed-recollement], whose triangle exists for
$\Qlb$-Weil sheaves by [prop-sf-open-closed-triangle-all-stages],
and the vanishing of $H_c^1$ on the single point from
[lem-a1-finite-boundary-cohomology] give a surjection
$H_c^1(U\setminus\{s\},\mathcal F)\to H_c^1(U,\mathcal F)$.
Transport by $\tau$ gives the asserted map in the convention of
[def-weil-ordinary-compact-cohomology].

attrs.title: Removing a regular point to arrange infinity

objects.body:
Let $j:U_0\hookrightarrow\mathbf A^1_{k_0}$ be a dense open immersion
and let $\mathcal M$ be a nonzero irreducible lisse Weil sheaf on
$U_0$. Suppose that $\mathcal M$ is unramified at infinity and not
geometrically constant, in the sense of [rem-dl-a1-conventions]. Then
$\mathcal M$ is constituent-nonexceptional in the sense of
[def-a1-constituent-nonexceptional]. Geometric irreducibility is not
assumed.

## Proof

Let $V=\mathcal M_{\bar\eta}$, let $W=W(U_0,\bar\eta)$ be the Weil group,
and let $G=\pi_1(U,\bar\eta)\triangleleft W$ be the geometric fundamental
group, as in [def-wf-fundamental-representation]. Since $\mathcal M$ is
irreducible, $V$ is a simple $W$-module. By
[lem-mg-normal-restriction-semisimple], $V|_G$ is semisimple. Hence
every geometric irreducible constituent of $\mathcal M$ is a
$G$-stable direct summand of $V$.

*Case $a\ne0$.* Suppose $\mathcal L_{\psi(ax)}|_U$ were a direct
summand of $V|_G$. The inertia group at
$\infty\in\mathbf P^1_k$ maps into $G$. Restricting from
$\mathbf A^1$ to $U$ does not change the local field at $\infty$. The
inertia group acts trivially on $V$ because $\mathcal M$ is unramified
at infinity, so it acts trivially on every summand. But
$\mathcal L_{\psi(ax)}$ is ramified at infinity by
[lem-a1-artin-schreier-ramified-infinity]. This is a
contradiction.

*Case $a=0$.* Suppose the trivial rank-one representation were a
geometric constituent. Then, being a direct summand, it gives
$V^G\neq0$. The subspace $V^G$ is $W$-stable because $G$ is normal: for
$w\in W$, $g\in G$ and $v\in V^G$,

$$
g\,(wv)=w\,(w^{-1}gw)\,v=wv .
$$

Since $V$ is a simple $W$-module, $V^G=V$. So $G$ acts trivially and
$\mathcal M$ is geometrically constant, contrary to hypothesis.

So no geometric constituent is of the form $\mathcal L_{\psi(ax)}|_U$
with $a\in k$.

attrs.title: Unramified at infinity and not geometrically constant implies nonexceptional

objects.body:
Let $k_0=\mathbf F_q$, let $k'_0=\mathbf F_{q^m}$ be a finite
extension of $k_0$, and let $(V,F)$ be as in
[def-weil-frobenius-module-weights], with the embedding $\iota$
and the prime power $q$ of that definition. Suppose that every
eigenvalue $\lambda$ of $F^m$ satisfies
$|\iota(\lambda)|^2\leq(q^m)^b$. Then every eigenvalue $\alpha$ of
$F$ satisfies $|\iota(\alpha)|^2\leq q^b$: the weight bound for the
target over the extended finite field implies the same bound over the
original field.

## Proof

For an extension of degree $m$, Frobenius becomes $F^m$
and the field cardinality becomes $q^m$, and the eigenvalues of
$F^m$ are the $m$-th powers of those of $F$ in the convention of
[def-weil-frobenius-module-weights].
Thus $|\iota(\alpha^m)|^2=|\iota(\alpha)|^{2m}\leq(q^m)^b=q^{mb}$ is
equivalent to $|\iota(\alpha)|^2\leq q^b$.

attrs.title: Weight bounds over a finite constant-field extension

objects.body:
Let $\mathcal G\subseteq\operatorname{GL}(V)$ over
$k=\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ be a closed subscheme of finite type, cut
out by a finitely generated, possibly nonradical, ideal, such that the
multiplication and inversion of $\operatorname{GL}(V)$ restrict to it.
Then $\mathcal G$ is smooth and reduced, so
$\mathcal G=\mathcal G_{\mathrm{red}}$ is a (smooth) closed matrix group. In particular, if a closed subgroup (a
stabilizer, a centralizer, or the kernel of a regular homomorphism) is
given by explicit equations, its Lie algebra in the sense of
[def-wf-lie-algebra-derivation] is the space of $X$ such that
$1+\varepsilon X$ satisfies those equations over
$k[\varepsilon]/\varepsilon^2$; no passage to the reduced structure
changes the tangent space.

## Proof

*Reduction and smoothness of reduced groups.* The reduction
$\mathcal G_{\mathrm{red}}$ has the same $k$-points as $\mathcal G$, since
nilpotents die in $k$, and those points form a subgroup. Its
multiplication is defined on a product of reduced varieties, which is
reduced by [lem-wf-affine-product-reduced], so multiplication and
inversion factor through the reduction by the vanishing principle
([lem-wf-affine-nullstellensatz-vanishing]); thus $\mathcal G_{\mathrm{red}}$ is a reduced
closed matrix group. Such a group is smooth by (2) of
[lem-wf-same-lie-closed-subgroup].

*Cartier's step.* Write $A=k[\mathcal G]$, $N=\sqrt0$ and
$\mathfrak m=\mathfrak m_e$. Then $N\subseteq\mathfrak m^2$. Indeed, let
$b\in N$ be nonzero in $A_{\mathfrak m}$ with least nilpotence exponent
$n\ge2$ there, arranged so that $b^n=0$ in $A$. The counit identities
give $\Delta(b)=b\otimes1+1\otimes b+w$ with
$w\in\mathfrak m\otimes_k\mathfrak m$. Expanding $0=\Delta(b)^n$ modulo
$A\otimes\mathfrak m^2$ kills every term with two factors from
$1\otimes b+w$ and leaves
$nb^{n-1}\otimes b+n(b^{n-1}\otimes1)w=0$; passing further to
$A/(b^{n-1}\mathfrak m)$ in the first coordinate leaves
$n\,\overline{b^{n-1}}\otimes\overline b=0$ with both factors nonzero.
Since $n\ne0$ in characteristic zero, this is a contradiction, and the
degenerate case $b=0$ in $A_{\mathfrak m}$ gives $b\in\mathfrak m^2$
directly. Hence
$\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2\simeq(\mathfrak m/N)/(\mathfrak m/N)^2$, so
$\mathcal G$ and its reduction have the same cotangent space at $e$;
primes contain nilpotents, so they also have the same local dimension.
Smoothness of the reduction therefore makes the local ring of
$\mathcal G$ at $e$ regular, and translations carry this to every closed
point.

*Reducedness.* A regular local ring is a domain
([Stacks 00NP](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00NP)), so every
local ring of $\mathcal G$ at a maximal ideal is reduced; a nonzero
global nilpotent would have a proper annihilator, hence survive in some
localization. Thus $\mathcal G$ is reduced, so
$\mathcal G=\mathcal G_{\mathrm{red}}$, which is smooth by (2) of
[lem-wf-same-lie-closed-subgroup].

*Subgroup schemes.* Stabilizer, centralizer and kernel loci are closed
subgroup schemes, so the reducedness just proved applies to them
verbatim: their defining equations already compute the tangent space,
and no passage to the reduced structure is involved.

Compare Milne, *Algebraic Groups* (2017), Cartier's Theorem 3.23.
Quoted rather than proved, all general geometry: density
([Stacks 0B8X](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0B8X)) and openness
([Stacks 01V5](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/01V5)) of the smooth
locus over a perfect field, with the regularity criterion
([Stacks 00TV](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00TV)), and the
regular-local-domain theorem.

attrs.title: Cartier: group schemes in characteristic zero are smooth and reduced

objects.body:
Let $L$ be a finite-dimensional Lie algebra over
$\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ whose radical is central,
$\operatorname{rad}L=Z(L)$, in the notation of
[def-wf-lie-radical-centre]. Then $L/Z(L)$ is semisimple and

$$
L=Z(L)+[L,L],
$$

where the plus sign denotes a sum of subspaces.

## Proof

The quotient $\bar L=L/Z(L)$ has zero radical. Let
$\bar I\subseteq\bar L$ be a solvable ideal and let $J\subseteq L$ be its
inverse image. Then $D^nJ\subseteq Z(L)$ for some $n$, and $Z(L)$ is
abelian, so $D^{n+1}J=0$. Thus $J$ is a solvable ideal, hence is contained
in the sum of all solvable ideals, $\operatorname{rad}L=Z(L)$, and
$\bar I=0$. So $\bar L$ is semisimple in the sense of
[def-wf-semisimple-lie-algebra].

By [lem-ag-killing-nondegenerate] the Killing form $B$ of $\bar L$ is
nondegenerate. Invariance of that form gives

$$
[\bar L,\bar L]^\perp
=\{x:B([x,y],z)=0\text{ for all }y,z\}
=Z(\bar L),
$$

so the orthogonal complement of the derived algebra lies in the centre.
The centre is an abelian, hence solvable, ideal of the semisimple
$\bar L$, so it is zero; nondegeneracy then gives
$[\bar L,\bar L]=\bar L$, i.e. the quotient is perfect.

Lift an expression of each quotient class as a sum of brackets; the
difference from these lifted brackets lies in $Z(L)$. This proves
$L=Z(L)+[L,L]$, including the zero-dimensional case.

attrs.title: Central radical gives centre plus derived algebra

objects.body:
For a represented degree datum as in [d-monodromy], $H$ is normal in
$G$, and

$$
aba^{-1}b^{-1}\in H\quad(a,b\in G),\qquad
[\operatorname{Lie}(G^\circ),\operatorname{Lie}(G^\circ)]\subseteq\operatorname{Lie}(H^\circ).
$$

## Proof

*Normality and commutators.* The kernel $P$ of the degree map in
[d-monodromy] is normal, so conjugation by an element of $\rho(W)$
preserves $\rho(P)$ and, being a homeomorphism, preserves its closure $H$
(as in [lem-wf-conjugation-geometric-monodromy]; both closures are
groups by [lem-wf-zariski-closure-subgroup]).
For fixed $h\in H$ the condition $ghg^{-1}\in H$ is closed in $G$ and
contains $\rho(W)$, hence contains $G$; applying it to $g^{-1}$ gives
$gHg^{-1}=H$. Since $\mathbf Z$ is abelian the degree map kills
commutators, so commutators of elements of $\rho(W)$ lie in $H$. Fixing
one variable, $a\mapsto aba^{-1}b^{-1}$ is regular, so the preimage of $H$
is closed and contains $\rho(W)$, hence $G$; fixing $a\in G$ and repeating
in the other variable gives the assertion on all of $G\times G$. No
quotient algebraic group is needed.

*The Lie inclusion.* Fix $a\in G$. The morphism
$b\mapsto aba^{-1}b^{-1}$ of the reduced variety $G$ sends every
$k$-point into the closed subvariety $H$, so by the vanishing principle
(a function on a reduced affine variety vanishing at every $k$-point is
zero) it factors through $H$. It sends $1$ to $1$; differentiating at
$b=1$ in the dual-number description of
[def-wf-lie-algebra-derivation] gives

$$
(\operatorname{Ad}(a)-1)\operatorname{Lie}(G)\subseteq\operatorname{Lie}(H).
$$

Now fix $X\in\operatorname{Lie}(G)$. The morphism
$a\mapsto(\operatorname{Ad}(a)-1)X$ from $G$ to the vector space
$\operatorname{Lie}(G)$ sends every $k$-point into the linear subspace
$\operatorname{Lie}(H)$, so again it factors through it. Its differential
at $a=1$ along $Y\in\operatorname{Lie}(G)$ is $[Y,X]$, since
$(1+\varepsilon Y)X(1-\varepsilon Y)-X=\varepsilon[Y,X]$. Hence
$[Y,X]\in\operatorname{Lie}(H)$. Finally, the identity components are
open by [lem-wf-algebraic-component-cosets], so
$\operatorname{Lie}(G^\circ)=\operatorname{Lie}(G)$ and
$\operatorname{Lie}(H^\circ)=\operatorname{Lie}(H)$. Spanning over all
such brackets gives the inclusion.

attrs.title: Normality, commutators and the Lie inclusion

objects.body:
For a semisimple represented degree datum as in [d-monodromy], $V$ is a
semisimple $G$-module and a semisimple $G^\circ$-module, in the sense of
[def-wf-simple-module] and [def-wf-semisimple-module].

## Proof

Write $V=\bigoplus_iV_i$ with each $V_i$ a simple $W$-representation.
The stabilizer of a subspace is Zariski closed, by the argument of
[lem-wf-stabilizer-density]; a $\rho(W)$-stable subspace is therefore
stable under the closure $G$, and conversely a $G$-stable subspace is
$\rho(W)$-stable. Hence each $V_i$ is $G$-stable, and a proper nonzero
$G$-stable subspace of $V_i$ would be $W$-stable, contradicting
simplicity. So the same decomposition exhibits $V$ as a semisimple
$G$-module. By [lem-wf-algebraic-component-cosets], $G^\circ$ is a
normal subgroup of finite index in $G$, so
[lem-wf-finite-index-restriction-semisimple] makes $V$ a semisimple
$G^\circ$-module.

attrs.title: A semisimple datum is semisimple for its closure and identity component

objects.body:
Let $G\subseteq\operatorname{GL}(V)$ be an irreducible closed matrix
group over $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$, and let $J\subseteq G$ be a
closed subgroup with $\dim J=\dim G$. Then $J=G$.

## Proof

The closed subset $J$ of the finite-type variety $G$ has finitely many
irreducible components, and its dimension is the maximum of their
dimensions, so some irreducible component $J_1$ of $J$ has
$\dim J_1=\dim G$. The matrix group $G$ is closed in the affine variety
$\operatorname{GL}(V)$, hence is an irreducible affine variety. If
$J_1\subsetneq G$, then [lem-wf-affine-dimension-drop] would give
$\dim J_1\le\dim G-1$; hence the closed subset $J_1$ equals $G$. Thus
$G=J_1\subseteq J\subseteq G$, and $J=G$.

attrs.title: A closed subgroup of full dimension is everything

objects.body:
Let $L$ be a finite-dimensional Lie algebra over
$\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$, and let $\rho:L\to\operatorname{End}(V)$ be
a Lie representation on a finite-dimensional vector space $V$, i.e. a
linear map with $\rho([x,y])=\rho(x)\rho(y)-\rho(y)\rho(x)$. Assume that
$\rho$ is faithful ($\ker\rho=0$) and semisimple: $V=\bigoplus_iM_i$ is a
direct sum of nonzero $\rho(L)$-stable subspaces $M_i$, each having no
$\rho(L)$-stable subspaces other than $0$ and $M_i$. Then, in the notation
of [def-wf-lie-radical-centre], $L$ has central radical and

$$
\operatorname{rad}L=Z(L),\qquad L=Z(L)+[L,L],
$$

where the plus sign denotes a sum of subspaces.

## Proof

Put $\mathfrak r=\operatorname{rad}L$, the sum of all solvable ideals
of [def-wf-lie-radical-centre]. As $L$ is finite-dimensional, this is
a finite sum of solvable ideals, so it is a solvable ideal by
[lem-wf-sum-of-solvable-ideals] and induction on the number of summands.
Write $xv$ for $\rho(x)v$. Fix one
summand $M=M_i$. The solvable Lie algebra $\mathfrak r$ acts on
$M\ne0$ through $\rho$, so [lem-wf-solvable-common-eigenvector] gives
a linear form $\lambda:\mathfrak r\to\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ for which

$$
M_\lambda=\{v\in M:av=\lambda(a)v\text{ for all }a\in\mathfrak r\}
$$

is nonzero.

We show that $M_\lambda$ is $\rho(L)$-stable. Let $x\in L$ and
$0\ne v\in M_\lambda$, and put $U_j=\operatorname{span}\{v,xv,\ldots,
x^{j-1}v\}$ and $U=\bigcup_jU_j$, a finite-dimensional $x$-stable
subspace of $M$. From

$$
ax^jv=x\,(ax^{j-1}v)+[a,x]x^{j-1}v
$$

and $[a,x]\in\mathfrak r$ (as $\mathfrak r$ is an ideal), induction on
$j$ shows that for every $a\in\mathfrak r$,

$$
ax^jv\equiv\lambda(a)x^jv\pmod{U_j}.
$$

Hence $U$ is $\mathfrak r$-stable and each $a\in\mathfrak r$ acts on $U$
by an upper-triangular matrix, in the ordered basis extracted from
$v,xv,x^2v,\ldots$, with constant diagonal entry $\lambda(a)$. For
$a\in\mathfrak r$, the element $[x,a]\in\mathfrak r$ acts on $U$ as the
commutator of the two endomorphisms $x|_U$ and $a|_U$, so

$$
0=\operatorname{tr}_U\bigl([x|_U,a|_U]\bigr)=(\dim U)\,\lambda([x,a]),
$$

and characteristic zero gives $\lambda([x,a])=0$. Consequently

$$
a(xv)=x(av)+[a,x]v=\lambda(a)\,xv+\lambda([a,x])\,v=\lambda(a)\,xv,
$$

so $xv\in M_\lambda$. Thus $M_\lambda$ is a nonzero
$\rho(L)$-stable subspace of $M$, and the simplicity of $M$ gives
$M_\lambda=M$. Moreover the computation shows that every $[x,a]$ with
$x\in L$, $a\in\mathfrak r$ acts on $M$ by the scalar
$\lambda([x,a])=0$.

Applying this to every summand $M_i$, the subspace $[L,\mathfrak r]$ acts
as zero on $V=\bigoplus_iM_i$. Faithfulness of $\rho$ gives
$[L,\mathfrak r]=0$, that is, $\mathfrak r\subseteq Z(L)$. Conversely,
$Z(L)$ is an ideal with $[Z(L),Z(L)]=0$, so it is solvable and is
contained in the sum of all solvable ideals: $Z(L)\subseteq\mathfrak r$.
Hence $\operatorname{rad}L=Z(L)$. The radical being central,
[lem-ag-central-radical-quotient] gives $L=Z(L)+[L,L]$.

attrs.title: A faithful semisimple Lie representation forces a central radical

objects.body:
Let $G\subseteq\operatorname{GL}(V)$ and $K\subseteq\operatorname{GL}(W)$
be closed reduced matrix groups over $k=\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$, and
let $\varphi:G\to K$ be a regular homomorphism, that is, a morphism of
varieties which is a group homomorphism on $k$-points. Then the image
$S=\varphi(G(k))$ is a closed subgroup of $K(k)$: it is the set of
$k$-points of a closed subgroup of $K$, which we equip with its reduced
structure.

## Proof

Since $\varphi$ is a homomorphism, $S$ is a subgroup of $K(k)$. For any
subgroup $H\subseteq K(k)$ its Zariski closure $\overline H$ is again a
subgroup: for fixed $y\in H$ the closed condition $xy\in\overline H$
holds on $H$, hence on $\overline H$; then for fixed $x\in\overline H$
the closed condition $xy\in\overline H$ holds on $H$, hence on
$\overline H$; inversion is the same argument.

First treat the identity component. By
[lem-wf-algebraic-component-cosets], $G^\circ$ is an irreducible closed
subset of the affine variety $\operatorname{GL}(V)$, hence an
irreducible affine variety. Put $S_0=\varphi(G^\circ(k))$, a subgroup of
$S$, and let $T=\overline{S_0}\subseteq K$ with its reduced structure.
Then $T$ is a closed subgroup; it is irreducible as the closure of the
image of an irreducible space, and it is affine, being closed in
$\operatorname{GL}(W)$. The morphism $\varphi|_{G^\circ}:G^\circ\to T$ is a
morphism of affine schemes of finite type over $k$, so by part (1) of
[lem-wf-affine-constructible-open] its image
$\varphi(G^\circ)\subseteq T$ is constructible. It is dense in $T$,
because its closed points $S_0$ are already dense; hence part (2)
of [lem-wf-affine-constructible-open] gives a nonempty open
$U\subseteq T$ contained in the image. On $k$-points: every closed
point $t\in U$ has a nonempty fibre, which is a nonempty finite-type
$k$-scheme and therefore has a $k$-point because $k$ is algebraically
closed; hence $U(k)\subseteq S_0$, and $U(k)\neq\varnothing$.

Now

$$
U(k)^{-1}U(k)=\bigcup_{u\in U(k)}u^{-1}U(k)
$$

is the set of $k$-points of an open neighbourhood of the identity in
$T$, and it lies in the subgroup $S_0$. Its translates $sU^{-1}U$ for
$s\in S_0$ show that $S_0$ is open in $T(k)$; the other cosets of $S_0$
in $T(k)$ are open for the same reason, so $S_0$ is also closed in
$T(k)$. Since $S_0$ is dense in $T$, we get $S_0=T(k)$. Thus
$\varphi(G^\circ(k))$ is the set of $k$-points of the closed subgroup
$T$.

Finally, by [lem-wf-algebraic-component-cosets] the group $G(k)$ is the
union of finitely many cosets $g_1G^\circ(k),\ldots,g_nG^\circ(k)$ (as
in [def-wf-algebraic-components], $G^\circ$ is the identity component).
Therefore

$$
S=\bigcup_{i=1}^n\varphi(g_i)\,T(k),
$$

a finite union of translates of the closed set $T(k)$. Each translate
is closed, so $S$ is the set of $k$-points of the closed reduced
subvariety $\bigcup_i\varphi(g_i)T$ of $K$, which is a subgroup because
$S$ is and closed subvarieties of $K$ are determined by their
$k$-points.

attrs.title: The image of a regular homomorphism is closed

objects.body:
Let $\mathfrak h$ be a finite-dimensional semisimple Lie algebra over
$\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ in the sense of
[def-wf-semisimple-lie-algebra]. Its Killing form

$$
B(X,Y)=\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{ad}(X)\operatorname{ad}(Y))
$$

is nondegenerate.

## Proof

To see this without a classification, let
$\mathfrak k=\operatorname{rad}(B)$. Invariance of $B$ makes
$\mathfrak k$ an ideal. Choose a vector-space decomposition
$\mathfrak h=\mathfrak k\oplus L$. If $X\in[\mathfrak k,\mathfrak k]$
and $Y\in\mathfrak k$, then $\operatorname{ad}(X)$ and
$\operatorname{ad}(Y)$ have zero lower-right block on
$\mathfrak h/\mathfrak k$, so

$$
\operatorname{tr}_{\mathfrak k}(\operatorname{ad}(X)|_{\mathfrak k}
\operatorname{ad}(Y)|_{\mathfrak k})=B(X,Y)=0.
$$

The trace criterion [lem-wf-cartan-trace-criterion], applied to
the image of $\mathfrak k$ in $\operatorname{End}(\mathfrak k)$,
shows that this image is solvable. Its kernel is the abelian centre of
$\mathfrak k$, so $\mathfrak k$ is solvable. Since $\mathfrak h$
is semisimple, $\mathfrak k=0$.

attrs.title: The Killing form of a semisimple Lie algebra is nondegenerate

objects.body:
Let $H\subseteq\operatorname{GL}(V)$ be a connected closed matrix group
over $\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$, with Lie algebra
$\mathfrak h=\operatorname{Lie}(H)$ as in
[def-wf-lie-algebra-derivation] and centre $\mathfrak z(\mathfrak h)$
as in [def-wf-lie-radical-centre]. Then

$$
Z(H)=\ker(\operatorname{Ad}:H\to\operatorname{GL}(\mathfrak h)),
\qquad
\operatorname{Lie}\bigl(Z(H)^\circ\bigr)=\operatorname{Lie}Z(H)=\mathfrak z(\mathfrak h).
$$

## Proof

For completeness, the adjoint kernel is the group centre. If
$g\in H$ acts trivially on $\mathfrak h$, the closed centralizer
$C_H(g)$ has Lie algebra $\mathfrak h$, so
[lem-wf-same-lie-closed-subgroup] gives $C_H(g)=H$ and
$g\in Z(H)$. The reverse inclusion is immediate; hence
$Z(H)=\ker(\operatorname{Ad}:H\to\operatorname{GL}(\mathfrak h))$.
For a dual-number matrix $1+\epsilon X$,

$$
\operatorname{Ad}(1+\epsilon X)(Y)
=Y+\epsilon[X,Y].
$$

Consequently the tangent equations of this kernel give

$$
\operatorname{Lie}Z(H)
=\ker(d\operatorname{Ad})
=\ker(\operatorname{ad})
=\mathfrak z(\mathfrak h).
$$
Here the centralizer $C_H(g)$ and the kernel of $\operatorname{Ad}$
are closed subgroup schemes defined by these equations, hence reduced
by [lem-ag-cartier-reduced], so their equations compute their Lie
algebras. Finally $Z(H)^\circ$ is open in $Z(H)$ by
[lem-wf-algebraic-component-cosets], hence has the same tangent space
at the identity, so $\operatorname{Lie}(Z(H)^\circ)=\operatorname{Lie}Z(H)$.

Let $H\subseteq\operatorname{GL}(V)$ be a connected closed matrix group
over $k=\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ (connected in the sense of
[def-wf-algebraic-components]), with Lie algebra
$\mathfrak h=\operatorname{Lie}(H)$ as in
[def-wf-lie-algebra-derivation], and let $r:H\to\operatorname{GL}(M)$ be
a rational representation, i.e. an algebraic-group module in the sense
of [def-wf-algebraic-representations]. Its differential
$dr:\mathfrak h\to\operatorname{End}(M)$ is defined by

$$
r(1+\varepsilon X)=1+\varepsilon\,dr(X)
\qquad\text{in }\operatorname{GL}(M)(k[\varepsilon]/\varepsilon^2),
\quad X\in\mathfrak h .
$$

Then a subspace $U\subseteq M$ is $H$-invariant if and only if
$dr(X)U\subseteq U$ for every $X\in\mathfrak h$.

## Proof

The entries of $r$ are regular functions on $H$, i.e. restrictions of
polynomials in the matrix entries and $\det^{-1}$; so $r$ may be
evaluated on $R$-points of $H$ for every commutative $k$-algebra $R$.
Since $r(1)=1$, the value $r(1+\varepsilon X)$ has the form
$1+\varepsilon Y$, so $dr$ is well defined and linear. The identities
$r(gh)=r(g)r(h)$ and $r(g^{-1})=r(g)^{-1}$ hold on $k$-points, hence
as identities of regular functions on the reduced varieties $H\times H$
and $H$; consequently they hold on $R$-points.

Choose a basis of $M$ whose first $u=\dim U$ vectors span $U$, and write
$r(g)$ in block form $\begin{pmatrix}a(g)&b(g)\\c(g)&d(g)\end{pmatrix}$,
with $c(g)$ the lower-left $(\dim M-u)\times u$ block. Let
$\mathcal S\subseteq\operatorname{GL}(V)$ be the closed subscheme cut
out by the ideal of $H$ together with the entries of $c$. Its $R$-points
are the $g\in H(R)$ such that $r(g)$ is block upper triangular. Block
upper triangular invertible matrices are closed under products and
inverses, and $r$ is multiplicative on $R$-points, so multiplication and
inversion of $\operatorname{GL}(V)$ restrict to $\mathcal S$. By
[lem-ag-cartier-reduced], $\mathcal S$ is reduced; it is the closed
subgroup

$$
S=\{g\in H:r(g)U\subseteq U\},
$$

and its Lie algebra is computed by the defining equations: $X\in
\operatorname{Lie}(S)$ exactly when $1+\varepsilon X$ is a
$k[\varepsilon]/\varepsilon^2$-point of $H$, i.e. $X\in\mathfrak h$
(again by [lem-ag-cartier-reduced] applied to $H$), and the lower-left
block of $r(1+\varepsilon X)=1+\varepsilon\,dr(X)$ vanishes. Thus

$$
\operatorname{Lie}(S)=\{X\in\mathfrak h:dr(X)U\subseteq U\}.
$$

If $U$ is $H$-invariant, then $S=H$, so
$\operatorname{Lie}(S)=\mathfrak h$ and every $dr(X)$ preserves $U$.
Conversely, if every $dr(X)$ preserves $U$, then
$\operatorname{Lie}(S)=\mathfrak h=\operatorname{Lie}(H)$. Since $H$ is
connected and $S\subseteq H$ is a closed algebraic subgroup,
[lem-wf-same-lie-closed-subgroup] gives $S=H$, i.e. $U$ is
$H$-invariant.

For $p_d:\mathbf A^d_S\to S$, let
$t_{p_d}:Rp_{d!}A(d)[2d]\to A_S$ be the counit of
the explicit affine-space adjunction at $A_S$. Then
$t_{p_d}$ is an isomorphism, compatible with arbitrary
base change between Noetherian schemes.
The notation refers to ordinary etale compact supports, and Tate twists.

## Proof

For $d=1$, apply the exact extension-by-zero triangle constructed in the proof
of [lem-amb-closed-support-hom] to the affine
open $j:\mathbf A^1_S\hookrightarrow\mathbf P^1_S$
and the infinity section $i$. It gives

$$
Rp_{1!}A\longrightarrow Rq_*A\longrightarrow A_S
\longrightarrow Rp_{1!}A[1].
$$

Under [thm-amb-p1-decomposition], the second arrow
is $(1,0)$. Its value on the unit is the identity;
its value on $h=c_1(\mathcal O(1))$ is zero because
$i^*\mathcal O(1)\cong\mathcal O_S$.
Consequently the trace of [def-amb-p1-trace]
restricts to an isomorphism
$Rp_{1!}A(1)[2]\to A_S$. This restricted trace is
exactly the counit obtained by composing
$j_!\dashv j^*$ with the projective-line adjunction
in [cor-amb-affine-space-adjunction].

For general $d$, use the tower of affine-line
projections from [cor-amb-affine-space-adjunction].
The projection formula of
[lem-amb-proper-coproducts-projection], applied on
the chosen compactifications, and the just-proved
one-dimensional isomorphism show successively that
$Rp_{d!}A(d)[2d]\cong A_S$. Under this
identification the composite counit is the composite
of $d$ identity maps. The base-change statement
follows either from the same tower and the natural
extension-by-zero triangle, or from the explicit
unit–counit compatibility proved in
[prop-asd-smooth-base-change].

attrs.title: The affine-space trace is an isomorphism

objects.body:
Let $i:D\hookrightarrow T$ be an effective Cartier divisor.
There is a natural morphism in the ordinary derived category

$$
c_D:i_*A_D\longrightarrow A_T(1)[2].
$$

Its image after forgetting support is
$c_1(\mathcal O_T(D))$. For any base change under which
the pullback divisor remains Cartier, the map pulls back to
the corresponding map for that divisor.
The notation refers to Kummer connecting maps, and Tate twists.

## Proof

First take coefficients $\mathbf Z/n$. Write
$v:T-D\hookrightarrow T$. The line bundle
$\mathcal O_T(D)$, together with its canonical trivialization
on $T-D$, defines an element of

$$
H^1\bigl(\operatorname{Cone}(R\Gamma(T,\mathbf G_m)
\longrightarrow R\Gamma(T-D,\mathbf G_m))[-1]\bigr).
$$

For completeness, choose local equations $f_a$ of $D$.
The transition units $f_a/f_b$ define the line bundle,
and the invertible functions $f_a$ on the complement give
its specified trivialization. The equality
$(f_a/f_b)(f_b/f_c)=f_a/f_c$ is the cocycle equation,
and restriction of the transition units is the coboundary of
these trivializing functions. These two assertions are exactly
the cocycle equation in the displayed relative cone. Replacing
$f_a$ by a unit times $f_a$ changes that cocycle by a
coboundary. Refining the covering preserves its class. One may
compute the cone on an injective resolution, or on etale
hypercovers refining this covering; the description gives the
same class in either computation.

Apply the connecting map of the Kummer sequence
[lem-amb-kummer-any-base] to this relative class. It gives
$c_D\in H_D^2(T,\mu_n)$. Forgetting the relative
trivialization sends it to the Kummer boundary of the line
bundle, namely its first Chern class. The support triangle in
[lem-amb-closed-support-hom] identifies

$$
H_D^2(T,\mu_n)
=\operatorname{Hom}_{D(T,\mathbf Z/n)}
(i_*\mathbf Z/n,\mu_n[2]).
$$

This identification uses the sheaf-level adjunction between
$i_*$ and sections supported on $D$, derived by
injective resolutions; it does not assert a purity isomorphism.
All the cone maps and Kummer boundaries commute with pullback
of the pair and its trivialized line bundle. This proves the
asserted base-change compatibility whenever the pulled-back
pair is again the Cartier pair of
[def-sc-effective-cartier-divisor].
Finally apply derived scalar extension from $\mathbf Z/n$
to $A$. Its source is $i_*A_D$, as seen on stalks,
and its target is $A_T(1)[2]$ by
[def-coefficient-twists-detailed]. No flatness of $A$ over
$\mathbf Z/n$ is needed.

attrs.title: A Cartier divisor gives a supported Kummer map

objects.body:
Let $i:D\hookrightarrow T$ be a closed immersion,
with complementary open immersion $v:V\hookrightarrow T$.
For a complex $K$ of etale $A$-module sheaves,
there is a natural isomorphism of ordinary derived
$A$-module complexes

$$
R\operatorname{Hom}_T(i_*A_D,K)
\cong\operatorname{Cone}\bigl(R\Gamma(T,K)
\longrightarrow R\Gamma(V,v^*K)\bigr)[-1].
$$

## Proof

The sequence
$0\to v_!A_V\to A_T\to i_*A_D\to0$ is exact:
at a geometric point of $V$ it is
$0\to A\xrightarrow{1}A\to0$, and at a point
of $D$ it is $0\to0\to A\xrightarrow{1}A\to0$.
This stalk computation uses exact closed direct image
from [lemma-weil-pbc-finite-direct-image-exact] and
conservativity from
[lemma-weil-pbc-geometric-stalk-conservative].
Apply derived Hom into $K$ to its triangle.
The open adjunction of
[lem-amb-etale-adjoint-locality] identifies
$R\operatorname{Hom}_T(v_!A_V,K)$ with
$R\Gamma(V,v^*K)$; both adjoints are exact, so
the derived identification holds on arbitrary complexes.
The resulting Hom triangle is exactly the asserted cone.

attrs.title: Closed support as a relative section complex

objects.body:
For a separated etale morphism $u:U\to X$ of finite type,
$u_!$ is exact and is left adjoint to $u^*$ on the whole
ordinary derived categories. If $f$ and $fu$ are
compactifiable, there is a canonical isomorphism

$$
u^*f^\times K\cong(fu)^\times K.
$$

The notation refers to ordinary etale compact supports.

## Proof

An etale morphism is a local homeomorphism of etale topoi.
For an etale test object $V\to X$, the sheaf $u_!F$
consists of sections on $U\times_XV$ with support proper
over $V$; after an etale covering which separates any finite
set of support points, this is the direct sum of the sections on
the corresponding sheets. This description is independent of
the covering by sheaf descent. It gives
$(u_!F)_{\bar x}=\bigoplus_{\bar z\in U_{\bar x}}F_{\bar z}$,
so $u_!$ is exact. Maps from these sums to $G$ are
precisely maps $F\to u^*G$, first on separated sheets and
then by sheaf descent. Thus $u_!\dashv u^*$ already on
sheaves. Both functors are exact, so the adjunction descends
termwise to ordinary derived categories.

For any complex $M$ on $U$, use the ambient adjunction
of [thm-amb-etale-exceptional-adjoint] and the composition
of compact supports in [lem-amb-etale-compact-comparisons]:

$$
\begin{split}
\operatorname{Hom}_U(M,u^*f^\times K)
&\cong\operatorname{Hom}_X(u_!M,f^\times K)\\
&\cong\operatorname{Hom}_S(Rf_!u_!M,K)\\
&\cong\operatorname{Hom}_S(R(fu)_!M,K).
\end{split}
$$

Yoneda gives the displayed isomorphism and its compatibility
with units, counits, and further etale localization.

attrs.title: Etale localization of the ambient adjoint

objects.body:
The proper-refinement comparisons for
[def-amb-etale-compact-support] are coherent
isomorphisms. Thus they identify its candidates canonically.
These identifications provide the usual composition
isomorphism $Rg_!Rf_!\cong R(gf)_!$ for composable
compactifiable separated finite-type morphisms between
Noetherian schemes.

## Proof

The etale refinement map is the map of
[lem-weil-pbc-proper-open-comparison-iso]; its
bounded-below proof tests only the open where it is
the identity and the complement, where proper base
The argument applies verbatim to bounded-below complexes, which is
the coefficient range in which the cited comparison lemmas of
the compactification-comparison chapter are stated; that is the range used below, and no
assertion is made here for complexes unbounded below.
[lem-weil-pbc-proper-open-comparison-composition]
likewise applies to them and proves identity and
composition for refinements. Given two compactifications,
the closure of the diagonal copy of $X$ in their
fibre product gives a common proper refinement of
the kind in [def-weil-compactifications-refinements].
Passing to a further such refinement compares any two
choices; the already-proved composition identity makes
the result independent of all choices.

Here is the composition construction. Compactify
$g:Y\to S$ as $Y\xrightarrow{v}\overline Y\to S$,
and compactify the map $vf:X\to\overline Y$ as
$X\xrightarrow{a}\overline X\xrightarrow{p}\overline Y$,
using [thm-nagata-compactification] if necessary.
Write $V=\overline X\times_{\overline Y}Y$, with
open immersion $b:V\to\overline X$ and proper map
$p_Y:V\to Y$. Then $X\hookrightarrow V\to Y$
is a compactification of $f$. For every bounded-below complex
$N$ on $V$, the map

$$
v_!Rp_{Y*}N\longrightarrow Rp_*b_!N
$$

is an isomorphism: over $Y$ it is proper base
change, and at a geometric point outside $Y$
both sides vanish, since the corresponding fibre
misses $V$. These assertions use
[prop-weil-proet-finite-proper-base-change], with the same
finite-amplitude extension as above. Apply this map
to the extension by zero of a complex on $X$,
then apply the proper direct image $R\overline g_*$.
Open extension by zero composes termwise, and proper
derived direct image composes
([lem-weil-derived-direct-image-composition], item (5)) by its adjunction to
the composite exact inverse image. The result is
$Rg_!Rf_!\cong R(gf)_!$. For three morphisms,
choose one common refinement of all compactifications;
the two composite maps restrict to the same identity
over the source and use the same proper base-change
maps on each Cartesian rectangle. Their pasting
identity, followed by the refinement composition
identity above, proves associativity.

Let $n$ be invertible on a scheme $T$. The sequence
of etale sheaves

$$
1\longrightarrow\mu_n\longrightarrow\mathbf G_m
\xrightarrow{z\mapsto z^n}\mathbf G_m\longrightarrow1
$$

is exact. It is the same Kummer sequence as
[def-sc-kummer-sequence], with the curve base replaced
by $T$.

## Proof

The kernel in the sequence of [def-sc-kummer-sequence]
is $\mu_n$ by its equation. To check surjectivity
as an etale sheaf, let $a\in R^\times$ on an affine
etale test object $\operatorname{Spec}R\to T$.
The algebra $R[z]/(z^n-a)$ is free of rank $n$,
and $z$ is a unit in it. The derivative $nz^{n-1}$
is therefore a unit. This algebra defines a finite
etale surjective cover, on which $a$ has the root
$z$. This proves exactness over any base. Pullback
preserves the equations and the root cover, so the
sequence and its connecting maps are natural in $T$.

attrs.title: The Kummer sequence on an arbitrary base

objects.body:
For every $g\in\operatorname{GL}_d(\mathcal O_S(S))$,
the linear automorphism of $\mathbf A^d_S$ induced
by $g$ preserves the affine-space trace
$t_{p_d}:Rp_{d!}A(d)[2d]\to A_S$.
The notation refers to Tate twists, and ordinary derived categories.

## Proof

Let $G=\operatorname{GL}_{d,S}$, the open subscheme
$\det\ne0$ of the affine scheme of $d$-by-$d$
matrices. Over $G$, the universal invertible matrix
defines an automorphism $a$ of $\mathbf A^d_G$.
Functoriality of compact supports from
[def-amb-etale-compact-support] gives an
automorphism of $Rp_{d!}A(d)[2d]$ over $G$.
By [lem-amb-affine-space-top-trace], this is an
automorphism of the sheaf $A_G$ in degree zero.
It is therefore multiplication by a locally constant
section $b$ of the finite constant sheaf $A$.
This uses ordinary sheaf endomorphisms, not cohomology
with support on a zero section.

Every geometric fibre of $G\to S$ is connected:
its coordinate ring is a polynomial ring over an
algebraically closed field with the determinant
inverted, hence an integral domain. The locally
constant section $b$ is constant on such a fibre.
At its identity matrix $a$ is the identity
automorphism, so $b=1$ there and therefore on the
whole fibre. Every geometric point of $G$ belongs
to one of these fibres; conservativity of stalks in
[lemma-weil-pbc-geometric-stalk-conservative] gives
$b=1$ globally. Finally the given matrix $g$
is a section $S\to G$. Pulling back this equality
and using the base-change compatibility in
[lem-amb-affine-space-top-trace] proves the assertion.

attrs.title: Linear changes of coordinates preserve integration

objects.body:
Put $W=P\times_SP$, let $p_1,p_2:W\to P$ be
the projections, and let $\Delta:P\hookrightarrow W$
be the diagonal. Its Cartier Kummer map
$\delta:\Delta_*A_P\to A_W(1)[2]$ satisfies, for
$a=1,2$,

$$
A_P=R(p_a)_*\Delta_*A_P
\xrightarrow{R(p_a)_*\delta}R(p_a)_*A_W(1)[2]
\xrightarrow{t_{p_a}} A_P
=\operatorname{id}_{A_P}.
$$

The notation refers to the projective line, projective-line integration, and Tate twists.

## Proof

The equation $x_0y_1-x_1y_0=0$ shows that $\Delta$
is an effective Cartier divisor. For either projection it is
a section. Apply [lem-amb-cartier-kummer-map].
Under [cor-weil-pbc-geometric-fiber-finite], the displayed
endomorphism restricts at every geometric point of $P$ to
integration of the class of a single rational point of
$\mathbf P^1$. Its associated line bundle has degree one,
so [thm-amb-p1-decomposition], [def-amb-p1-trace] make this
value $1$. An endomorphism of the sheaf $A_P$, placed
in degree zero, is determined by its stalks. Hence the
displayed endomorphism is the identity for both projections.

attrs.title: The two integrals of the diagonal class

objects.body:
Let $r:V\to T$ be a proper
morphism of finite type between Noetherian schemes. On the
ordinary derived categories
of etale $A$-module sheaves, $Rr_*$ preserves arbitrary coproducts.
The notation refers to derived direct images.

## Proof

Choose a common finite bound $e$ for the dimensions of the
geometric fibres of the finite-type morphism $r$.
The stalk formula of [cor-weil-pbc-geometric-fiber-finite]
and the bound [thm-sc-finite-type-torsion-cd] give
$R^a r_*F=0$ for $a>2e$, for every sheaf $F$.
The functors $R^a r_*$ commute with filtered colimits: on each
geometric fibre this is
[lem-weil-pbc-cohomology-filtered-colimit], and
[lemma-weil-pbc-geometric-stalk-conservative] detects the comparison.
They therefore commute with direct sums, a direct sum being the
filtered colimit of its finite subsums. The finite acyclic-resolution argument of
[lem-exc-direct-image-coproducts] applies on the unbounded
ordinary category. Its hypercohomology spectral
sequence has only the columns $0,\ldots,2e$. For each total
degree it thus uses a finite interval of cohomology sheaves of the
input. Applying this spectral sequence to the coproduct comparison
proves the assertion, including for unbounded complexes. It
also extends the geometric-fibre formula to unbounded complexes by
the same finite-interval argument.

attrs.title: Proper direct image preserves arbitrary coproducts

objects.body:
Let $r:V\to T$ be a proper
morphism of finite type between Noetherian schemes. For all complexes
$L$ on $V$ and $K$ on $T$, the canonical
derived tensor projection map is an
isomorphism in the ordinary
derived category:

$$
K\otimes_A^LRr_*L\longrightarrow Rr_*(r^*K\otimes_A^LL).
$$

The notation refers to derived direct images, and inverse images.
