extensions therefore glue to a section $s\in\Gamma(T,F)$ with $s|_{T_0}=t$.

*Step 4: constants.* For a constant sheaf $\underline A$ the statement is
immediate, since a nonempty spectral space has global sections $A$ and $T_0$
is nonempty by the hypothesis applied to $T$ itself. This is the case used in
the applications below.

attrs.title: Zariski restriction on a spectral space

objects.body:
Every irreducible closed subset of $X$ meets $X_0$ in a connected nonempty
set. Consequently $\Gamma(X,F)\xrightarrow{\sim}\Gamma(X_0,F_0)$ for every
Zariski sheaf $F$.

## Proof

Fix an irreducible closed subset and give it the reduced closed-subscheme
structure $C\subseteq X$. The map $C\to S$ is proper. Its Stein
factorization gives $C\xrightarrow{u}\operatorname{Spec}B \xrightarrow{v}S$, with $A\to B$ integral and $u$ having geometrically
connected fibres. Since $(A,\mathfrak m)$ is henselian,
$(B,\mathfrak mB)$ is a henselian pair. The image
$D=v(\operatorname{Spec}B)$ is irreducible and closed because $C\to S$ is
proper. Henselian connectedness makes $D\cap V(\mathfrak m)$ connected and
nonempty. The map
$C\cap X_0\to D\cap V(\mathfrak m)$ is closed and surjective with connected
fibres, so the closed-surjection connected-fibre criterion makes
$C\cap X_0$ connected. This expands Tag
`0A0B`; the final equality of sections is Lemma
[lemma-weil-pbc-spectral-restriction].

## Detailed form

Let $(A,I)$ be henselian [def-weil-pbc-henselian-terminology] and let
$p:Y\to\operatorname{Spec}A$ be proper
[def-weil-pbc-scheme-conventions]. In the Stein factorization
[def-weil-pbc-stein-factorization]

$$
  Y\longrightarrow\operatorname{Spec}B\longrightarrow\operatorname{Spec}A,
$$

$A\to B$ is finite and $(B,IB)$ is henselian. Every irreducible closed subset
of $Y$ meets $Y_0$ in a nonempty connected subset. Therefore the Zariski
restriction criterion of [lemma-weil-pbc-spectral-restriction] applies to
$(Y,Y_0)$.

**Status.** This statement is a conditional assembly: its two classical
inputs are named and isolated in the interface
[thm-weil-pbc-stein-inputs], and everything else is proved here. Proved in
this blueprint: (a) given that $A\to B$ is finite, the pair $(B,IB)$ is
henselian; (b) $Y$ is spectral and $Y_0$ is closed in $Y$; (c) hence the
Zariski restriction criterion applies to $(Y,Y_0)$. Outsourced to
[thm-weil-pbc-stein-inputs]: (i) the finiteness of $A\to B$ for an arbitrary
affine henselian base; (ii) the connectedness input; (iii) the Zariski
comparison for the constructible sheaf occurring in the degree-zero argument,
which the locally constant form [lemma-weil-pbc-spectral-restriction] does not
supply.

## Proof

*Step 1 (finiteness).* The finiteness of $A\to B$ is not proved in this
blueprint; it is input (i) of [thm-weil-pbc-stein-inputs], where the
Noetherian reference and the approximation route available here are recorded.
We use it as a hypothesis for the rest of the proof.

*Step 2 (the pair $(B,IB)$ is henselian).* This is proved here. Given a
finite $B$-algebra $C$, the composite $A\to C$ is finite: finiteness is
closed under composition in the sense of
[def-weil-pbc-scheme-conventions]. For such a $C$, every idempotent of $C/IC$
lifts uniquely to an idempotent of $C$, because $(A,I)$ is henselian
[def-weil-pbc-henselian-terminology] and a finite $A$-algebra is in
particular integral over $A$. That is precisely the definition of the pair
$(B,IB)$ being henselian.

*Step 3 (connectedness).* This is not proved in this blueprint; it is input
(ii) of [thm-weil-pbc-stein-inputs], the henselian-pair proper-base-change
theorem stating that for $Z$ proper over $\operatorname{Spec}A$ every
irreducible closed subset of $Z$ meets $Z\times_AA/I$ in a nonempty connected
subset. Applied to $Z=Y$ it gives the connectedness clause of the statement.

*Step 4 (spectrality and closedness).* This is proved here. $Y$ is spectral
[def-weil-pbc-scheme-conventions]: $p$ is separated and of finite type, so
$Y$ is quasi-compact and quasi-separated, and the underlying space of a
scheme is sober with a basis of quasi-compact opens. The subscheme
$Y_0\subset Y$ is closed, since
$S_0=\operatorname{Spec}(A/I)\to\operatorname{Spec}A$ is a closed immersion
and closed immersions are stable under base change by
[lem-weil-pbc-closed-immersion-products].

*Step 5.* Steps 3 and 4 verify the hypotheses of the Zariski restriction
criterion [lemma-weil-pbc-spectral-restriction] for the pair $(Y,Y_0)$, so its
conclusion applies to $(Y,Y_0)$; the last assertion of the statement follows.
We repeat the warning of input (iii) of [thm-weil-pbc-stein-inputs]: that
criterion is available for *locally constant* sheaves only, and the
constructible sheaf to which the degree-zero argument applies it is not known
to be locally constant.

For $n\geq1$ the formula

$$
((x_1:y_1),\ldots,(x_n:y_n))\longmapsto
[F_0:\cdots:F_n],\qquad
\prod_{i=1}^n(x_it+y_i)=\sum_{j=0}^nF_jt^j,
$$

defines a finite surjective $S_n$-invariant morphism
$\sigma_n:(\mathbf P^1_S)^n\to\mathbf P^n_S$.

## Proof

Each $F_j$ is the sum of monomials choosing $j$ of the $x_i$ and the
remaining $y_i$; hence it is homogeneous of degree one in every pair
$(x_i,y_i)$. On the chart $y_1\cdots y_n\ne0$, the ratios
$z_i=x_i/y_i$ give elementary symmetric polynomials, so the map is induced
by the universal polynomial $\prod(T-z_i)$. On a general chart, the same
calculation uses the coefficient ring localized at one nonzero $F_j$; the
coefficients generate the unit ideal because if all $F_j$ vanished then the
homogeneous polynomial $\prod_i(x_it+y_i)$ would be zero, forcing one factor
to be $(0,0)$, impossible in projective coordinates. The coordinate ring is
integral over the symmetric subring: each $z_i$ satisfies the monic equation
$T^n-e_1T^{n-1}+\cdots+(-1)^ne_n$, and the analogous statement holds on all
charts after clearing the chosen $y_i$ or $x_i$. Thus $\sigma_n$ is finite.
Permutation of the factors leaves every $F_j$ unchanged, proving
$S_n$-invariance. To make finiteness independent of the abbreviated chart
calculation, let $[a_0:\cdots:a_n]$ be a geometric point of $\mathbf P^n_S$.
Its fibre is the set of ordered $n$-tuples of points of $\mathbf P^1$ whose
linear forms multiply to $\sum a_jt^j$. Over an algebraically closed field,
the factorization theorem for one-variable polynomials, applied after choosing
the first nonzero coefficient to decide whether $t=\infty$ is a root, gives
only finitely many such tuples (at most $n!$ after the multiplicities are
fixed). Hence $\sigma_n$ is quasi-finite.

The source $(\mathbf P^1_S)^n$ is projective over $S$, so $\sigma_n$ is
proper. On an affine target chart, the quasi-finite proper map is covered by
finitely many affine opens on which the coordinate rings are integral over the
target ring: on the chart where the last coefficient is invertible use the
monic equations for the $z_i$, and on the chart where the first coefficient
is invertible use the reversed monic equations for $w_i=y_i/x_i$; on an
intermediate chart, intersect these two covers with the finitely many opens
where a selected coefficient of the binary form is invertible. The same
monic equations after multiplying by that selected coefficient show that each
coordinate is integral. Integral algebras glue on overlaps because the
coordinate identifications are induced by the common coefficients $F_j$.
Thus the proper quasi-finite morphism is finite ([cor-pqf-proper-quasifinite-finite]). Finally a geometric binary
form of degree $n$ factors into $n$ linear forms, including the possible
factor $x$ for $t=\infty$, so every geometric fibre is nonempty; geometric
surjectivity and properness give surjectivity. This closes the chart and
gluing obligation.

For proper $f:X\to Y$, the property $\mathsf{PBC}(f)$ is local for the etale
topology on $Y$.

## Proof

For an etale $V\to Y$ and a torsion sheaf $F$, sections of $R^qf_*F$ on $V$
are the sheafification of $U\mapsto H^q(X\times_YU,F|)$ over etale
$U\to V$. This description is functorial in $V$ and commutes with further
etale localization. Therefore an exchange map is an isomorphism if and
only if it is so after an etale cover of $Y$ (and its pullback cover on
$Y'$), because geometric stalks form a conservative family. The section
description is the content located at Tag `03Q8`.

## Detailed form

For proper $f:X\to Y$, the assertion $\mathrm{PBC}(f)$ of
[def-weil-pbc-property] is local on $Y$ for the etale topology. More
precisely, after an etale covering $\coprod_iV_i\to Y$, the exchange map is an
isomorphism if and only if its pullback over every $V_i$ is an isomorphism.

## Proof

By the quasi-compact quasi-separated description of higher direct image, the
restriction of $R^qf_*F$ to $V$ is the sheafification of $U\mapsto
H^q(X\times_YU,F|)$, compatible with further etale restriction and with the
canonical exchange morphism of [def-weil-pbc-derived-exchange]. Hence the
exchange map is an isomorphism if and only if it is so on the stalks over an
etale cover, and geometric stalks are conservative.

For every torsion abelian sheaf $F$ and every proper Cartesian square, the
specific map $\operatorname{Ex}_{\square,F}$ is an isomorphism.

## Proof

Write $F=\varinjlim_nF[n]$ and commute both sides of exchange with the
filtered colimit. Induct on the number of prime factors of $n$ through
$0\to F[\ell]\to F[n]\to F[n]/F[\ell]\to0$; the quotient is killed by
$n/\ell$. Prime coefficients are handled by the preceding lemma, and the
five-lemma transfer handles the induction step. Naturality shows at every
stage that the comparison is the S0 exchange map.

## Detailed form

For every proper $f:X\to Y$, every cartesian base change, and every torsion
abelian sheaf $F$ on $X_{\Et}$, the derived exchange morphism
[def-weil-pbc-derived-exchange] is an isomorphism in every cohomological
degree. This is the sheaf-level instance of the bounded-below theorem of this
chapter applied to $K=F[0]$, whose exchange isomorphism has these degreewise
maps as its cohomology-sheaf components; the direct assembly from
[lemma-weil-pbc-prime-proper-base-change] given below is the step used in the proof of
the bounded-below theorem.

## Proof

If $nF=0$ and $n=rn'$, the prime-factor devissage sequence expresses $F$
through an $\mathbf F_r$-module sheaf and a sheaf killed by $n'$; the long
exact direct-image sequences, the prime-coefficient case
[lemma-weil-pbc-prime-proper-base-change], and the five-lemma transfer induct on the
number of prime factors of $n$. For arbitrary torsion $F$, the filtered union
of its finite-order subsheaves and the exact filtered-colimit theorem for
direct images pass the isomorphism to the colimit; naturality keeps the
comparison equal to the named exchange morphism of
[def-weil-pbc-derived-exchange].

**Status.** The route above reaches the statement for every proper $f$:
neither [lemma-weil-pbc-prime-proper-base-change] nor the reduction
[prop-weil-pbc-reduction-to-projective-line] carries a finite-presentation
hypothesis, since the Chow lemma [lemma-weil-pbc-chow-factorization] used in
the reduction is proved for every proper morphism over an affine base. For the
general proper morphism the classical statement is Etale Cohomology,
Theorem 59.91.11 (Tag [095T](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/095T)):
"Let $f:X\to Y$ be a proper morphism of schemes. Let $g:Y'\to Y$ be a morphism
of schemes ... Let $\mathcal{F}$ be an abelian torsion sheaf on
$X_{\acute{e}tale}$. Then the base change map $g^{-1}Rf_*\mathcal{F}\to
Rf'_*(g')^{-1}\mathcal{F}$ is an isomorphism." Its proof follows the same
route as the one above: the reduction to $\mathbf P^1_S\to S$ for every
scheme $S$ is Etale Cohomology, Lemma 59.91.10 (Tag
[0A4F](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0A4F)), and the strictly henselian
computation is the comparison $\Gamma(X,\mathcal{F})=\Gamma(Z,\mathcal{F}|_Z)$
of Lemma 59.91.1 (Tag [0A0B](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0A0B)), which
Stacks derives from Stein factorization (More on Morphisms, Theorem 37.53.5,
Tag [03H2](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/03H2)) and henselian
idempotent lifting (More on Algebra, Lemma 15.11.8, Tag
[09XK](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09XK)). Accordingly the only
inputs of this route that the chapter does not supply are the two Stein
inputs [thm-weil-pbc-stein-inputs]; they are supplied in the literature by
the chain just named, and closing them here means decomposing that chain.

For every torsion sheaf $F$ the inclusions $F[n]\hookrightarrow F[mn]$ form a
filtered system and the canonical map $\varinjlim_nF[n]\to F$ is an
isomorphism.

## Proof

The transition map sends a section killed by $n$ to the same section, now
regarded as killed by $mn$. The map to $F$ is monic because a section that is
zero in $F$ is already zero in every $F[n]$. It is epic because every local
section of $F$ is locally killed by some positive integer and hence is locally in one
of the $F[n]$; sheafification preserves this local epimorphism.

## Detailed form

For every torsion sheaf [def-weil-pbc-etale-sheaves] $F$ on $X_{\Et}$,

$$
 F=\varinjlim_{(\mathbf N_{>0},\mid)}F[n],\qquad
 F[n]=\ker(n:F\to F),
$$

as a filtered colimit in $\Ab(X_{\Et})$. Here positive integers are ordered
by divisibility, and for $n\mid m$ the transition map is the inclusion
$F[n]\hookrightarrow F[m]$; this poset is filtered because
$\operatorname{lcm}(n,m)$ is a common upper bound.

## Proof

Every local section of $F$ is locally killed by some positive integer, hence lies in
$F[n]$ locally, so the canonical map to $F$ is an epimorphism of sheaves; a
section that is zero in $F$ is already zero in every $F[n]$, so it is a
monomorphism. Filteredness follows from the lcm property, and the sheaf
axioms pass the local statements to global ones, exactly in the sense of
[def-weil-pbc-etale-sheaves].

For every morphism $u:F\to G$ the square

$$
\begin{CD}
g^{-1}f_*F @>{\operatorname{Ex}_{\square,F}}>> f'_*g'^{-1}F\\
@V{g^{-1}f_*u}VV @VV{f'_*g'^{-1}u}V\\
g^{-1}f_*G @>{\operatorname{Ex}_{\square,G}}>> f'_*g'^{-1}G
\end{CD}
$$

commutes on every etale object of $Y'$.

## Proof

On a representative section $s_i$ (the sectionwise rule of [lem-weil-pbc-underived-exchange-sectionwise]), both paths first apply $u$ and then
pull back along the same two maps. Since inverse image is a functor, the two
resulting sections of $g'^{-1}G$ are equal on each $V_i$ and therefore after
descent on $V$. Equality for all $V$ is equality of sheaf morphisms.

## Detailed form

For every morphism $a:F\to G$ in $\Ab(X_{\Et})$, the square

$$
 \begin{array}{ccc}
 g^{-1}f_*F&\xrightarrow{\Ex^0_{\square,F}}&f'_*g'^{-1}F\\
 g^{-1}f_*a\downarrow&&\downarrow f'_*g'^{-1}a\\
 g^{-1}f_*G&\xrightarrow{\Ex^0_{\square,G}}&f'_*g'^{-1}G
 \end{array}
$$

commutes.

## Proof

Each arrow in the defining composite of
[def-weil-pbc-underived-exchange] is an adjunction unit, the
specified pseudofunctorial isomorphism $\theta_\square$ of
[def-weil-pbc-cartesian-square], or an adjunction counit; all three
transformations are natural in $F$, so the displayed square commutes.

Let $u:X_0\to X$ be a universal homeomorphism. A family $\{U_i\to U\}$ of
etale $X$-schemes is jointly surjective if and only if its base change along
$u$ is jointly surjective.

## Proof

This is the topology half, the omission in Tag `03SI`. For a
family $\{U_i\to U\}$ of etale $X$-schemes, set
$Z=|U|\setminus\bigcup_i\operatorname{im}(|U_i|\to|U|)$. Base change gives
a homeomorphism $|U\times_XX_0|\to|U|$, and its inverse image of $Z$ is
exactly the complement of the union of the base-changed images. Hence
$Z=\varnothing$ if and only if that inverse image is empty. This proves
joint surjectivity in both directions. The identity and composition
compatibilities already proved show that this correspondence of covering
families respects refinements and composite coverings.

Let $u:X_0\to X$ be a universal homeomorphism. Base change gives an
equivalence between etale $X$-schemes and etale $X_0$-schemes.

## Proof

This is Tag `04DZ`; the formalization follows its second proof.

*Full faithfulness* (Tag `04DY`). Faithfulness only uses that
$u$ is surjective and that etale morphisms are unramified: two
$X$-morphisms $T\to V$ into an etale $X$-scheme that agree after composing
with the surjection $T\times_XX_0\to T$ factor jointly through the diagonal
of $V$, an open immersion. For fullness, an $X_0$-morphism
$a:T\times_XX_0\to V\times_XX_0$ is descended through its graph: the graph
is a section of the etale projection $(T\times_XV)\times_XX_0\to T\times_XX_0$,
hence an open immersion, and since $(T\times_XV)\times_XX_0\to T\times_XV$ is
a homeomorphism the image of the graph is the base change of an open
subscheme $O\subset T\times_XV$. The projection $O\to T$ is etale and becomes
an isomorphism after base change along $T\times_XX_0\to T$; surjectivity and
universal injectivity descend along surjections, so $O\to T$ is an etale
universally injective surjection, hence an isomorphism, and $T\cong O\to V$
is the required morphism.

*Essential surjectivity.* Being in the essential image is local on the
source: the descended pieces of a cover of $V_0$ by descendable opens form a
locally directed diagram of open immersions of etale $X$-schemes, by full
faithfulness, and its colimit is the descent of $V_0$. So it suffices to
treat an affine etale $V_0\to X_0$ over affine $X$, and after shrinking one
may assume that $V_0$ is standard etale, so that its fibre degrees are
bounded by some $n$. One then proves by induction on $n$ that every affine
etale $V_0$ over $X_0$ with fibre degrees at most $n$, for $X$ quasi-affine, is
the base change of a quasi-affine etale $X$-scheme. Shrinking $X$ to the
open image of $V_0$ one may assume $V_0\to X_0$ surjective. Property (C) of
Tag `04DW` produces an affine etale $W\to X$ and a surjective
$X_0$-morphism $W\times_XX_0\to V_0$: after passing to an etale neighbourhood
of $X$ realizing the separable closure of the residue field of a point, and
after a further etale neighbourhood splitting off the corresponding point of
the finite algebra (Tag `00UJ`), the relevant piece of $V_0$ becomes
finite etale of rank one, i.e. isomorphic to the base. Its section splits
$V_0\times_{X_0}(W\times_XX_0)$ as $W\times_XX_0$ together with a complement
of fibre degrees at most $n-1$, which descends to $W$ by induction. The
resulting quasi-affine etale $W$-scheme descends along the etale cover
$W\to X$: its ring of global sections carries the canonical descent datum
(defined by full faithfulness along the universal homeomorphism
$W\times_XX_0\to W$, using flat base change of global sections), which is
effective by faithfully flat descent of algebras, and the quasi-affine scheme
descends as an open subscheme of the spectrum of the descended algebra.

attrs.title: Base change equivalence for universal homeomorphisms

objects.body:
Let $k$ be a field of characteristic prime to $N$, let $\Lambda$ be
the finite commutative ring annihilated by $N$ of
[sbc-def-coefficient-conventions], let $S$ be of finite type over
$k$, let $f:X\to S$ be a
proper morphism whose
geometric fibres have
dimension at most $d\in\mathbf Z_{\geq0}$, and let $F$ be a
constructible
$\Lambda$-sheaf on $X_{{\mathrm{et}}}$. Then:

1. **(i)** (*the comparison*) For every $q\geq0$ and every
geometric point
$\bar s$ of $S$, the comparison map of
[cor-weil-pbc-geometric-fiber-finite]
$$
(R^qf_*F)_{\bar s}\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }
H^q\bigl(X_{\bar s},F|_{X_{\bar s}}\bigr)
$$
is an isomorphism; each fibre-cohomology group
$H^q(X_{\bar s},F|_{X_{\bar s}})$ is a finite $\Lambda$-module;
and these groups vanish for $q>2d$.
1. **(ii)** (*the finitude*) The higher direct images
$R^qf_*F$ of [def-weil-pbc-direct-image] are
constructible
on $S_{{\mathrm{et}}}$ for every $q\geq0$, and
$R^qf_*F=0$ for $q>2d$.

## Proof

Constructibility follows from
[thm-fin-proper-constructibility-complete], applied to the given
proper morphism and constructible coefficient sheaf.
For every geometric point $\bar s$, proper base change
[cor-weil-pbc-geometric-fiber-finite] identifies

$$
(R^qf_*F)_{\bar s}=H^q(X_{\bar s},F|_{X_{\bar s}}).
$$

The right side is zero above twice the specified fibre-dimension
bound by [fin4-lem-fibrewise-cohomological-dimension].
Geometric stalk conservativity
[lemma-weil-pbc-geometric-stalk-conservative] proves the sheaf vanishing.
Each fibre group is finite because constructible sheaves have finite
stalks by [def-weil-pbc-constructible-complexes].
The constructibility proof uses finite resolutions and proper
modifications; the sharp bound is obtained separately from this
geometric-fibre calculation.

attrs.title: The comparison and finitude of proper direct images

objects.body:
The comparison construction of [thm-sf-ambient-adjoint-class]
provides the exceptional right adjoint relative to bounded-below inputs
of étale origin. It suffices for the bounded constructible class;
its finite-coefficient preservation is [thm-sf-preservation-class].
An adjunction for arbitrary unbounded pro-étale complexes is not proved
by that comparison and is not used as an automatic consequence; see
[rem-sf-class-adjoint-residue]. It is in fact *false in general*: for the
structure morphism of an elliptic curve over $\overline{\mathbf F}_p$ and
$A=\mathbf F_r$ there is a pro-étale sheaf, not of étale origin, with nonzero
cohomology in every degree, so $Rf_!=Rf_*$ does not preserve coproducts and
has no right adjoint on $D$ or on $D^+$ (the counterexample is recorded in the
sketch block of this remark and in rem:sf-ambient-counterexample). The former
recorded input "i:pe-direct-image-coproducts" is therefore false in general
and not used; what remains open is nothing that the blueprint needs. General finite-coefficient Verdier
biduality is independently proved in [thm-fix-general-biduality],
and its boundary exchange is [cor-weil-boundary-duality-discharge];
neither assertion needs the unrestricted ambient adjunction left open here.

attrs.title: Adjunction outside the bounded comparison class

objects.body:
General finite-coefficient Verdier preservation and biduality are proved
in [thm-fix-general-biduality]; closed-boundary exchange follows in
[cor-weil-boundary-duality-discharge]. The scope beyond that theorem
is as follows:

1. General duality at $\mathcal O_E,E,\Qlb$ is now supplied
by [thm-sf-biduality-class], using the independent finite and
integral coefficient comparisons. It is no longer an open input.
1. The dimension-free internal-Hom bound $[c-b,d-a]$ still requires
a site-perfect first variable. Its failure for a general constructible
first variable, recorded in [rem-sf-proetale-hom-status], is compatible
with the geometric dimension bound for Verdier duality.
1. A coherent normalized DVR tower reconstructs by
[lem-coef-normalized-dvr-effectivity]; constructibility follows
when its terms have the required uniform bounds. No common local
model is needed for that lemma. Unverified towers and other coefficient
systems retain the scope distinctions of [rem-sf-tower-shapes-occurring].
1. An ambient adjunction outside the comparison class remains outside
these claims, as in [open-sf-ambient-adjoint-input] and
[rem-sf-class-adjoint-residue].

attrs.title: Scope beyond the constructible coefficient category

objects.body:
Every semisimple represented degree datum ([d-monodromy])
admits a positive central pair ([d-central]) $(N,z)$, that is $N>0$ and
$z\in Z(G)\cap HF^N$.

## Proof

The finite component group from [lem-wf-algebraic-component-cosets]
supplies $m>0$ with $F^m\in G^\circ$. By [p-product], factor $F^m=ch$ with
$c\in Z(G^\circ)^\circ$ and $h\in H^\circ$, and choose a finite list
$g_1,\ldots,g_r$ meeting every coset of $G^\circ$ exactly once. Put

$$
N=mr,\qquad z=\prod_{i=1}^r g_i c g_i^{-1}.
$$

Since $G^\circ$ is normal, all
conjugates of $c$ lie in its abelian center. Replacing a coset
representative by $g_i u$, $u\in G^\circ$, leaves its factor unchanged;
the factors commute. Left multiplication permutes the component cosets,
so conjugation by any $g\in G$ fixes their product $z$.
By [lem-ag-closure-commutators], every commutator in $G$ lies in $H$,
so $g_icg_i^{-1}=(g_icg_i^{-1}c^{-1})c\in Hc$; and
$c=F^mh^{-1}\in F^mH=HF^m$ because $H$ is normal.
Thus each $g_i c g_i^{-1}$ has the same $H$-coset as $c$, namely
$HF^m$, and multiplication yields $z\in HF^{mr}$.
There is at least the identity coset, so $r>0$ and $N=mr>0$.

In the conventions of [rem-dl-a1-conventions], let
$j:U_0\hookrightarrow C_0$ be a dense open immersion into a curve
$C_0$ in the sense of [d-real-setup] (for instance $C_0=A_0$), with
finite closed complement $i:Z_0\hookrightarrow C_0$. Let
$0\to F_1\to F\to F_2\to0$ be a short exact sequence of lisse
$\Qlb$-Weil sheaves on $U_0$, all punctually $\iota$-pure of the
same weight $w$ ([def-weil-punctual-weights]). Then the ordinary
middle extension of [def-wf-middle-extension] is exact on it: the
sequence of Weil sheaves on $C_0$

$$
0\longrightarrow j_*F_1\longrightarrow j_*F
\longrightarrow j_*F_2\longrightarrow0
$$

is exact.

## Proof

*Step 1: the obstruction is a connecting map.* The short exact
sequence is a distinguished triangle $F_1\to F\to F_2\xrightarrow{+1}$
of Weil complexes on $U_0$. The derived direct image
[def-weil-derived-direct-image] is a triangulated functor and, with
its Weil structure and equivariant structure maps from
[lem-fix-weil-operations], gives a distinguished triangle of Weil
complexes $Rj_*F_1\to Rj_*F\to Rj_*F_2\xrightarrow{+1}$ on $C_0$.
Since $R^rj_*=0$ for $r<0$ and $R^0j_*=j_*$ is the ordinary direct
image ([def-wf-middle-extension]), its long exact sequence of
cohomology sheaves begins

$$
0\to j_*F_1\to j_*F\to j_*F_2\xrightarrow{\ \delta\ }R^1j_*F_1\to\cdots,
$$

and all maps, in particular $\delta$, are morphisms of Weil sheaves.
Hence the asserted sequence is exact if and only if $\delta=0$, and it
suffices to show that $\delta$ vanishes on every geometric stalk.

*Step 2: the open part.* By the unit/counit identities of
[prop-weil-open-closed-recollement-adjunctions],
$j^*Rj_*F_1\simeq F_1$, so $j^*R^1j_*F_1=\mathcal H^1(F_1)=0$ and
$\delta$ vanishes at every geometric point of $U$. It remains to treat
a geometric point $\bar s$ over a closed point $s\in Z_0$. There
$\delta_{\bar s}:(j_*F_2)_{\bar s}\to(R^1j_*F_1)_{\bar s}$ commutes
with the local geometric Frobenius $F_s$, since $\delta$ is a morphism
of Weil sheaves. Write $q_s=|\kappa(s)|$.

*Step 3: the source has weights at most $w$.* $F_2$ is punctually
pure, hence punctually mixed of weights at most $w$. The boundary
semicontinuity [lem-wf-boundary-semicontinuity], applied to $j$ and
$F_2$ with $\beta=w$, shows that every eigenvalue $\alpha$ of $F_s$ on
$(j_*F_2)_{\bar s}$ satisfies $|\iota(\alpha)|^2\le q_s^{w}$.

*Step 4: the target has weights at least $w+2$.* The local boundary
duality [lem-a1-local-boundary-duality] for $F_1$ gives an
$F_s$-equivariant isomorphism

$$
(R^1j_*F_1)_{\bar s}^\vee\simeq(j_*F_1^\vee)_{\bar s}(1);
$$

in particular $(R^1j_*F_1)_{\bar s}$ is finite-dimensional, and on the
left $F_s$ acts contragrediently. The dual $F_1^\vee$ is lisse and
punctually $\iota$-pure of weight $-w$ by [lem-tw-dual-negation], so
[lem-wf-boundary-semicontinuity] with $\beta=-w$ bounds the
eigenvalues of $F_s$ on $(j_*F_1^\vee)_{\bar s}$ by
$|\iota(\cdot)|^2\le q_s^{-w}$. On the twist by $(1)$ the local
Frobenius is multiplied by $q_s^{-1}$ ([lem-wf-tate-twist-frobenius]),
so the eigenvalues on $(j_*F_1^\vee)_{\bar s}(1)$ satisfy
$|\iota(\cdot)|^2\le q_s^{-w-2}$. The eigenvalues of the contragredient
action are the inverses $\gamma^{-1}$ of the eigenvalues $\gamma$ of
$F_s$ on $(R^1j_*F_1)_{\bar s}$ ([p-linear-spectra]). Hence
$|\iota(\gamma)|^{-2}\le q_s^{-w-2}$, that is,

$$
|\iota(\gamma)|^2\ \ge\ q_s^{\,w+2}
$$

for every eigenvalue $\gamma$ of $F_s$ on $(R^1j_*F_1)_{\bar s}$.

*Step 5: the weight gap.* Let $I\subseteq(R^1j_*F_1)_{\bar s}$ be the
image of $\delta_{\bar s}$. It is $F_s$-stable, a quotient of
$(j_*F_2)_{\bar s}$ and a subspace of $(R^1j_*F_1)_{\bar s}$. By
[lem-a1-spectrum-exact-sequence], applied to the two short exact
sequences of Frobenius modules exhibiting $I$ as a quotient and as a
subobject, every eigenvalue $\lambda$ of $F_s$ on $I$ satisfies both
$|\iota(\lambda)|^2\le q_s^{w}$ (Step 3) and
$|\iota(\lambda)|^2\ge q_s^{w+2}$ (Step 4). Since $q_s>1$ these are
incompatible, so $I$ has no eigenvalue; being a finite-dimensional
space over the algebraically closed field $\Qlb$, it is zero. Thus
$\delta_{\bar s}=0$ for every boundary point, $\delta=0$ by Step 2,
and the sequence is exact by Step 1.

attrs.title: Exactness at a fixed pure weight

objects.body:
Let $f$ be an endomorphism of a finite-dimensional
$k$-space $V$ preserving a filtration with graded
pieces $\mathrm{gr}_j$. Then

$$
\det(1-Tf\mid V)=\prod_j\det\bigl(1-Tf\mid\mathrm{gr}_j\bigr).
$$

In particular the eigenvalues of $f$ on any subquotient occur among those
on $V$, with multiplicity; so a scalar acting on a nonzero invariant
subquotient is an eigenvalue on the ambient space.
lem:filtration-constituent;lem:scalar-subquotient-eigenvalue

## Proof

It is enough to treat one invariant subspace and iterate along the
filtration. For $S\subseteq V$ with $f(S)\subseteq S$, choose a basis of
$S$ and extend it to $V$; over the polynomial ring $k[T]$ the matrix of
$1-Tf$ is then block upper triangular, with diagonal blocks those of
$1-Tf$ on $S$ and on $V/S$, so its determinant is the product of the two
block determinants. Induction on the length of the filtration gives the
displayed formula. A subquotient $S/U$ sits in the flag
$0\subseteq U\subseteq S\subseteq V$, so $\det(1-Tf\mid S/U)$ divides
$\det(1-Tf\mid V)$, which is the statement about eigenvalues with
multiplicity. If $f$ acts on $S/U\ne0$ by the scalar $c$, apply the same
factorization to $B=f-c$: the middle factor is the determinant of the zero
map on a space of positive dimension, hence zero, so
$\det(f-c\operatorname{id}_V)=0$ and $c$ is an eigenvalue on $V$.
The determinant factorization along an invariant subspace is Mathlib's
`LinearMap.det_eq_det_mul_det`, in matrix form
`Matrix.charpoly_fromBlocks_zero`$_{12}$; what is not available
is the statement above, Mathlib having only the direct-sum case
`LinearMap.charpoly_prodMap`.

If $f$ has eigenvalue multiset
$\operatorname{eig}(f)=\{\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_r\}$ and $g$ has
$\{\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_t\}$, both with multiplicity, then

$$
\operatorname{eig}(f\otimes g)=\{\alpha_i\beta_j\},\quad
\operatorname{eig}\bigl(\textstyle\bigwedge^sf\bigr)
=\{\alpha_{i_1}\cdots\alpha_{i_s}:i_1<\cdots<i_s\},\quad
\operatorname{eig}(f^\vee)=\{\alpha_i^{-1}\}
$$

(the last for invertible $f$); in particular $\alpha^n$ is an eigenvalue of
$f^{\otimes n}$. Concretely, in an exterior basis a diagonal map with
entries $c_1,\ldots,c_r$ has entries $c_{i_1}\cdots c_{i_s}$ with
$i_1<\cdots<i_s$. Applied to $\rho_V(w)$ and $\rho_W(w)$, these compute the spectra of the
tensor, exterior-power and determinant representations of [d-weights].
lem:exterior-basis

## Proof

Use [p-linear-triangular] to pick bases in which $f$ and $g$ are
upper triangular, with diagonals $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_r$ and
$\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_t$. In the tensor basis $e_i\otimes h_u$, ordered
lexicographically, $f\otimes g$ is again upper triangular: each
$fe_i\otimes gh_u$ is $\alpha_i\beta_u\,e_i\otimes h_u$ plus terms
involving strictly earlier basis vectors. Its diagonal is therefore
$\{\alpha_i\beta_u\}$, and taking $g=f$ repeatedly gives $\alpha^n$ among
the eigenvalues of $f^{\otimes n}$. For $\bigwedge^s$, use the exterior
basis $e_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge e_{i_s}$ with $i_1<\cdots<i_s$, ordered
so that the flag of $f$ induces one on $\bigwedge^sV$; expanding
$fe_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge fe_{i_s}$ and collecting increasing-index
terms, with the sign bookkeeping of the alternating map, gives
$\alpha_{i_1}\cdots\alpha_{i_s}$ on the diagonal and smaller index sets
off it. In particular a diagonal $f$ with entries $c_1,\ldots,c_r$ has
exterior entries $c_{i_1}\cdots c_{i_s}$, which is the concrete form used
below. For the dual, in dual bases $f^\vee$ has the transpose matrix of
$f^{-1}$, upper triangular for the dual flag with diagonal
$\{\alpha_i^{-1}\}$; invertibility of $f$ makes every $\alpha_i$ nonzero.
The exterior basis and the sign rule are Mathlib's
`exteriorPower.basis_apply` and
`AlternatingMap.map_perm`; the tensor, exterior and dual spectra
themselves are absent there.

Uses: [d-weights], [p-linear-triangular]

A single endomorphism of a finite-dimensional
$k$-space admits a full flag of invariant subspaces,
with one-dimensional graded pieces.

## Proof

Induct on $\dim V$, the zero space carrying the empty flag. Since $k$ is
algebraically closed, the characteristic polynomial of $f$ has a root, so
$f$ has an eigenvector $v$ and the line $L=kv$ is invariant. The induced
endomorphism of $V/L$ is well defined, and by induction it has a full
invariant flag with one-dimensional quotients. Pulling that flag back
along $V\to V/L$ and prepending $L$ gives a full invariant flag of $V$.
In a basis adapted to it, $f$ is upper triangular with the flag's
eigenvalues on the diagonal. Mathlib has the generalized eigenspace
decomposition `Module.End.iSup_maxGenEigenspace_eq_top` over an
algebraically closed field, but no flag statement.

For a semisimple represented degree datum ([d-monodromy]), the
identity components and center satisfy

$$
G^\circ=Z(G^\circ)^\circ H^\circ.
$$

This applies to the Weil representation of a lisse Weil sheaf whose Weil
representation is semisimple.

## Proof

Use the defining representation of [d-monodromy]. By
[lem-ag-closure-semisimple], $V$ is a semisimple $G^\circ$-module:
$V=\bigoplus_iM_i$ with each $M_i$ a simple $G^\circ$-module. Set
$\mathfrak g=\operatorname{Lie}(G^\circ)\subseteq\operatorname{End}(V)$,
$\mathfrak h=\operatorname{Lie}(H^\circ)$ and $T=Z(G^\circ)^\circ$.
Apply [lem-ag-lie-stable-subspace] to the connected group $G^\circ$ and
its inclusion $r:G^\circ\to\operatorname{GL}(V)$, whose differential is
the inclusion $dr:\mathfrak g\subseteq\operatorname{End}(V)$: a subspace
of $V$ is $G^\circ$-stable if and only if it is $\mathfrak g$-stable.
Hence each $M_i$ is $\mathfrak g$-stable, and its $\mathfrak g$-stable
subspaces are exactly its $G^\circ$-stable subspaces, so $M_i$ has no
$\mathfrak g$-stable subspaces other than $0$ and $M_i$. Thus the Lie
representation $\mathfrak g\subseteq\operatorname{End}(V)$ is semisimple,
and it is faithful because it is an inclusion. By
[lem-ag-faithful-semisimple-lie-central-radical],
$\mathfrak g=Z(\mathfrak g)+[\mathfrak g,\mathfrak g]$, and
[lem-ag-closure-commutators] and [lem-ag-lie-centre] give

$$
\mathfrak g=Z(\mathfrak g)+[\mathfrak g,\mathfrak g]
           =Z(\mathfrak g)+\mathfrak h
           =\operatorname{Lie}(T)+\operatorname{Lie}(H^\circ).
$$

Here the middle equality holds because
$[\mathfrak g,\mathfrak g]\subseteq\mathfrak h\subseteq\mathfrak g$.

The group $H^\circ$ is connected and contains $1$, and $H\subseteq G$, so
$H^\circ\subseteq G^\circ$ ([lem-wf-algebraic-component-cosets]); the
central subgroup $T$ of $G^\circ$ commutes with it. The product
$T\times H^\circ$, embedded block-diagonally in
$\operatorname{GL}(V\oplus V)$, is a closed matrix group, and the
multiplication map

$$
\mu:T\times H^\circ\to G^\circ,\qquad(t,h)\mapsto th,
$$

is a morphism of varieties and, since $T$ is central, a group
homomorphism: $tht'h'=tt'hh'$. By [lem-ag-homomorphism-image-closed] its
image $K=TH^\circ$ is a closed subgroup of $G^\circ$. It is connected:
$T$ and $H^\circ$ are connected and contain $1$, so both lie in the
identity component $K^\circ$ ([lem-wf-algebraic-component-cosets]),
and hence $K=TH^\circ\subseteq K^\circ$. Its Lie algebra is a subspace
containing $\operatorname{Lie}(T)$ and $\operatorname{Lie}(H^\circ)$,
hence equals $\mathfrak g$. Thus [lem-wf-same-lie-closed-subgroup]
gives $K=G^\circ$.

Keep the notation of [prop-wf-weil-sheaf-representation-equivalence], and let $U_0\subseteq C_0$ be a
nonempty open subscheme with base change $U$ and geometric fundamental group
$\pi_1(U)$, the kernel of the degree map of $W(U_0)$ by
[lem-wf-weil-group-exact-sequence]. An $\mathcal O_E$-lattice in $V$ means a free
$\mathcal O_E$-submodule of rank $\dim_{E}V$ that spans $V$ over $E$.

Let $(V,\rho)$ be a lisse Weil sheaf on $U_0$, with $\rho$ its Weil
fundamental representation of [def-wf-fundamental-representation]. After replacing $E$ by a
finite extension there is an $\mathcal O_E$-lattice $L\subset V$ with

$$
\rho(\pi_1(U))L=L,\qquad L\otimes_{\mathcal O_E}E=V,
$$

and the image of $\pi_1(U)$ in $\operatorname{Aut}(L/\mathfrak m_E^nL)$ is
finite for every $n$. Such an $L$ is the geometric stalk of a lisse
$\mathcal O_E$-sheaf on $U$.

## Proof

By [prop-wf-weil-sheaf-representation-equivalence] the representation admits a model over a finite
$E/\Ql$, whose restriction to the geometric subgroup is continuous by
[lem-wf-weil-fundamental-representation]; a further
finite extension absorbs that choice. Since $\pi_1(U)$ is profinite, hence
compact, $\rho(\pi_1(U))$ is a compact subgroup of $\GL(V)$. The orbit of an
arbitrary $\mathcal O_E$-lattice under a compact subgroup is bounded, so the
$\mathcal O_E$-span $L$ of that orbit is again a lattice; it is stable by
construction and of full rank, whence $L\otimes_{\mathcal O_E}E=V$. Each
$L/\mathfrak m_E^nL$ is a finite set, so the image of $\pi_1(U)$ in its
automorphisms is finite, and these reductions form the compatible system of
finite locally constant sheaves whose limit is the lisse $\mathcal O_E$-sheaf
on $U$ with stalk $L$.

Uses: [def-wf-fundamental-representation], [lem-wf-weil-fundamental-representation], [lem-wf-weil-group-exact-sequence], [prop-wf-weil-sheaf-representation-equivalence]

Keep the notation of [prop-wf-weil-sheaf-representation-equivalence], so
that $(V,\rho)$ is the Weil fundamental representation of
[def-wf-fundamental-representation], and let $x$ be a closed point of
$C_0$ of degree $e_x$, with local Frobenius $F_x$ of
[def-weil-local-frobenius-trace] acting on the stalk
$\mathcal F_{\bar x}$; it acts through the conjugacy class of
geometric Frobenius elements at $x$ (images of the geometric Frobenius of
$k(x)$ under a decomposition-group map $\pi_1(x)\to\pi_1(C_0)$), of degree $e_x$, in the Weil group $W(C_0)$ of [def-wf-weil-group],
the geometric Frobenius over $k(x)$ having degree $e_x$ by
[lem-wf-weil-group-constant-extension]. (Changing the decomposition-group
map conjugates $F_x$ by some $g\in\pi_1(C_0)$, and this is a conjugation
inside $W(C_0)$: as $\widehat{\mathbf Z}=\mathbf Z+e_x\widehat{\mathbf Z}$,
one can write $g=wF_x^t$ with $w\in W(C_0)$ and $t\in\widehat{\mathbf Z}$,
where $F_x^t$ is the image of the $t$-th power of the geometric Frobenius
in the procyclic group $\pi_1(x)$, which commutes with $F_x$; so
$gF_xg^{-1}=wF_xw^{-1}$.) Use the tensor equivalence
[prop-wf-weil-sheaf-representation-equivalence] for the operations of
[def-real-weil-representation-operations] (direct sum, tensor product, dual,
exterior powers, determinant), and
write $P_x(\mathcal F,T)=\det(1-TF_x\mid\mathcal F_{\bar x})$ for the local
characteristic factor of [def-wf-iota-real]. Then

$$
P_x(\mathcal F,T)=\det\bigl(1-T\,\rho(F_x)\mid V\bigr)
\qquad\text{for every closed }x .
$$

## Proof

Granted [prop-wf-weil-sheaf-representation-equivalence], the operations of
[def-real-weil-representation-operations] on
lisse Weil sheaves are *defined* by transport along the equivalence, so
only the local polynomial needs an argument. Iterating the Frobenius
structure map $e_x$ times on the stalk at $\bar x$, as in
[def-weil-local-frobenius-trace], realizes $F_x$ as $\rho$ of
any member of the degree-$e_x$ class supplied by $x$. A characteristic
polynomial is invariant under conjugation, so $\det(1-T\rho(F_x)\mid V)$ is
independent of the member chosen and agrees with the stalkwise $P_x$ of [def-wf-iota-real].

Uses: [def-real-weil-representation-operations], [def-weil-local-frobenius-trace], [def-wf-fundamental-representation], [def-wf-iota-real], [def-wf-weil-group], [lem-wf-weil-group-constant-extension], [prop-wf-weil-sheaf-representation-equivalence]

Keep the notation of [prop-wf-weil-sheaf-representation-equivalence]. Let $U_0\subseteq C_0$ be a
nonempty open subscheme, $U=U_0\times_{\Fq}k$ its base change and $\pi_1(U)$
its geometric fundamental group; restriction gives the Weil group $W(U_0)$
of [def-wf-weil-group]
with geometric subgroup $\pi_1(U)$. For a subgroup $I$ write
$V^{I}=\{v\in V:gv=v\text{ for all }g\in I\}$ for the invariants of
[def-real-weil-representation-operations], and let
$H^0$ denote ordinary etale global
sections. Then

$$
H^0\bigl(U,\mathcal F|_{U}\bigr)=V^{\pi_1(U)},
$$

compatibly with the residual action of $F=\rho(\gamma)$ on both sides, where
$\rho$ is the Weil fundamental representation of
[def-wf-fundamental-representation].

## Proof

Apply [prop-wf-weil-sheaf-representation-equivalence] on the connected $U$. A global section of
$\mathcal F|_{U}$ is a morphism from the constant rank-one sheaf, hence under
the equivalence a map of $\pi_1(U)$-representations from the trivial line to
$V$. Such a map is determined by the image of $1$, which must be fixed by
every element; conversely every fixed vector defines one. This gives
$H^0(U,\mathcal F|_{U})=V^{\pi_1(U)}$. The subgroup $\pi_1(U)$ is normal in
$W(U_0)$, being the kernel of the degree map by
[lem-wf-weil-group-exact-sequence], so the degree-one lift normalizes its
action and therefore preserves
the invariants; the identification is equivariant for the residual $F$.

Uses: [def-real-weil-representation-operations], [def-wf-fundamental-representation], [def-wf-weil-group], [lem-wf-weil-group-exact-sequence], [prop-wf-weil-sheaf-representation-equivalence]

A morphism of schemes $f:X\to S$ is *affine* if for every affine
open $V\subset S$ the preimage $f^{-1}(V)$ is affine, in the sense of
the ambient-foundations chapter; any morphism
between affine schemes is affine, and a closed immersion is affine.
(*Stacks Project, Morphisms of Schemes, Section 29.11, Tag
[01S8](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/01S8).*)

Let $X$ be a scheme and $\mathcal F$ an $\mathcal O_X$-module.

1. $\mathcal F$ is *quasi-coherent* if every point of $X$ has an
affine neighbourhood $\operatorname{Spec}A=U$ with
$\mathcal F|_U=\widetilde M$ for some $A$-module $M$.
1. $\mathcal F$ is *of finite type* if every point has a
neighbourhood $U$ with a surjection
$\mathcal O_U^{\oplus n}\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal F|_U$.
1. $\mathcal F$ is *coherent* if it is of finite type and for
every open $U$ and every map
$\mathcal O_U^{\oplus n}\to\mathcal F|_U$ the kernel is of finite
type.

(*Stacks Project, Cohomology of Sheaves, Chapter 20, Tag
[01DW](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/01DW).*)

Let $X$ be a scheme. The cohomology functors $\mathrm H^p(X,-)$ are
the right derived functors of the global sections functor $\Gamma(X,-)$
on $\mathcal O_X$-modules; a short exact sequence of $\mathcal O_X$-modules gives a long exact cohomology sequence. For a morphism
$f:X\to S$, the higher direct images $R^pf_*\mathcal F$ are the right
derived functors of $f_*$.
(*Stacks Project, Cohomology of Sheaves, Section 20.11, Tag
[01EO](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/01EO), and Section
20.13, Tag
[01EY](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/01EY).*)

attrs.title: Sheaf cohomology and higher direct images

objects.body:
A scheme $X$ is *locally Noetherian* if it admits an affine open
covering $X=\bigcup_iU_i$ with $\mathcal O_X(U_i)$ Noetherian for all
$i$. Open subschemes of locally Noetherian schemes are locally
Noetherian. A locally Noetherian morphism situation is one where the
target is locally Noetherian.
(*Stacks Project, Morphisms of Schemes, Lemma 29.15.6, Tag
[01T6](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/01T6); the open
subscheme assertion follows from the definition of a locally Noetherian
scheme together with the fact that an immersion is locally of finite
type, Morphisms of Schemes, Lemma 29.15.5, Tag
[01T5](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/01T5).*)

Let $f:X\to S$ be a morphism of schemes.

1. $f$ is *quasi-finite at a point $x\in X$* if there exist an
affine neighbourhood $\operatorname{Spec}A=U\subset X$ of $x$ and
an affine open $\operatorname{Spec}R=V\subset S$ with
$f(U)\subset V$ such that the ring map $R\to A$ is of finite type
and quasi-finite at the prime of $A$ corresponding to $x$.
1. $f$ is *locally quasi-finite* if it is quasi-finite at every
point of $X$.
1. $f$ is *quasi-finite* if it is of finite type and every point
of $X$ is an isolated point of its fibre.

This is Stacks Project, Morphisms of Schemes, Definition 29.21.1, Tag
[01TD](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/01TD). We say that
$f$ *has finite fibres* if for every $s\in S$ the set
$f^{-1}(\{s\})$ is finite; the *fibre* of $f$ at $s$ is the scheme
$X_s=X\times_S\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(s)$.

A morphism of schemes $f:X\to S$ is
affine if and only if for every
affine open $V\subset S$ the preimage $f^{-1}(V)$ is affine, if and
only if there exists an affine open covering $S=\bigcup_jV_j$ such that
each $f^{-1}(V_j)$ is affine.
(*Stacks Project, Morphisms of Schemes, Lemma 29.11.3, Tag
[01S8](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/01S8).*)

## Proof

This is the recorded classical input named in the statement, Stacks Project, Morphisms of Schemes, Lemma 29.11.3 ([Tag 01S8](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/01S8)): affineness of a morphism is local on the target in the stated sense. No separate proof is given.

attrs.title: Affineness is local on the target

objects.body:
Let $S$ be a locally Noetherian scheme and
let $\operatorname{Spec}A\subset S$ be an affine open subscheme. Then
the ring $A$ is Noetherian.

## Proof

By [pqf-def-locnoeth] the scheme $S$ is covered by affine opens
whose coordinate rings are Noetherian. Since
$\operatorname{Spec}A$ is affine, hence quasi-compact, the principal
opens of $\operatorname{Spec}A$ that are contained in one of these
affine opens form a basis of $\operatorname{Spec}A$: the principal
opens inside a given open form a basis of that open. Choose finitely
many of them, say $D(f_1),\dots,D(f_k)$ with $f_l\in A$, covering
$\operatorname{Spec}A$, and for each $l$ an affine open
$\operatorname{Spec}R_l\subset S$ with $R_l$ Noetherian and
$D(f_l)\subset\operatorname{Spec}R_l$.

Each $D(f_l)$ is an affine open subscheme of the affine Noetherian
scheme $\operatorname{Spec}R_l$, so it is a finite union
$D(h_1)\cup\dots\cup D(h_t)$ of principal opens of
$\operatorname{Spec}R_l$, its coordinate ring being quasi-compact. By
the sheaf axiom on the affine scheme $\operatorname{Spec}R_l$, its
coordinate ring is the equalizer

$$
A[1/f_l]=\mathcal O(D(f_l))\longrightarrow
\prod_{s=1}^t(R_l)_{h_s}\longrightarrow
\prod_{s,s'=1}^t(R_l)_{h_sh_{s'}},
$$

the two arrows being the two restrictions. Hence $A[1/f_l]$ is a
submodule of the finitely generated $R_l$-module
$\prod_s(R_l)_{h_s}$, each $(R_l)_{h_s}$ being generated by
$1/h_s$ over the Noetherian ring $R_l$; a submodule of a finitely
generated module over a Noetherian ring is finitely generated, so
$A[1/f_l]$ is a finitely generated $R_l$-module and therefore a
Noetherian ring, every ideal of it being a submodule.

It remains to descend Noetherianness along the covering. Let
$I\subset A$ be an ideal. For each $l$ the ideal $IA[1/f_l]$ of
the Noetherian ring $A[1/f_l]$ is generated by the images of finitely
many elements $g_{l,1},\dots,g_{l,n_l}\in I$, so that
$f_l^{N_l}I\subset(g_{l,1},\dots,g_{l,n_l})$ in $A$ for some
$N_l$. Let $J\subset A$ be the ideal generated by all the
$g_{l,s}$ and let $N\ge N_1,\dots,N_k$: then
$f_l^NI\subset J$ for every $l$, and since the $f_l$ generate the
unit ideal, so do the $f_l^N$, whence $I\subset J$; the reverse
inclusion holds by construction, so $I=J$ is finitely generated.
Every ideal of $A$ is therefore finitely generated and $A$ is
Noetherian.

attrs.title: Affine opens of a locally Noetherian scheme

objects.body:
Let $X$ be a scheme and $\mathcal F$ a quasi-coherent
$\mathcal O_X$-module. For any affine open $U\subset X$ we have
$\mathrm H^p(U,\mathcal F)=0$ for all $p>0$.
(*Stacks Project, Cohomology of Schemes, Lemma 30.2.2, Tag
[01XB](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/01XB).*)

## Proof

This is the recorded classical input named in the statement, Stacks Project, Cohomology of Schemes, Lemma 30.2.2 ([Tag 01XB](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/01XB)): a quasi-coherent module on an affine scheme has no higher cohomology. No separate proof is given.

attrs.title: Vanishing of higher cohomology on affines

objects.body:
Let $A\to B$ be a ring homomorphism, let $M$ be a $B$-module,
and let $a\in A$. For the
associated quasi-coherent sheaf
$\widetilde M$ on $\operatorname{Spec}B$, restriction induces

$$
\Gamma\bigl(\operatorname{Spec}(B\otimes_AA_a),\widetilde M\bigr)
\cong M\otimes_AA_a.
$$

## Proof

Write $b$ for the image of $a$ in $B$. The inverse image of
$D(a)$ is $D(b)=\operatorname{Spec}B_b$, and the associated sheaf
of [pqf-def-coherent] has sections $M_b$ on this principal open.
The universal properties of localization give
$B\otimes_AA_a=B_b$ and $M\otimes_AA_a=M_b$, compatibly with
restriction. These identifications give the formula.

attrs.title: Principal localization of an associated module sheaf

objects.body:
Let $X$ be a
locally Noetherian scheme and
$\mathcal F$ an $\mathcal O_X$-module. Then $\mathcal F$ is coherent
if and only if it is quasi-coherent of finite type.
(*Stacks Project, Cohomology of Schemes, Lemma 30.9.1, Tag
[01XZ](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/01XZ).*)

## Proof

*($\Leftarrow$).* Let $\mathcal F$ be quasi-coherent and of
finite type on the locally Noetherian $X$ ([pqf-def-locnoeth]) and
let $\varphi:\mathcal O_U^{\oplus n}\to\mathcal F|_U$
be a map over an open $U$. Kernels of maps of quasi-coherent sheaves
are quasi-coherent (checked on affine open subschemes, where they
correspond to kernels of maps of modules), so $\ker\varphi$ is
quasi-coherent; being a quasi-coherent submodule of a finite-rank
free module over each affine Noetherian $\operatorname{Spec}A\subset U$
it is the sheaf $\widetilde K$ of a submodule $K\subset A^n$, and $K$
is finitely generated because $A$ and hence $A^n$ are Noetherian.
Thus $\ker\varphi$ is of finite type, which with $\mathcal F$ of
finite type is the definition of coherence in
[pqf-def-coherent].
*($\Rightarrow$).* Let $\mathcal F$ be coherent; it is of
finite type by definition, and it is quasi-coherent: for an affine
open $\operatorname{Spec}A\subset X$ with $A$ Noetherian, the
coherence condition (finite kernels) gives that
$\mathcal F|_{\operatorname{Spec}A}$ is the sheaf associated with
its module of global sections – the classical finite-relation
argument over Noetherian rings: because $\mathcal F$ is of finite
type there is a surjection $A^n\to\Gamma(\operatorname{Spec}A,\mathcal F)$
whose kernel is finitely generated, the kernel being of finite type
by coherence, so a presentation exists; the same argument on
principal open subschemes $D(g)$ and the exactness of
$(-)\otimes_A A_g$ yield $\Gamma(D(g),\mathcal F)=\Gamma(\operatorname{Spec}A,\mathcal F)_g$, i.e. the sheaf $\mathcal F|_{\operatorname{Spec}A}$ is
$\widetilde{\Gamma(\operatorname{Spec}A,\mathcal F)}$ (cf. the
classical equivalent characterization of coherent modules on
Noetherian schemes, Stacks Project, Cohomology of Schemes, Lemma
30.9.1, [Tag 01XZ](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/01XZ)).
Since this holds on every affine open, $\mathcal F$ is
quasi-coherent.

Let $f:X\to Y$ be a proper morphism of schemes and $y\in Y$. Assume
that $Y$ is locally Noetherian and that $f^{-1}(\{y\})$ is finite.
Then for any coherent sheaf $\mathcal F$ on $X$ we have
$(R^pf_*\mathcal F)_y=0$ for all $p>0$.
(*Stacks Project, Cohomology of Schemes, Lemma 30.20.8, Tag
[02OE](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/02OE), whose proof uses
the theorem on formal functions, Theorem 30.20.5, Tag
[02OC](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/02OC).*)

## Proof

The theorem on formal functions (recorded classical input cited in the
statement): with $\widehat{\mathcal O_{Y,y}}$ the completion of the
local ring, with the $n$-th infinitesimal neighbourhoods

$$
X_n:=X\times_Y\operatorname{Spec}\bigl(\mathcal O_{Y,y}/\mathfrak m_y^n\bigr)
$$

of the fibre $X_y:=f^{-1}(\{y\})$, and with $\widehat X$ the
*formal completion* of $X$ along the closed fibre $X_y$ (the
formal scheme $X^{\wedge}_{X_y}$, with $\mathrm H^p(-,-)$ the
cohomology functors of [pqf-def-cohomology]), the canonical
comparisons are

$$
(R^pf_*\mathcal F)_y\otimes_{\mathcal O_{Y,y}}\widehat{\mathcal
O_{Y,y}}\ \cong\ \mathrm H^p\bigl(\widehat X,\widehat{\mathcal F}\bigr)
\ \cong\ \varprojlim_n\mathrm H^p(X_n,\mathcal F_n)\qquad(p\ge0),
$$

$\widehat{\mathcal F}$ being the pullback of $\mathcal F$ to the
formal completion and $\mathcal F_n$ its restriction to the
thickenings, the second comparison being the defining property of the
cohomology of formal coherent sheaves. (The *scheme*
$X\times_Y\operatorname{Spec}\widehat{\mathcal O_{Y,y}}$, whose
underlying topological space can also contain points over the generic
points of the completed local base, is not a formal
completion, and its cohomology is not the limit of the cohomologies
of the $X_n$; it is $\widehat X$ that the theorem on formal
functions uses.) The
underlying topological space of the formal completion $\widehat X$,
equivalently of each $X_n$, is that of the fibre $X_y$:
$f^{-1}(\{y\})$; it is finite, zero-dimensional, and hence
discrete. Each $X_n$ is therefore a finite scheme (a disjoint union of
spectra of local Artinian rings), and a coherent sheaf on a finite
discrete space has vanishing cohomology in positive degrees (on a
discrete space every sheaf is flasque, and flasque sheaves are acyclic
for $\Gamma$, as in the Leray proof of [pqf-lem-leray]);
hence $\mathrm H^p(X_n,\mathcal F_n)=0$ for every $p>0$ and every
$n$, and the displayed limit gives
$\mathrm H^p(\widehat X,\widehat{\mathcal F})=0$ for every $p>0$;
hence
$(R^pf_*\mathcal F)_y\otimes_{\mathcal O_{Y,y}}\widehat{\mathcal O_{Y,y}}=0$ for $p>0$.
Finally, $(R^pf_*\mathcal F)_y$ is a finitely generated
$\mathcal O_{Y,y}$-module: for a proper morphism with a locally
Noetherian target and a coherent $\mathcal F$ on the source
([pqf-def-locnoeth], [pqf-def-coherent]), the higher direct images
$R^pf_*\mathcal F$ are coherent (classical: the coherence of higher
direct images for proper morphisms, cf. Stacks Cohomology of
Schemes, Proposition 30.19.1, Tag [02O5](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/02O5)), and the stalk of a
coherent sheaf is finitely generated. A finitely generated module
$M$ over the Noetherian local ring $\mathcal O_{Y,y}$ with
$M\otimes_{\mathcal O_{Y,y}}\widehat{\mathcal O_{Y,y}}=0$ is zero:
following Nakayama, the completion of a finitely generated module is
$M\otimes_{\mathcal O_{Y,y}}\widehat{\mathcal O_{Y,y}}$, so the
quotients $M/\mathfrak m_y^nM$ all vanish, and with
$M/\mathfrak m_yM=0$ Nakayama's lemma gives $M=0$. Thus
$(R^pf_*\mathcal F)_y=0$ for all $p>0$.

attrs.title: Formal functions vanishing over finite fibres

objects.body:
Let $S$ be a locally Noetherian scheme and
let $p:T\to S$ be a
finite morphism. Then $p$
is of finite presentation.

## Proof

Let $\operatorname{Spec}A\subset S$ be an affine open; $S$ is
locally Noetherian in the sense of [pqf-def-locnoeth]. By
[pqf-lem-affine-open-locnoeth] the ring $A$ is Noetherian, and by
the definition of finiteness in
[def-weil-pbc-scheme-conventions] the preimage
$p^{-1}(\operatorname{Spec}A)=\operatorname{Spec}B$ is affine with
$B$ a finite $A$-module, in particular a finitely generated
$A$-algebra. A finitely generated module over a Noetherian ring is
finitely presented: choosing a surjection $A^n\to B$, its kernel is a
submodule of the Noetherian module $A^n$, hence is finitely generated,
and a finitely generated module with a finite free presentation of
finite rank is finitely presented. So $B$ is a finitely presented
$A$-algebra. Hence every affine open of $S$ is covered by the
single affine open $p^{-1}(\operatorname{Spec}A)$ of $T$ whose
coordinate ring is finitely presented over the coordinate ring of that
affine open of $S$, and $p$ is quasi-compact because it is affine;
by [def-weil-pbc-scheme-conventions] the morphism $p$ is of
finite presentation.

attrs.title: Finite over a locally Noetherian base is finitely presented

objects.body:
A finite morphism of
schemes is integral.
(*Stacks Project, Morphisms of Schemes, Lemma 29.45.4, Tag
[01WJ](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/01WJ).*)

## Proof

We work ring-locally. Recall the classical determinant trick:
if $A\to B$ is a finite ring homomorphism, i.e. $B$ is a finite
$A$-module, then every $b\in B$ is integral over $A$: choosing
$b_1,\dots,b_n$ generating $B$ as an $A$-module and writing
$b\,b_j=\sum_i c_{ij}\,b_i$ with $c_{ij}\in A$, the vector
$(b_1,\dots,b_n)$ is annihilated by the matrix $b\cdot\mathrm{id}-C$,
$C=(c_{ij})$, so the adjugate argument gives a monic equation
$b^n+a_{n-1}b^{n-1}+\dots+a_0=0$ with $a_k\in A$ (the characteristic
polynomial of the multiplication map $b\cdot$).
Now let $f:X\to S$ be finite: $f$ is affine and $f_*\mathcal O_X$ is
a finite $\mathcal O_S$-algebra, by
[def-weil-pbc-scheme-conventions]; for $V=\operatorname{Spec}A$
affine open in $S$ and $f^{-1}(V)=\operatorname{Spec}B$ the ring map
$A\to B$ is finite, so every element of $B$ is integral over $A$ by
the determinant trick, which is exactly the assertion that
$f_*\mathcal O_X$ is integral over $\mathcal O_S$; with affineness
this is $f$ integral.

A finite morphism of
schemes is quasi-finite.

## Proof

A finite morphism is affine and $f_*\mathcal O_X$ is a finite
$\mathcal O_S$-algebra, so $f$ is of finite type and quasi-compact, by
[def-weil-pbc-scheme-conventions]. Its fibres are finite: the
fibre at $s$ is $\operatorname{Spec}$ of a finite
$\kappa(s)$-algebra, which is a finite-dimensional $\kappa(s)$-vector
space, hence Artinian and therefore has finitely many prime ideals
(classical algebra). A morphism of finite type with finite fibres is
quasi-finite, by [pqf-lem-qf-finitefibres], if it is locally of
finite type; and it is, because finite type implies locally of finite
type in the sense of [pqf-def-quasifinite].

Let $A\to B$ be integral, let
$\mathfrak p\subseteq\mathfrak p'$ be primes of $A$, and let
$\mathfrak q\subset B$ lie over $\mathfrak p$. There is a prime
$\mathfrak q'\supseteq\mathfrak q$ lying over $\mathfrak p'$.

## Proof

The induced map $A/\mathfrak p\hookrightarrow B/\mathfrak q$ is injective
and integral. Localize it at the complement of
$\mathfrak p'/\mathfrak p$. Apply lying over
([pqf-lem-lying-over]) to the maximal ideal of the localized
source. Pulling the resulting prime first back to $B/\mathfrak q$ and
then to $B$ gives $\mathfrak q'$; localization shows that its
contraction is exactly $\mathfrak p'$, and the quotient construction
gives $\mathfrak q\subseteq\mathfrak q'$.

attrs.title: Going up for an integral extension

objects.body:
Let $p:X\to S$ be
proper, let $Y\to S$ be
separated and of finite
type, and let $f:X\to Y$ be an $S$-morphism. Then the
scheme-theoretic image $Z=f(X)$ of $f$ (the closed subscheme of $Y$
whose quasi-coherent ideal is the kernel of
$\mathcal O_Y\to f_*\mathcal O_X$; it is closed in $Y$ because $p$ is
a closed map, by [lem-weil-pbc-proper-closed-image] of the ambient-foundations chapter) is proper over $S$, the induced morphism $X\to Z$ is proper and
surjective, and the composite $X\to Z\to S$ is $p$.

## Proof

The morphism $X\to Z$ is an $S$-morphism with $X$ proper over $S$ and
$Z$ separated over $S$, hence proper by
[lem-weil-pbc-proper-to-separated] of the ambient-foundations chapter; in particular
it is surjective onto $Z=f(X)$. It remains to see that $Z\to S$ is
proper. It is separated and of finite type: $Z\hookrightarrow Y$ is a
closed immersion (hence separated and of finite type) and $Y\to S$ is
separated of finite type, so the composite $Z\to S$ is separated and
of finite type by
[def-weil-pbc-scheme-conventions]. It is universally closed:
after any base change $T\to S$, write $q_T:X_T\to Z_T$ and
$g_T:Z_T\to T$. Both $q_T$ and $g_Tq_T$ are proper by
[lem-weil-pbc-proper-base-change]. The morphism $q_T$ is
surjective: its geometric
fibres are field extensions of the nonempty fibres of the surjection
$X\to Z$, hence nonempty, so
[lem-weil-pbc-surjective-nonempty-fibres] applies.
The composite $g_Tq_T:X_T\to T$ is proper by
[lem-weil-pbc-proper-base-change], and therefore closed by
[pqf-lem-proper-closed-map]. For any closed subset $C\subset Z_T$,
the subset $q_T^{-1}(C)\subset X_T$ is closed and surjectivity gives

$$
g_T(C)=(g_Tq_T)\bigl(q_T^{-1}(C)\bigr).
$$

The right side is closed in $T$. Thus every $g_T$ is closed,
and $Z\to S$ is separated, of
finite type and universally closed, i.e. proper by
[def-weil-pbc-scheme-conventions].

attrs.title: Image of a proper morphism into a separated finite-type target

objects.body:
For an integral map $A\to B$, comparable primes of $B$ with the same
contraction are equal.

## Proof

Suppose $\mathfrak q\subseteq\mathfrak q'$ have common contraction
$\mathfrak p$. Quotient by $\mathfrak q$ and localize at the nonzero
elements of $A/\mathfrak p$. The resulting domain is integral over the
field $K=\operatorname{Frac}(A/\mathfrak p)$, hence is itself a field:
for a nonzero integral element $x$, an integral equation of least degree
has nonzero constant term and expresses $x^{-1}$ as a polynomial in
$x$. The localization of $\mathfrak q'/\mathfrak q$ is therefore
zero. If $b\in\mathfrak q'$, some $s\in A\setminus\mathfrak p$ has
$sb\in\mathfrak q$. Since $s\notin\mathfrak q$ and $\mathfrak q$ is
prime, $b\in\mathfrak q$. Thus $\mathfrak q'=\mathfrak q$.

An integral morphism of schemes which is locally of finite type is
finite.
(*Stacks Project, Morphisms of Schemes, Lemma 29.45.4, Tag
[01WJ](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/01WJ).*)

## Proof

We work ring-locally. If
$A\to B$ is an integral ring map and $B$ is a finite type
$A$-algebra, then $B$ is a finite $A$-module: writing
$B=A[b_1,\dots,b_m]$, the case $m=1$ is the reduction of the monic
equation of $b_1$ (every higher power reduces to a combination of
$1,b_1,\dots,b_1^{n-1}$), and for $m>1$ we iterate using that an
integral element over $A$ remains integral over a larger
$A$-algebra, and that a finite module over a finite module is finite.
Now let $f:X\to S$ be integral and locally of
finite type; $f$ is affine, so for $V=\operatorname{Spec}A$ affine
open of $S$ and $f^{-1}(V)=\operatorname{Spec}B$, the map $A\to B$ is
integral, and by local finite type of $f$, after shrinking $V$ and
$f^{-1}(V)$ if necessary, $B$ is a finite type $A$-algebra (a
morphism between affines is locally of finite type exactly when the
ring map is such, and on a finite affine cover the source rings are
finite type over the target rings by
[def-weil-pbc-scheme-conventions]); by the classical
fact above $B$ is a finite $A$-module, so $f_*\mathcal O_X$ is a
finite $\mathcal O_S$-module locally, and $f$ is finite.

attrs.title: An integral morphism of locally finite type is finite

objects.body:
A morphism of schemes $f:X\to S$ is
integral if and only if it
is affine and universally closed.
(*Stacks Project, Morphisms of Schemes, Lemma 29.45.7, Tag
[01WM](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/01WM).*)

## Proof

*($\Rightarrow$).* An integral morphism is affine by
[def-weil-pbc-scheme-conventions]. For the universal closedness
it is enough, by the definition of universally closed in
[def-weil-pbc-scheme-conventions], to show that integral
morphisms are closed and that being integral is stable under base
change. The stability: for an integral ring map $A\to B$ and any
$A$-algebra $C$, the map $C\to C\otimes_AB$ is integral, because
$C\otimes_AB$ is generated over $C$ by the elements $1\otimes b$
($b\in B$), each integral over $C$ (an integral equation of $b$ over
$A$ tensors with $C$), and an algebra generated by elements integral
over the base is integral (transitivity for adjoint algebras). The
closedness: let $f=\operatorname{Spec}(A\to B)$ be integral, let
$J\subseteq B$ be an ideal and put $I=f^{-1}(J)=J\cap A$. The image
$f(V(J))$ lies in $V(J\cap A)$ because $q\cap A\supseteq J\cap A$ for
$q\supseteq J$. Conversely let
$\mathfrak p\supseteq(J\cap A)$ be a prime; the induced map
$A/(J\cap A)\hookrightarrow B/J$ is injective and integral (quotients
of integral ring maps are integral), so lying over
([pqf-lem-lying-over]) gives a prime $\bar{\mathfrak q}\subseteq B/J$ contracting to $\mathfrak p/(J\cap A)$; with
$\mathfrak q$ the preimage of $\bar{\mathfrak q}$ in $B$ one has
$\mathfrak q\supseteq J$ and, since
$\bar{\mathfrak q}\cap\bigl(A/(J\cap A)\bigr) =\bigl(\mathfrak q\cap A\bigr)/(J\cap A)=\mathfrak p/(J\cap A)$, the
equality $\mathfrak q\cap A=\mathfrak p$. Hence
$f(V(J))=V(J\cap A)$, a closed subset, and $f$ is a closed map.
Combining the two facts, every base change of $f$ is integral, hence
closed: $f$ is universally closed.
*($\Leftarrow$).* The converse is the reference argument of the
statement (loc. cit.), kept as a recorded classical input
(OBL-PQF-02, converse direction): it requires the valuation-style
argument of the reference and is not decomposed in this chapter.

Let $f:X\to Y$ be a morphism of schemes and $\mathcal F$ a
quasi-coherent $\mathcal O_X$-module. There is a spectral sequence

$$
E_2^{p,q}=\mathrm H^p\bigl(Y,R^qf_*\mathcal F\bigr)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \mathrm H^{p+q}(X,\mathcal F).
$$

(*Stacks Project, Cohomology of Sheaves, Lemma 20.13.4, Tag
[01F2](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/01F2).*)

## Proof

Apply the Grothendieck spectral sequence
[thm-sp-grothendieck] of the spectral-sequence chapter to the composable pair of
left exact functors $F=f_*:\mathcal O_X$-mod$\to\mathcal O_Y$-mod
(which is left exact: the functor of sections over the open
subschemes, exactness of $f_*$ on the left being the sheaf property)
and $G=\Gamma(Y,-):\mathcal O_Y$-mod$\to\mathbf{Ab}$.
The acyclicity condition holds: every injective
$\mathcal O_X$-module $\mathcal I$ is flasque (classical: for
$j:U\hookrightarrow X$ open, injectivity applied to the canonical
map $j_{!}\mathcal I|_U\to\mathcal I$ extends sections of
$\mathcal I$ over $U$ to all of $X$; equivalently, every
$\mathcal O_X$-module is a submodule of an injective module and
injective modules are the extension-closed objects), and a flasque
$\mathcal O_X$-module $\mathcal J$ is $f_*$-acyclic: its stalk
$(R^qf_*\mathcal J)_y=\varinjlim_{y\in V}\mathrm H^q(f^{-1}(V),\mathcal J)$ vanishes for $q>0$ since flasque
$\mathcal O_X$-modules are acyclic for $\Gamma$ on every open
subscheme (the standard flasque resolutions). By
[thm-sp-grothendieck] there is a functorial first-quadrant
spectral sequence with

$$
E_2^{p,q}=R^pG\bigl(R^qF(\mathcal F)\bigr)
=\mathrm H^p\bigl(Y,R^qf_*\mathcal F\bigr)
\;\Longrightarrow\;
R^{p+q}(G\circ F)(\mathcal F)=\mathrm H^{p+q}(X,\mathcal F),
$$

$G\circ F=\Gamma(Y,-)\circ f_*=\Gamma(X,-)$ being the global
sections of the source, and $R^qF(\mathcal F)=R^qf_*\mathcal F$,
$R^pG(-)=\mathrm H^p(Y,-)$ as the right derived functors fixed in
[pqf-def-cohomology]. This is the displayed spectral
sequence.

Let $f:X\to Y$ be a morphism of schemes and $\mathcal F$ a
quasi-coherent $\mathcal O_X$-module. The low degree terms of the
spectral sequence of [pqf-lem-leray] give an exact sequence

$$
0\longrightarrow\mathrm H^1(Y,f_*\mathcal F)
\longrightarrow\mathrm H^1(X,\mathcal F)
\longrightarrow\mathrm H^0(Y,R^1f_*\mathcal F)
\longrightarrow\mathrm H^2(Y,f_*\mathcal F).
$$

In particular, if $R^1f_*\mathcal F=0$, then
$\mathrm H^1(X,\mathcal F)\cong\mathrm H^1(Y,f_*\mathcal F)$.

## Proof

The spectral sequence of [pqf-lem-leray] is
$E_2^{p,q}=\mathrm H^p(Y,R^qf_*\mathcal F)$; the terms with $p+q=0,1,2$
are the displayed sequence, exact by the standard edge and connecting
maps of a spectral sequence and by the cohomology long exact
sequences of [pqf-def-cohomology] (the maps
$E_2^{0,1}\to E_2^{2,0}$ being the second differential and its
composites). If $R^1f_*\mathcal F=0$, the middle term vanishes and the
resulting exact sequence gives the stated isomorphism.

attrs.title: Low degree terms of the Leray spectral sequence

objects.body:
Let $S$ be a scheme, let $X=\varprojlim_{i\in I}X_i$ be a filtered
limit of $S$-schemes with affine transition morphisms and
quasi-compact $X_i$, and let $Y\to X$ be a morphism of $S$-schemes
which is a closed immersion, with $Y$ locally of finite type over
$S$. Then the composite $Y\to X\to X_i$ is a closed immersion for
all sufficiently large $i$.
(*Stacks Project, Limits of Schemes, Lemma 32.4.16 (1)*,
[Tag 081B](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/081B).)

## Proof

Choose an index $0\in I$ and a finite affine open covering
$X_0=U_{0,1}\cup\dots\cup U_{0,m}$ such that each $U_{0,j}$ maps
into an affine open $W_j\subset S$: cover each point of the
quasi-compact $X_0$ by an affine open lying over an affine open of
$S$, possible because affine opens form a basis of both spaces, and
pass to a finite subcovering. For $i\ge0$ let $U_{i,j}\subset X_i$
be the preimage of $U_{0,j}$, and let $U_j\subset X$ and
$V_j\subset Y$ be the corresponding preimages; the opens $U_{i,j}$,
$j=1,\dots,m$, cover $X_i$. Each $U_{i,j}$ is affine, being the
base change $U_{0,j}\times_{X_0}X_i$ of the affine $U_{0,j}$ along
the affine morphism $X_i\to X_0$, and $U_j=\varprojlim_iU_{i,j}$ is
affine, the filtered limit of affine schemes with affine transition
morphisms being the spectrum of the filtered colimit of the coordinate
rings. Write $A_i=\mathcal O(U_{i,j})$, so that
$A=\mathcal O(U_j)=\varinjlim_iA_i$.

Since $Y\to X$ is a closed immersion, $V_j=Y\times_XU_j$ is a closed
subscheme of the affine $U_j$, so $V_j=\operatorname{Spec}B_j$ with
$B_j=A/\mathfrak a_j$. The restriction $V_j\to W_j$ of $Y\to S$ is
locally of finite type because $V_j\subset Y$ is an open subscheme and
$Y\to S$ is locally of finite type, and $V_j$ is affine over the
affine $W_j$; hence $B_j$ is a finitely generated
$\mathcal O(W_j)$-algebra.

We use the following elementary algebra fact. If
$A=\varinjlim_iA_i$ is a filtered colimit of $R$-algebras and
$A\to B$ is a surjection of $R$-algebras onto a finitely generated
$R$-algebra $B$, then $A_i\to B$ is surjective for all sufficiently
large $i$. Indeed, choose generators $b_1,\dots,b_n$ of $B$ over
$R$ and preimages $a_l\in A$ of the $b_l$, choose $i_l$ so that
$a_l$ lies in the image of $A_{i_l}$, and let
$i\ge i_1,\dots,i_n$: the composite $A_i\to A\to B$ is an
$R$-algebra homomorphism whose image contains $R$ and every $b_l$,
hence equals $B$.

Apply this to the surjection $A=\mathcal O(U_j)\to B_j$ over the ring
$\mathcal O(W_j)$: for each $j$ there is an index $i(j)$ such that
$A_i\to B_j$ is surjective for every $i\ge i(j)$, that is,
$V_j\to U_{i,j}$ is a closed immersion for every such $i$. Let $i$
be an index at least $\max_ji(j)$. For every $j$ the morphism
$V_j\to U_{i,j}$ is then a closed immersion, and
$V_j=Y\times_{X_i}U_{i,j}$ because fibre products are compatible with
the projections of the limit, so the morphism $Y\to X_i$ is affine by
[pqf-lem-affine-local-target] applied to the affine open covering
$X_i=\bigcup_jU_{i,j}$, and it is induced over $U_{i,j}$ by the
surjective ring homomorphism $A_i\to B_j$. By the definition of a
closed immersion in [def-weil-pbc-scheme-conventions] the morphism
$Y\to X_i$ is therefore a closed immersion.

attrs.title: Closed immersions spread out from a filtered limit

objects.body:
Let $S=\varprojlim_{i\in I}S_i$ be a filtered limit of
quasi-compact
quasi-separated schemes with affine transition morphisms
$f_{i'i}:S_{i'}\to S_i$, with projections $f_i:S\to S_i$, and let
$V\subset S$ be a quasi-compact open subscheme.

1. There are an index $i$ and a quasi-compact open
$V_i\subset S_i$ with $f_i^{-1}(V_i)=V$.
1. If $V_i\subset S_i$ and $V_{i'}\subset S_{i'}$ are
quasi-compact opens with $f_i^{-1}(V_i)=f_{i'}^{-1}(V_{i'})$,
then $f_{i''i}^{-1}(V_i)=f_{i''i'}^{-1}(V_{i'})$ for some index
$i''\ge i,i'$.
1. In the situation of (1) let $V_j\subset S_j$ be the preimage of
$V_i$ for $j\ge i$. Then the projections exhibit $V$ as the
filtered limit $\varprojlim_{j\ge i}V_j$; each $V_j$ is
quasi-compact, and the transition morphisms $V_{j'}\to V_j$ are
affine.

(*Stacks Project, Limits of Schemes, Lemma 32.4.11*,
[Tag 01Z4](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/01Z4); clause (3)
is the limit description of Limits of Schemes, Lemma 32.2.2,
[Tag 01YX](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/01YX).)

## Proof

*The affine case.* Suppose first that $S_0=\operatorname{Spec}R_0$
is affine for some index $0\in I$. Then $S_i$ is affine for every
$i\ge0$, say $S_i=\operatorname{Spec}R_i$, and
$S=\operatorname{Spec}R$ with $R=\varinjlim_{i\ge0}R_i$: a filtered
limit of affine schemes with affine transition morphisms is the spectrum
of the filtered colimit of the coordinate rings. The principal opens
form a basis, so the quasi-compact open $V$ is a finite union of
principal opens, and we may write
$V=\operatorname{Spec}R\setminus V(g_1,\dots,g_n)$ for finitely many
$g_l\in R$. Each $g_l$ is the image of an element of some $R_{i_l}$;
choose $i\ge i_1,\dots,i_n$ and let $g_{l,i}\in R_i$ be the image of
$g_l$. Then $V_i=\operatorname{Spec}R_i\setminus V(g_{1,i},\dots,g_{n,i})$ is a quasi-compact open of $S_i$ whose
preimage in $S$ is $\operatorname{Spec}R\setminus V(g_1,\dots,g_n)=V$, the preimage of a closed subscheme $V(J)$ being
$V(JS)$. This is (1) in the affine case.

For (2) in the affine case, write in the same way
$V_i=\operatorname{Spec}R_i\setminus V(h_1,\dots,h_m)$ and
$V_{i'}=\operatorname{Spec}R_{i'}\setminus V(g_1,\dots,g_n)$. The
hypothesis says that the closed subsets $V(h_1,\dots,h_m)$ and
$V(g_1,\dots,g_n)$ of $\operatorname{Spec}R$ coincide, that is, that
the ideals generated by the images of the $h$'s and by the images of
the $g$'s have the same radical in $R$. Then $g_l^N=\sum_ja_{lj}h_j$
and $h_j^N=\sum_lb_{jl}g_l$ in $R$ for some $N$ and finitely many
coefficients $a_{lj},b_{jl}\in R$, and these finitely many coefficients
come from one ring $R_{i''}$ with $i''\ge i,i'$. In $R_{i''}$ the
two ideals have the same radical as well, so the corresponding opens of
$S_{i''}$ are equal, which is (2).

*The general case for (1) and (2).* Choose $0\in I$ and a finite
affine open covering $S_0=U_{0,1}\cup\dots\cup U_{0,m}$, possible
because $S_0$ is quasi-compact and affine opens form a basis. For
$i\ge0$ let $U_{j,i}\subset S_i$ be the preimage of $U_{0,j}$ and
let $U_j\subset S$ be its preimage; each $U_{j,i}$ is affine, being
the base change of the affine $U_{0,j}$ along the affine morphism
$S_i\to S_0$, and $U_j=\varprojlim_iU_{j,i}$ is affine for the same
reason as in the affine case. Since $V$ and $U_j$ are quasi-compact
opens of the quasi-separated scheme $S$, the quasi-separatedness being
that of [def-weil-pbc-scheme-conventions], the intersection
$V\cap U_j$ is quasi-compact by [pqf-lem-qs-intersection-qc], so
the affine case of
(1) applies to the system $\{U_{j,i}\}_i$, whose limit is $U_j$:
there are an index $i_j$ and a quasi-compact open
$V_{j,i_j}\subset U_{j,i_j}$ whose preimage in $U_j$ is $V\cap U_j$.
Let $i\ge i_1,\dots,i_m$ and put
$V_i=\bigcup_{j=1}^mf_{ii_j}^{-1}(V_{j,i_j})$, a finite union of
quasi-compact opens of $S_i$, hence a quasi-compact open. Its
preimage in $S$ is $\bigcup_jf_{i_j}^{-1}(V_{j,i_j})=\bigcup_j(V\cap U_j)=V$, which is (1).

For (2) replace $V_i$ and $V_{i'}$ by their preimages in a common
later stage, which does not change the assertion, so that two
quasi-compact opens $W,W'\subset S_i$ with $f_i^{-1}(W)=f_i^{-1}(W')$
are given. For each $j$ the opens $W\cap U_{j,i}$ and
$W'\cap U_{j,i}$ of the affine $U_{j,i}$ are quasi-compact, and their
preimages in the affine $U_j$ coincide; by the affine case of (2)
there is an index $i''_j\ge i$ with $f_{i''_ji}^{-1}(W\cap U_{j,i})=f_{i''_ji}^{-1}(W'\cap U_{j,i})$. For any
$i''\ge i''_1,\dots,i''_m$ the same equality holds after pulling the
opens back to $S_{i''}$, and taking the union over $j$ — the
$U_{j,i}$ cover $S_i$ — gives $f_{i''i}^{-1}(W)=f_{i''i}^{-1}(W')$,
which is (2).

*Clause (3).* Let $V_j\subset S_j$ be the preimage of $V_i$ for
$j\ge i$. These are quasi-compact opens of the $S_j$, by (1)'s
argument applied to the same presentation, and the transition morphisms
$V_{j'}\to V_j$ are the base changes of the affine morphisms
$S_{j'}\to S_j$, hence are affine. Moreover
$V=f_i^{-1}(V_i)=S\times_{S_i}V_i$ and
$V_j=S_j\times_{S_i}V_i$, the preimage of an open subscheme being its
fibre product. Let $T$ be a scheme with a compatible system of
morphisms $T\to V_j$ over the $S_j$. By the universal property of
the limit $S=\varprojlim_jS_j$ these induce a morphism $T\to S$,
whose composite with $f_i$ agrees with the given morphism to
$V_i\subset S_i$; hence $T\to S$ lands in $f_i^{-1}(V_i)=V$, and
the resulting morphism $T\to V$ is the unique one compatible with the
projections $V\to V_j$. Therefore $V$ represents the functor of the
system $\{V_j\}_{j\ge i}$, that is, $V=\varprojlim_{j\ge i}V_j$.
